PCE does not prove gradual passage among them. Theorem A.0.2 has its own reliability branch, while a positive CC label requires Theorem 34's strict-improvement and realization package; no observer-level label activates another automatically.

### P.5.8.4 Perspectival Information and the Observer

The observer hierarchy supplies a family of conditional operational descriptions. The quantities $\sigma_S(E)$ and $\mu_S(E)$ are defined only when the system carries the Effective Operational Property-R, identifiable self-model splitting, and prediction-map certificates of Definitions M.10.1--M.10.3. They therefore remain undefined for a Level-0 or Level-1 label lacking those certificates. An interaction has a Landauer ledger only when it implements the registered reset of Theorem 31.

For a certified Level-2 or Level-3 pattern family, Theorem M.10.3's asymptotic processing bound additionally requires its pattern-specific reduction and implementation certificates. Theorem M.10.7 supplies a conditional mean reset-heat export bound under its complete implementation, entropy and summation hypotheses; a positive total entropy-production bound requires a separate production certificate. Definition B.8 supplies a stress-energy model term only after its coefficients and retained-energy map are registered.

The external-evaluation and screening statements of Theorems M.10.5 and M.10.8 likewise require their explicit model-access, decision, finite-family, and insulation certificates. Neither a bare aggregate-complexity ordering nor faithful replay proves sender-flat processing cost. The perspectival profile $\mathcal P_S(E)$ is therefore a descriptor of a fully specified receiver, pattern, update map, and implementation branch.

### <a id="p585-conditional-same-basis-wigner-friend-record-consistency"></a>P.5.8.5 Conditional Same-Basis Wigner--Friend Record Consistency

The perspectival formalism supplies a conditional same-basis record-reading consistency theorem for Wigner's-friend-type protocols (Theorem M.6.1). Suppose that $F$ already carries a registered outcome $k$ on an independently supplied instrument, Born-selector, and actualization branch. If $W$ later satisfies the strong-readout hypotheses of Lemma M.6.1 for that record basis, the resulting record pair is supported on matching values of $k$.

A definite outcome requires the instrument, Born-selector, and actualization branch; a physical-reset cost requires Theorem 31's registered-reset hypotheses; and a stochastic arrow requires the separate Appendix O pathwise certificate. Definition 24 indexes retained states by perspective, and the cross-perspective import obstruction is stated below.

Definition M.6.2 requires a record-sharing or perspective-invariance certificate before an actualized record may be imported across distinct perspectives, and Lemma M.6.2a proves the corresponding import normal form for the retained calculus. Theorem M.6.2b applies this rule to the displayed Frauchiger–Renner-style import: when neither certificate exists, that import is ill typed. This establishes a precise obstruction to any argument containing such an import, and Theorem M.6.2c applies it to both certainty routes of the complete four-laboratory Frauchiger–Renner protocol when their edges connect distinct perspective indices.

### P.5.8.6 Comparison with Existing Frameworks

The following status ledger records PU's own construction:

| PU item | Internal conclusion | Required branch |
|:--------|:--------------------|:----------------|
| Observer | finite prediction, registered verification, and outcome-conditioned update | Definitions 4--5 and P.5.8.1 |
| Minimal observer candidate | threshold full-loop implementation | nonempty attained Definition-23 implementation class |
| Quantum measurement ledger | trace-form weights and a normalized outcome instrument | Principles 8.0b--8.0c, Theorem 8.0d, and the accepted actualization branch |
| Sharp repeatable case | Lüders instrument | Proposition 9's ideal nondegenerate branch |
| Reflexive limitation | no one uniformly exact predictor | Theorems 10--11 on their diagonal-closed class |
| Cross-perspective consistency | same-basis matching record | Theorem M.6.1 under its strong-readout hypotheses |

These entries define PU's comparison class. They do not establish that Copenhagen, Everettian, decoherence, QBist, relational, or collapse frameworks have no observer criterion, or that PU's operational criterion uniquely resolves their ontological questions.

Two distinct interpretive criteria are used here. The temporal rule is an explicit PU admissibility criterion directed at ontic future-to-present inputs and all-at-once replacements of the predictive loop; finite pre/post-selection and weak-value calculations remain ordinary conditional process-tensor statistics. The Artifact Identification Criterion can classify proposed surplus structure only relative to a stated finite-response branch. Finite capacity, a conditional reset ledger, SPAP, and finite resolution do not by themselves prove that a continuum ontology is unreal or empirically exclude an interpretation.

Accordingly, the framework can quotient response-null labels and compare operational predictions, but it cannot infer the falsity of Everettian, Bohmian, GRW, or other ontologies from resource bounds alone. Theorem E.9.5 is itself conditional on its closed-system, retained-algebra, and ND-RID hypotheses and supplies neither the Born selector nor an actualization rule.

PU supplies a complete operational specification on its explicit physical principle set: Definition P.5.8.1 defines an observer; Definition 23 defines a minimal qualifying full-loop implementation; Theorems 10–11 delimit universally exact reflexive prediction; Principle 11b and Theorem 11b close the binary invariant response law; Principles 8.0b–8.0c and Theorem 8.0d close the complex carrier, Born ledger, quantum instrument, and single-outcome registration; and Theorems 31–31a supply the general and full-context reset ledgers. Each conclusion is tied to the exact principle or theorem that establishes it.

## P.6 Physical Instantiation: The Bridge from Logic to Physics

### P.6.1 The Principle of Physical Instantiation (PPI)

<a id="definition-p62-principle-of-physical-instantiation-ppi"></a>**Definition P.6.2 (Principle of Physical Instantiation – PPI).**
Any derivable, self-consistent logical or mathematical structure, when physically instantiated by a system composed of finite resources and operating in finite time, will manifest in the physical world with properties and dynamics shaped by the irreducible thermodynamic costs and resource-optimization imperatives inherent in its implementation. When multiple physically admissible implementations realize the same abstract structure with the same operational functionality, the realized implementation is the one minimizing the relevant resource cost over that admissible class (PPI-optimality).

In the finite-response formulation, PPI is not an additional copy map from pure mathematics into physics. It is the operational representation rule for physical content: a structure is physically instantiated exactly through the finite protocol-response presheaf it induces after response-null labels are quotiented and PCE-minimal representatives are selected. It explains why the physical world is not a direct copy of abstract structures, but the finite-response, cost-minimal representative of those structures whenever the bridge-collapse conditions of Theorem P.6.1b.7 are satisfied and, after Theorem P.6.1b.8a, represented in the finite operational quotient with nondegenerate uniqueness still requiring the strictness clauses of Theorem P.6.1b.7.

<a id="definition-p62a-thermodynamically-dressed-mathematical-object"></a>**Definition P.6.2a (Thermodynamically Dressed Mathematical Object).** Let $\mathfrak M$ be the domain of mathematical objects. A bare mathematical object is denoted $X\in\mathfrak M$. A thermodynamically dressed object is a tuple
$$
X^\Theta=(X,\Pi_X,R_X,V_X,C_X,\tau_X),
$$
where $\Pi_X$ is a finite physicalization protocol, $R_X$ is the finite record produced by the protocol, $V_X$ is a finite verifier, $C_X$ is the thermodynamic or resource cost of producing and maintaining the record, and $\tau_X$ is the update-ordering datum of the instantiation. The protocol and verifier records fix the encoding and decoder for $R_X$, the accepted witness fields, the verification tolerance, and the resource units. When verification is certificate-relative, the witness travels in $R_X$: $\Pi_X$ bears the production or search obligation, while $V_X$ is charged as checking with the supplied witness. A finite verifier-time bound therefore supplies no bound on the discovery cost of $R_X$.

Bare mathematical existence is the condition $X\in\mathfrak M$. PPI-physicalizable existence is the existence of at least one admissible dressing $X^\Theta$ with finite cost.

<a id="definition-p62b-ppi-physicalizable-sector"></a>**Definition P.6.2b (PPI-Physicalizable Sector).** Define $\mathfrak P\subseteq\mathfrak M$ by
$$
X\in\mathfrak P
$$
when there exist finite data
$$
(\Pi_X,R_X,V_X,C_X)
$$
such that $\Pi_X$ instantiates an operational aspect of $X$ as a finite physical record or process, $V_X$ verifies the record relative to the intended aspect of $X$, $C_X<\infty$, and $R_X$ can enter a finite retained predictive, causal, or verification update.

Let $\mathfrak A(t)\subseteq\mathfrak P$ be the actually instantiated physical records or processes at time $t$, represented by their dressed operational aspects, and let $\mathfrak E_S(t)\subseteq\mathfrak A(t)$ be the actualized sector accessible to predictor $S$ at time $t$. Then
$$
\mathfrak E_S(t)\subseteq\mathfrak A(t)\subseteq\mathfrak P\subseteq\mathfrak M.
\tag{P.6.2a}
$$

<a id="theorem-p62c-finite-cost-physicalizability-criterion"></a>**Theorem P.6.2c (Finite-Cost Physicalizability Criterion).** A mathematical object $X\in\mathfrak M$ is PPI-physicalizable only through finite recordability, finite verification, finite maintenance, and finite update-use. Equivalently,
$$
X\in\mathfrak P
\Longleftrightarrow
X\text{ admits a finite thermodynamic dressing }X^\Theta
$$
relative to the retained operational aspect being instantiated.

*Proof.* By Definition P.6.2, physical instantiation is finite-resource implementation shaped by thermodynamic cost and PCE/PPI optimality. If $X$ is physically instantiated, then the instantiation must be carried by some finite protocol, finite record or process, finite verifier, finite maintenance budget, and finite update role; otherwise it is not an MPU-admissible finite physical implementation. Conversely, if such finite data exist, they define a PPI-admissible thermodynamic dressing of the operational aspect of $X$. ∎

**Domain and budget scope.** The biconditional classifies a nominated $X$ once an admissible dressing is supplied; it does not furnish a uniform terminating decision procedure for membership in $\mathfrak P$ over arbitrary $X\in\mathfrak M$. Such a procedure requires a declared presentation of $\mathfrak M$ and a completeness proof for the dressing test. Membership in $\mathfrak P$ is existential at the finiteness level: some finite dressing exists. It does not assert that one predictor or one fixed budget can maintain every member of $\mathfrak P$. A fixed-budget claim uses a declared protocol, outcome, tolerance, verification, and cost restriction such as Definition P.16d.0.1; an object may admit a finite dressing while remaining unavailable at the nominated budget.

<a id="definition-p62d-operational-latent-mathematics"></a>**Definition P.6.2d (Operational Latent Mathematics).** The global operational-latent sector at time $t$ is
$$
\mathfrak W_{\mathrm{OLM}}(t)=\mathfrak P\setminus\mathfrak A(t).
$$
It consists of mathematical structures that can in principle be physicalized at finite cost but have not been actualized as physical records or processes at $t$.

The predictor-relative operational-latent sector is
$$
\mathfrak W_{\mathrm{OLM}}(S,t)=\mathfrak P\setminus\mathfrak E_S(t).
$$
It consists of physicalizable, and possibly already actualized, structures not currently accessible to predictor $S$.

<a id="proposition-p62e-non-nested-ppi-status-taxonomy"></a>**Proposition P.6.2e (Non-Nested PPI Status Taxonomy).** The following status taxonomy separates mathematical existence from physical actualization and observer access:

| Class | Name | Formal condition | Example | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $C_0$ | Bare mathematical | $X\in\mathfrak M$ | arbitrary formal structure | mathematical only |
| $C_1$ | Finitely describable | finite code $\ulcorner X\urcorner$ | $\pi$, $\mathbb N$, $\Omega$ | nameable, not necessarily physicalizable |
| $C_2$ | Generator-physicalizable | finite rule generates finite approximants | successor rule, digits of $\pi$ to bound $N$ | finite prefixes physicalizable |
| $C_3$ | Certificate-physicalizable | finite certificate and finite verifier | proof code, computation trace | directly PPI-admissible |
| $C_4$ | Predictor-accessible | $\operatorname{Adm}_S(t,p,e)$ | proof usable by $S$ | perspectival information |
| $C_5$ | Phase-unlockable | inaccessible at $t$, accessible after update | $E_{B,t}$ of A.5.6a | context-update dependent |
| $C_6$ | PCE-stable | retained predictive value | law, stable record, error-corrected bit | physically meaningful |
| $C_7$ | Actualized | $X\in\mathfrak A(t)$ via some $X^\Theta$ | stored bit, written proof | physical actuality |
| $C_8$ | Experienced | $X\in\mathfrak E_S(t)$ via some $X^\Theta$ | observed fact, known proof | observer-accessed reality |

These labels are independent audit coordinates, not a chain of inclusions. For example, an actual finite record need not be PCE-stable, a finite generator need not make a completed infinite object physically recordable, and a certificate may be inaccessible to a nominated predictor. The only universal inclusions asserted here are the typed sets in (P.6.2a): $\mathfrak E_S(t)\subseteq\mathfrak A(t)\subseteq\mathfrak P\subseteq\mathfrak M$. A physical claim must state which additional status coordinates it needs.

*Proof.* Equation (P.6.2a) follows from the definitions of accessibility, actualization, physicalizability, and mathematical existence. No further inclusion follows from the table without an explicit implication certificate. $\square$

<a id="corollary-p62f-completed-infinity-is-not-a-completed-physical-record"></a>**Corollary P.6.2f (Completed Infinity Is Not a Completed Physical Record).** Completed infinite totalities may be legitimate mathematical objects in $\mathfrak M$, but they are not PPI-complete as physical records unless a finite dressing specifies the operational aspect being instantiated. Thus the successor rule and finite numerals can be physicalized, while $\mathbb N$ as a completed physical record is not a finite PPI object.

*Proof.* A completed physical record of all natural numbers would require infinite memory, infinite distinguishability, and infinite verification. This violates the finite-cost condition in Theorem P.6.2c. A successor rule, by contrast, is a finite generator, and any finite prefix has finite record and finite verification cost. ∎

<a id="corollary-p62g-finite-dressing-obligations-for-physical-structure"></a>**Corollary P.6.2g (Finite-Dressing Obligations for Physical Structure).** An abstract order, metric, dependency relation, or discrete set becomes a PU physical observable only after a finite protocol specifies its record, verifier, error tolerance, implementation cost, and update use. The required bridge data are type-specific:

- a physical clock requires a calibrated duration/rate observable and stability record;
- a spatial metric requires separating probes, metric reconstruction, conditioning, and geometric realization;
- causal influence requires an intervention-response map and a registered propagation cone;
- operational discreteness requires a finite distinguishability quotient at the stated budget.

A registered reset and its irreversible heat ledger may orient histories on Appendix O's additional pathwise branch, but irreversibility is not required merely for physical time or event order. Finite dependency alone is not causation, and finite distinguishability alone is not a theorem that the underlying ontology is discrete.

*Proof.* Theorem P.6.2c supplies the common finite-dressing requirement. The additional bullets are precisely the independent clock, metric, intervention, and quotient certificates required by the corresponding source theorems; none follows from the common dressing alone. $\square$

**Remark: Dynamical Descent.** Theorems K.10.25a–K.10.25b make the information requirement explicit. Positive separation entropy forces the number of retained history bits to grow and prevents exact deterministic descent to every finite partition below the stated cell diameter. This identifies ambiguity somewhere in the chosen quotient. A stochastic law additionally specifies a measure and memory treatment; an ontically exhaustive finite-state interpretation adds a physical principle.

**Remark: Relation to PCE.** PPI defines the admissible finite-response domain and PCE supplies a cost schema on a declared comparison class. A selected stable attractor requires a nonempty class, a complete commensurate cost, existence or attainment, the strictness needed for uniqueness, and Appendix D's independent dynamical hypotheses; its physical realization requires a separate realization certificate.

### P.6.1a PPI-Contract Rigidity

<a id="definition-p61a1-ppi-contract"></a>**Definition P.6.1a.1 (PPI Contract).** A PPI contract is a quadruple
$$
\mathcal C=(\mathcal I,\mathcal O,\pi,\eta)
$$
where $\mathcal I$ is a finite list of PU-internal invariants, $\mathcal O$ is a finite list of operational observables, $\pi:\mathcal I\to\mathcal O$ is the interpretation map, and $\eta$ is the finite-resolution error budget assigning a tolerance to each observable comparison. A registered equivalence relation $\sim_{\mathrm{op}}$ on contracts specifies the operational quotient and must have the following soundness property: equivalent contracts produce outcome distributions agreeing within $\eta$ for every MPU-admissible protocol after applying their interpretation maps. Pairwise agreement within a positive tolerance alone does not define this quotient, because that relation need not be transitive. The equivalence classes and their compatibility with the retained protocol maps are additional finite-resolution data.

<a id="definition-p61a2-contract-cost"></a>**Definition P.6.1a.2 (Contract Cost).** On an admissible class $\mathfrak C$ of PPI contracts, define
$$
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{PPI}}(\mathcal C)
=
L_{\mathrm{desc}}(\mathcal C)
+
L_{\mathrm{viol}}(\mathcal C)
+
L_{\mathrm{regret}}(\mathcal C),
\tag{P.6.1a.1}
$$
where $L_{\mathrm{desc}}$ is the description length of the interpretation map and branch data, $L_{\mathrm{viol}}$ is the nonnegative penalty for violating already-derived PU constraints, and $L_{\mathrm{regret}}$ is the predictive regret against admissible protocols. The cost descends to the quotient $\mathfrak C/\sim_{\mathrm{op}}$ whenever all three terms are invariant under operational equivalence.

<a id="theorem-p61a3-ppi-contract-rigidity-on-a-strict-pce-branch"></a>**Theorem P.6.1a.3 (PPI-Contract Rigidity on a Strict PCE Branch).** Suppose the quotient $Q=\mathfrak C/\sim_{\mathrm{op}}$ is nonempty and compact in the finite-resolution topology induced by the protocol family, and suppose the descended cost
$$
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}:Q\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}
$$
is lower semicontinuous and strictly convex along every nontrivial operational interpolation in $Q$, and assume any two distinct minimizers in $Q$ can be joined by such an interpolation. Then there is a unique minimizing PPI contract up to operational equivalence:
$$
[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{phys}}]
=
\operatorname*{argmin}_{[\mathcal C]\in Q}
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([\mathcal C]).
\tag{P.6.1a.2}
$$

*Proof.* Put
$$
m=\inf_{q\in Q}\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q).
$$
Because $Q$ is nonempty and the cost is finite and nonnegative, $m\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$. For every integer $n\ge1$, define
$$
F_n=
\left\{q\in Q:
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q)
\le m+\frac1n
\right\}.
$$
The definition of the infimum makes $F_n$ nonempty. Lower semicontinuity makes $F_n$ closed, and $F_{n+1}\subseteq F_n$. Each $F_n$ is therefore compact. The nested family has the finite-intersection property, so compactness of $Q$ gives a point $q_*\in\bigcap_{n\ge1}F_n$. Then
$$
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_*)
\le m+\frac1n
$$
for every $n$, whence $\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_*)\le m$. The reverse inequality follows from the definition of $m$, so $q_*$ is a minimizer.

Suppose $[\mathcal C_1]$ and $[\mathcal C_2]$ are distinct minimizers with common value $m$. The interpolation hypothesis supplies a nontrivial $[\mathcal C_t]$, $0<t<1$, between them. Strict convexity gives
$$
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([\mathcal C_t])
<
(1-t)\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([\mathcal C_1])
+t\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([\mathcal C_2])
=m,
$$
contradicting the definition of $m$. Thus the minimizer is unique in $Q$. Representatives of its quotient class differ only by operationally null reparameterization, so the contract is unique up to PPI-equivalence. ∎

<a id="corollary-p61a4-no-free-interpretive-branches-at-identical-predictive-content"></a>**Corollary P.6.1a.4 (No Free Interpretive Branches at Identical Predictive Content).** If two admissible PPI mappings have identical operational predictions and the same predictive-regret term, and one has strictly larger sum $L_{\mathrm{desc}}+L_{\mathrm{viol}}$, that mapping cannot minimize the complete cost (P.6.1a.1) in a comparison class containing the other.

*Proof.* The predictive-regret terms cancel in the cost difference. The strictly positive difference in $L_{\mathrm{desc}}+L_{\mathrm{viol}}$ therefore gives a strictly larger complete objective value. An increase in one component alone is insufficient when another component decreases by an offsetting amount. ∎

### P.6.1b Operational Yoneda Reconstruction

<a id="definition-p61b1-protocol-response-presheaf"></a>**Definition P.6.1b.1 (Protocol Response Presheaf).** Let $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}$ be the finite category of MPU-admissible protocols at fixed resolution, with morphisms given by admissible protocol refinements, coarse-grainings, and pre/post-processing maps. Let $\mathsf{Prob}_{\mathrm{fin}}$ be the category of finite probability spaces and stochastic maps. For a PPI-admissible internal invariant $X$, define its operational response presheaf
$$
\mathcal R_X:\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}^{op}\to\mathsf{Prob}_{\mathrm{fin}}
$$
by assigning to each protocol $P$ the finite outcome distribution
$$
\mathcal R_X(P)=\Pr_X(\cdot\mid P).
$$
A protocol family is separating when
$$
\mathcal R_X(P)=\mathcal R_Y(P)
\quad
\text{for every }P\in\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}
$$
implies $X\sim_{\mathrm{op}}Y$. For the reconstruction branch, additionally register an operational quotient category in which $\mathcal R$ is a functor, operational equivalence makes its response objects and induced arrows agree, and isomorphic quotient objects are identified. The last condition chooses the quotient at object-isomorphism level; equality of outcome distributions alone does not supply it. Protocol-completeness in Definition P.6.1b.2 is imposed on the resulting morphism classes.

<a id="definition-p61b2-protocol-complete-ppi-branch"></a>**Definition P.6.1b.2 (Protocol-Complete PPI Branch).** A PPI branch is protocol-complete when every natural transformation
$$
\eta:\mathcal R_X\Rightarrow\mathcal R_Y
$$
between response presheaves is induced by a PPI-admissible transformation $X\to Y$, unique up to operational equivalence.

<a id="theorem-p61b3-operational-yoneda-reconstruction"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.3 (Operational Yoneda Reconstruction).** On a separating protocol-complete PPI branch, the assignment
$$
\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}:
X\longmapsto\mathcal R_X
$$
descends to a fully faithful functor
$$
\mathsf{Inv}_{\mathrm{PPI}}/{\sim_{\mathrm{op}}}
\hookrightarrow
[\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}^{op},\mathsf{Prob}_{\mathrm{fin}}].
\tag{P.6.1b.1}
$$
Consequently,
$$
\mathcal R_X\simeq\mathcal R_Y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X\sim_{\mathrm{op}}Y.
\tag{P.6.1b.2}
$$

*Proof.* The assignment is well-defined on the quotient because operationally equivalent invariants give the same outcome distributions for every admissible protocol. If
$$
\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}([X])=\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}([Y]),
$$
then $\mathcal R_X(P)=\mathcal R_Y(P)$ for all protocols $P$. Since the protocol family is separating, $X\sim_{\mathrm{op}}Y$, proving faithfulness on objects.

Protocol-completeness states that every natural transformation is induced by a unique operational morphism class. Thus the response functor induces a bijection on each Hom-set and is fully faithful. A natural isomorphism between $\mathcal R_X$ and $\mathcal R_Y$ lifts, together with its inverse, to two quotient morphisms. Faithfulness sends their composites to the corresponding identities, so the lifted morphisms are inverse. The object-isomorphism identification registered in Definition P.6.1b.1 then gives $X\sim_{\mathrm{op}}Y$. The reverse implication follows from the quotient compatibility of the response functor. This proves (P.6.1b.2). ∎

<a id="corollary-p61b4-no-observable-without-a-protocol-presheaf"></a>**Corollary P.6.1b.4 (No Observable Without a Protocol Presheaf).** An internal PU invariant has physical content exactly to the extent that it defines a nontrivial operational response presheaf. If two invariants define naturally isomorphic response presheaves, PPI identifies them as the same physical invariant.

*Proof.* Theorem P.6.1b.3 embeds physical invariants into the presheaf category of protocol responses. A trivial or naturally redundant presheaf gives no distinction in the quotient. ∎

<a id="definition-p61b5-finite-pce-completion-datum"></a>**Definition P.6.1b.5 (Finite-PCE Completion Datum).** Let $X$ be an abstract, continuum, or internal PU invariant with operational response presheaf
$$
\mathcal R_X:\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}^{op}\to\mathsf{Prob}_{\mathrm{fin}}
$$
on the finite protocol category of Definition P.6.1b.1, with each fixed protocol carrying its fixed finite outcome set. A finite-PCE completion datum for $X$ is a directed family
$$
\{(X_h,\mathcal R_h,\mathcal C_h)\}_{h\in I}
$$
such that:

1. $X_h$ is a finite MPU implementation with PPI contract $\mathcal C_h$.

2. $\mathcal R_h$ is the finite protocol-response presheaf induced by $X_h$.

3. For every finite protocol $P\in\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}$, after identifying all responses with the fixed finite outcome set of $P$,
$$
\lim_{h}
d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal R_h(P),\mathcal R_X(P)\right)=0,
\tag{P.6.1b.3}
$$
and the convergence is natural under protocol refinements and coarse-grainings.

4. The PPI contract costs are uniformly finite on every fixed finite protocol family:
$$
\sup_h
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{PPI}}(\mathcal C_h\vert_{\mathsf P_0})
<\infty
\quad
\text{for every finite }
\mathsf P_0\subset\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}.
\tag{P.6.1b.4}
$$

5. If two directed subfamilies induce the same limiting protocol-response presheaf, they are identified in the operational quotient.

<a id="theorem-p61b6-operational-limit-of-a-finite-pce-completion"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.6 (Operational Limit of a Finite-PCE Completion).** On a separating protocol-complete PPI branch, every finite-PCE completion datum for an invariant $X$ determines the limiting protocol-response presheaf $\mathcal R_X$ and its natural-isomorphism class
$$
[X]_{\mathrm{comp}}
:=
[\mathcal R_X]_{\simeq}.
\tag{P.6.1b.5}
$$
Two completion data determine the same operational completion class exactly when their limiting protocol-response presheaves are naturally isomorphic. This response-class definition requires no bonding morphisms between the $X_h$. A categorical colimit of those objects requires a separately supplied diagram and its colimit universal property.

This completion class is a physical identity class only under both of the following additional hypotheses:

1. the limiting response presheaf lies in the essential image of $\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}$, so it is induced by a PPI-admissible invariant;
2. at least one such realizing invariant has globally finite PPI implementation cost.

If, in addition, the quotient of realizing contracts satisfies the nonemptiness, compactness, lower-semicontinuity, interpolation, and strict-convexity hypotheses of Theorem P.6.1a.3, that physical class has a unique PCE-minimizing contract up to operational equivalence. A PPI-instantiated invariant supplies a finite-PCE completion datum only when its finite records form a directed family satisfying all five clauses of Definition P.6.1b.5.

*Proof.* Let $\{(X_h,\mathcal R_h,\mathcal C_h)\}_{h\in I}$ be a finite-PCE completion datum. For each retained protocol $P$, clause 3 gives convergence in total variation to $\mathcal R_X(P)$. The simplex over the specified finite outcome set of $P$ is closed, so $\mathcal R_X(P)$ is a probability distribution. If $T$ is any retained stochastic push-forward, then
$$
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(T_\#\mu,T_\#\nu)
\le
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu).
$$
Indeed, for every event $A$ in the target outcome set,
$$
|(T_\#\mu)(A)-(T_\#\nu)(A)|
=
\left|\sum_x T(A\mid x)(\mu(x)-\nu(x))\right|
\le
d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mu,\nu),
$$
and taking the supremum over $A$ gives the contraction. Every naturality square for the approximants therefore remains commutative after taking the limit. The datum consequently determines a limiting response presheaf. The operational completion class is the natural-isomorphism class of this limiting presheaf. Thus two completion data define the same completion class exactly when their limiting presheaves are naturally isomorphic, by definition, including limits outside the essential image. Clause 5's identification of subfamilies with the same limit is consistent with this definition.

Definition P.6.1b.2 states only that natural transformations between presheaves $\mathcal R_Y$ and $\mathcal R_Z$ already arising from PPI-admissible invariants are induced by admissible transformations. It does not assert that an arbitrary limiting presheaf is $\mathcal R_Y$ for some admissible $Y$. The essential-image hypothesis supplies precisely that object-level existence. Once a realizing $Y$ exists, separation makes its operational class unique. The global finite-cost hypothesis places at least one representative in the physical PPI domain; the bounds in (P.6.1b.4), taken separately on finite protocol families, are not used as a substitute for that hypothesis. Under the further hypotheses of Theorem P.6.1a.3, that theorem gives the unique cost-minimizing contract within the realizing class. Finally, physical instantiation yields a completion datum only when the required directed approximants, convergence, uniform local cost bounds, naturality, and quotient identification are supplied; these are exactly clauses 1--5 of Definition P.6.1b.5. ∎

<a id="theorem-p61b7-ppi-bridge-collapse-theorem"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.7 (PPI Bridge-Collapse Theorem).** Let $\mathfrak B$ be a nonempty admissible finite-resolution family of bridge maps from a specified list of PU-internal invariants $\mathcal I$ to a specified list of operational observables $\mathcal O$. For each bridge $B\in\mathfrak B$, let $\mathcal R_B$ be its protocol-response presheaf on $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}$, and write
$$
B\sim_{\mathrm{op}}B'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal R_B\simeq\mathcal R_{B'}
$$
by exact natural isomorphism of the registered finite-resolution response presheaves. The finite-resolution equivalence and protocol-compatibility data satisfy Definition P.6.1a.1; approximate pairwise agreement alone is not used as an equivalence relation. Suppose:

1. the protocol family is separating and protocol-complete in the sense of Definitions P.6.1b.1-P.6.1b.2;
2. the quotient $Q_{\mathfrak B}:=\mathfrak B/{\sim_{\mathrm{op}}}$ is compact in the finite-resolution protocol topology;
3. the three nonnegative cost components descend to lower-semicontinuous functions on $Q_{\mathfrak B}$;
4. one of the following nondegeneracy conditions holds:
   - **scalar branch:** every two distinct points of $Q_{\mathfrak B}$ can be joined by a nontrivial operational interpolation, and $\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}=L_{\mathrm{desc}}+L_{\mathrm{viol}}+L_{\mathrm{regret}}$ is strictly convex along every such interpolation;
   - **lexicographic branch:** the map
     $$
     [B]\longmapsto
     \bigl(L_{\mathrm{viol}}([B]),L_{\mathrm{regret}}([B]),L_{\mathrm{desc}}([B])\bigr)
     $$
     is injective, and selection minimizes this ordered triple lexicographically;
5. every bridge degree of freedom invisible to all finite protocols has positive description length unless it is quotiented out.

On the scalar branch there is a unique scalar-cost minimizer,
$$
[B_{\mathrm{phys}}]
=
\operatorname*{argmin}_{[B]\in Q_{\mathfrak B}}
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([B]).
\tag{P.6.1b.6}
$$
On the lexicographic branch there is a unique lexicographic minimizer of $(L_{\mathrm{viol}},L_{\mathrm{regret}},L_{\mathrm{desc}})$. These are different selection rules; the lexicographic conclusion does not assert that the scalar argmin is a singleton.

*Proof.* Put $Q=Q_{\mathfrak B}$. On the scalar branch, let
$$
m=\inf_{q\in Q}\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q).
$$
For each $n\ge1$, the set
$$
F_n=\left\{q\in Q:\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q)\le m+\frac1n\right\}
$$
is nonempty by the definition of $m$, closed by lower semicontinuity, and nested. Compactness gives a point $q_*\in\bigcap_{n\ge1}F_n$. Hence $\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_*)\le m$, so equality holds and a minimizer exists. If distinct minimizers $q_1,q_2$ existed, hypothesis 4 supplies an interpolation $q_t$, $0<t<1$, and strict convexity gives
$$
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_t)
<
(1-t)\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_1)
+t\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}(q_2)
=m,
$$
a contradiction.

On the lexicographic branch, first minimize $L_{\mathrm{viol}}$ on $Q$. The same compact-sublevel argument gives a nonempty compact minimizer set $M_1$. Minimize $L_{\mathrm{regret}}$ on $M_1$ to obtain a nonempty compact set $M_2$, and minimize $L_{\mathrm{desc}}$ on $M_2$ to obtain a nonempty compact set $M_3$. Every point of $M_3$ is a lexicographic minimizer. If $q_1,q_2\in M_3$, all three cost coordinates agree at $q_1$ and $q_2$; injectivity of the triple map gives $q_1=q_2$. Thus the lexicographic minimizer is unique. Condition 5 and Corollary P.6.1a.4 remove positive-cost response-null symbols from a representative without changing its quotient point. ∎

<a id="corollary-p61b8-no-response-surplus-principle"></a>**Corollary P.6.1b.8 (No-Response-Surplus Principle).** On a separating protocol-complete PPI branch, an additional branch label, field, family copy, bridge normalization, or geometric refinement is physically retained only if it changes a finite protocol-response presheaf or lowers an already-defined PPI cost. If it changes no finite response and lowers no cost, PCE quotients it out.

*Proof.* A response-null addition defines the same object of $Q_{\mathfrak B}$ by Theorem P.6.1b.3. If it has positive description length and no compensating decrease in $L_{\mathrm{viol}}$ or $L_{\mathrm{regret}}$, Corollary P.6.1a.4 removes it. If it changes a finite protocol response, it is not response-null and must be evaluated in the separating quotient. These two alternatives exhaust the finite-response cases. ∎

<a id="theorem-p61b8a-finite-operational-response-closure"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8a (Finite Operational Response Closure).** Work at a specified finite resolution, so $\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}$ is finite and every retained protocol $P$ has a specified finite outcome set $\Omega_P$. On this branch, every protocol arrow $\alpha:P\to Q$ has one registered stochastic map $T_\alpha:\Omega_Q\to\Omega_P$, shared by every response presheaf in the family; these maps satisfy the identity and contravariant composition laws. Thus a response presheaf is determined by its outcome laws subject to the equations $T_\alpha\mathcal R(Q)=\mathcal R(P)$. Let $\mathfrak B_0$ be any raw family of finite PPI bridge descriptions with these response maps and a prefix-free finite description code for which every bounded-length code sublevel is finite. Let
$$
\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}(B)=\mathcal R_B
$$
be the induced protocol-response presheaf, and define
$$
B\sim_{\mathrm{op}}B'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal R_B\simeq\mathcal R_{B'}.
$$
Let
$$
Q_{\mathfrak B}:=
\overline{\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathfrak B_0)}/\simeq,
\tag{P.6.1b.7}
$$
where the closure is taken in the finite product of retained protocol-outcome simplexes. Assume that natural isomorphism is induced by the continuous action of the finite group of protocol-compatible outcome relabellings. Assume also that $L_{\mathrm{viol}}$ and $L_{\mathrm{regret}}$ are continuous operational functions of the response presheaf, and define
$$
\bar{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{PPI}}([R])
=
L_{\mathrm{viol}}(R)+L_{\mathrm{regret}}(R)
+
\inf\{L_{\mathrm{desc}}(B):\mathcal R_B\simeq R\}.
\tag{P.6.1b.8a}
$$
Then $Q_{\mathfrak B}$ is compact Hausdorff, finite protocols separate its distinct points, the cost descends and is lower semicontinuous, and positive-cost response-null surplus is absent from a cost-minimal representative.

The object closure (P.6.1b.7) does not by itself imply protocol-completeness. A formally morphism-complete response category can be defined by taking the objects in the closure and all finite natural transformations between them as morphisms. Identifying that formal category with PPI-admissible transformations additionally requires the realizability hypothesis that every retained natural transformation is induced by a PPI-admissible transformation. Neither the scalar nor the lexicographic nondegeneracy condition of Theorem P.6.1b.7 follows from response closure.

*Proof.* Let
$$
X=\prod_{P\in\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}}\Delta(\Omega_P).
$$
Every factor is a compact Hausdorff simplex, and the product is finite, so $X$ is compact Hausdorff. The set $\overline{\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathfrak B_0)}$ is closed in $X$ and hence compact Hausdorff. Let $G$ be the finite group of protocol-compatible relabellings. The orbit relation is
$$
\mathcal R_G=\bigcup_{g\in G}\{(R,gR):R\in\overline{\mathcal Y_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathfrak B_0)}\}.
$$
For each $g$, the displayed graph is closed because the action is continuous and the space is Hausdorff. The union is finite, so $\mathcal R_G$ is closed. The quotient by a closed equivalence relation on a compact Hausdorff space is compact Hausdorff. Thus $Q_{\mathfrak B}$ is compact Hausdorff.

If two response classes are distinct, their presheaves are not naturally isomorphic. Hence at least one retained outcome coordinate, restriction map, relabelling, conditioning map, or composition response differs. That finite datum separates the two quotient points.

The cost is constant on each response class by construction, so it descends. The first two terms are continuous by hypothesis. For the description envelope, define
$$
D([R])=\inf\{L_{\mathrm{desc}}(B):\mathcal R_B\simeq R\}.
$$
Description lengths are nonnegative integers. Whenever a response class has a coded representative, the nonempty set of its code lengths has a least element, so the infimum is attained. For every integer $N\ge0$, the sublevel $\{[R]:D([R])\le N\}$ is the image of the finite bounded-length code set. It is a finite subset of the Hausdorff quotient and is therefore closed. Thus $D$ is lower semicontinuous, and so is its sum with the two continuous nonnegative terms.

A response-null symbol leaves the quotient point, $L_{\mathrm{viol}}$, $L_{\mathrm{regret}}$, and the envelope $D$ unchanged. If an admissible deletion preserves every retained response and certificate while strictly decreasing the representative's complete description length, that representative does not attain the envelope $D$ and cannot be a shortest representative of its class. The strict exclusion concerns the representative cost, not a decrease of the already minimized class function.

Finally, (P.6.1b.7) specifies only a set of response objects modulo isomorphism; it contains no morphism set. Declaring all finite natural transformations to be morphisms defines a formal response category, but Definition P.6.1b.2 requires those morphisms to be induced by PPI-admissible transformations. That implication is exactly the additional realizability hypothesis stated above. Response closure also places no strict inequality between costs of distinct quotient points, so the nondegeneracy alternatives of Theorem P.6.1b.7 remain separate hypotheses. ∎

<a id="theorem-p61b8d-fixed-code-completion-and-strict-selector-classification"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8d (Fixed-Code Completion and Strict-Selector Classification).** On the following fixed finite-prefix-code datum, Theorems W4-P1–P3 and the dyadic sampler prove the stated finite-sublevel, selector-gap and bounded-cost completion results. The interpolation obstruction has its displayed continuity premise. Global physical identification, empirical-input maps and categoricity remain separate obligations. Section numbers are local.

## 2. Typed datum and conventions

Let $C$ be the registered prefix-free subset of words over a finite alphabet of size $b\ge 2$, with a single-valued decoding/response map $r:C\to Q$. The binary specialization has $b=2$; the arguments requiring only finite bounded-length sublevels also apply to any registered description-length convention with that property. Here $Q$ is the finite-protocol response closure modulo the registered relabelling equivalence; by the owner's theorem $Q$ is Hausdorff. Codes may be redundant. A code decodes exactly one response class; probabilistic decoding is instead part of that response law, not a different class chosen by decoding luck.

For $q\in Q$ set

$$
D(q)=\min\{|s|: s\in C \text{ and } r(s)=q\},
$$

with $D(q)=+\infty$ when the set is empty. The minimum exists whenever there is a code since lengths are nonnegative integers. Let $\alpha>0$ be the registered cost per code symbol and $A:Q\to[0,+\infty]$ the sum of all other registered nonnegative cost terms. Define

$$
V(q)=\alpha D(q)+A(q).
$$

The manuscript's equation P.6.1b.8a is the specialization $\alpha=1$, $A=L_{\mathrm{viol}}+L_{\mathrm{regret}}$. An explicit symbol-to-resource conversion $\alpha$ is retained if physical cost units are claimed. We never identify description bits with joules or physical time without a supplied unit bridge.

Every compared implementation in this theorem must be represented by a code in this fixed family and charged its full registered description length in the complete representative cost. For a representative $s$ with cost $\alpha|s|+A(r(s))$, its class cost satisfies $V(r(s))\le\alpha|s|+A(r(s))$; the same bound therefore applies to uniformly bounded representative costs. The global quantifiers below range over this declared response closure, not over unencoded physical implementations or another cost ledger.

Write $F_N=\{q:D(q)\le N\}$, for integers $N\ge 0$. The quotient may be uncountable; $F_{N}$ is finite. No assumption that an uncoded limit is physically realized is made.

## 3. Theorem W4-P1: exact finite-sublevel and strict-selector classification

For every datum of Section 2:

1. $|F_N|\le b^N$ (in particular $2^N$ for binary codes). Every finite $V$-sublevel is finite.
2. If any $q_{b}$ has $V(q_b)=U<\infty$, put $N=\lfloor U/\alpha\rfloor$. The global minimum $m=\min_Q V$ exists and all global minimizers are exactly

   $$
   M=\{q\in F_N:V(q)=\min_{p\in F_N}V(p)\}.
   $$

   In particular the minimum is finite and M is finite and nonempty. No compactness, lower semicontinuity, interpolation or strict convexity is needed for this assertion beyond the supplied exact code and nonnegative complete cost.
3. Put

   $$
   \delta_{\mathrm{in}}=\min\{V(q)-m:q\in F_N\setminus M\},
   $$

   with the minimum of the empty set equal to +∞, and

   $$
   \delta=\min\{\delta_{\mathrm{in}},\alpha(N+1)-m\}.
   $$

   Then $\delta>0$ and $V(q)\ge m+\delta$ for every $q\notin M$. If $Q\setminus M$ is empty the same inequality is vacuous and $\delta$ remains a valid positive bound.
4. Thus unique selection is equivalent to one response class winning the finite census $F_{N}$. A finite positive-gap certificate is automatic after that uniqueness check. Ties are exactly the finite set $M$, not an uncontrolled continuum of minimizers.
5. Any perturbation $\tilde{V}$ on the same response domain, retaining $\tilde{V}(q)=+\infty$ wherever $V(q)=+\infty$ and satisfying $|\tilde{V}(q)-V(q)|\le\varepsilon$ at every finite-cost $q$ with $2\varepsilon<\delta$ cannot select a point outside $M$. If $M=\{q_*\}$, $q_*$ remains its unique minimizer. This robustness conclusion is global because the perturbation bound is global.

### Proof

For each $q\in F_N$ choose one shortest code $s_{q}$; the semantic decoder assigns the whole exact response law to that code, not the outcome of one random execution. These are distinct elements of a prefix-free language. Extend every selected word to length $N$ in all possible ways. Prefix-freeness makes these extension sets disjoint and a word $s_{q}$ has $b^{N-|s_q|}$ extensions. Hence

$$
\sum_{q\in F_N}b^{N-D(q)}\le b^N.
$$

Every summand is at least one, proving $|F_N|\le b^N$. Equivalently, the shortest representatives obey Kraft's inequality. Since $V\ge\alpha D$, a finite $V$-sublevel at $U$ lies in $F_{\lfloor U/\alpha\rfloor}$.

Given $q_{b}$ and $U$, $q_b\in F_N$. For every $q\notin F_N$, either $D(q)=\infty$ or $D(q)\ge N+1$; hence $V(q)\ge\alpha(N+1)>U$. The finite set $F_{N}$ contains a point of cost $U$, so minimizing its finitely many values yields a finite $m\le U$. No point outside $F_{N}$ can match or improve it. This proves the exact global minimizer formula.

Each cost difference in the finite nonempty set defining $\delta_{\mathrm{in}}$ is strictly positive, or $\delta_{\mathrm{in}}=\infty$ if there is no such point. Also $\alpha(N+1)-m\ge\alpha(N+1)-U>0$. Their minimum is therefore positive. The two cases $q\in F_N\setminus M$ and $q\notin F_N$ give the gap assertion.

For $q\notin M$ and $p\in M$,

$$
\tilde{V}(q)-\tilde{V}(p)\ge V(q)-V(p)-2\varepsilon\ge\delta-2\varepsilon>0.
$$

All points outside M are strictly worse than every point in M. The remaining assertions follow. ∎

### What an executable selector actually requires

The finite bound is a theorem, not a decision algorithm for arbitrary programs. Definition P.6.2a explicitly separates finite witness checking from discovery, and the “Domain and budget scope” paragraph after Theorem P.6.2c explicitly withholds a uniform terminating membership procedure without an additional complete test. The cost in P.6.1b.8a bounds description length; it supplies no numerical bound on execution time, physical clock duration, thermodynamic production cost, or numerical precision. P.6.1d's frozen finite-model route separately supplies versioned total parsers and exact decidable semantic tables. Neither a universal algorithm nor an undecidability theorem for that owner follows from the length bound alone. To execute the census, one must supply a total test for admitted codes of length $\le N$, exact finite response equivalence, and comparable cost values or certified intervals. These are populated explicitly in Section 6. For general computable real costs an exact tie test can remain undecidable; the theorem does not replace it with floating-point equality.

A rigorous interval certificate suffices: exhibit a candidate $q_*$ with certified upper cost $U$, enumerate all admissible codes of length $\le\lfloor U/\alpha\rfloor$, merge response-equivalent codes, and prove every other class has a lower cost endpoint strictly above the upper endpoint for $q_*$. Outside the census the bound $\alpha(N+1)>U$ proves exclusion. For a parameter-dependent $U$ choose a single certified upper bound before enumerating; no sample-based cutoff is allowed.

## 4. Theorem W4-P2: bounded-cost completion rigidity

Let $(q_{h})$ be any net of coded response classes converging in $Q$, with one common code/decoder and common $\alpha>0$. Suppose $V(q_h)\le U<\infty$ for every $h$, or eventually. Then its limit $q$ belongs to $F_{\lfloor U/\alpha\rfloor}$ and $q_h=q$ eventually. Consequently:

- the limiting response class has an actual finite source code;
- a genuinely new, uncoded response limit requires unbounded description cost;
- a limit distinct from every fixed finite-cost class cannot be obtained with a uniform bound of this cost;
- changing the number of retained protocols with h falls outside this fixed-budget assertion.

### Proof

Discard an initial segment if necessary. Every $q_{h}$ lies in the finite set $F_{N}$. Finite subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed, so their limit $q$ lies in $F_{N}$. Because $F_N\setminus\{q\}$ is a finite closed set, its complement is an open neighborhood of $q$ that intersects $F_{N}$ only in $q$. Convergence makes $q_{h}$ lie in that neighborhood eventually, hence $q_h=q$ eventually. A shortest source code for $q$ provides the exact finite response realizer. ∎

### Application to the owner's finite-PCE completions

At a fixed finite protocol budget, combine Definition P.6.1b.5 with the *same* prefix-code envelope of Theorem P.6.1b.8a and a uniform bound on its complete cost. The whole retained protocol category is one of the finite protocol families to which the bound applies. W4-P2 then makes the retained response class eventually stationary. When every decoded source implementation is PPI-admissible, the limit lies in that same admissible essential image by its existing finite source representative. Its additional global physical cost, any unretained protocols, and transformations not supplied by decoding are not inferred from that fixed-budget result.

A varying code, omitted source-description charge, an $\alpha$ tending to zero, or bounds applying only to progressively different protocol subfamilies would not satisfy this theorem's common datum. This is a quantifier boundary, not an added historical gate.

## 5. Theorem W4-P3: continuous interpolation obstruction

Suppose $\gamma:[0,1]\to Q$ is continuous, $\gamma(0)\ne\gamma(1)$, and both endpoints have finite cost. There is no cost-convex interpolation inequality

$V(\gamma(t))\le(1-t)V(\gamma(0))+tV(\gamma(1))$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.

In particular no strictly convex continuous interpolation between response-distinct finite-cost endpoints exists for this exact code cost. If the operational interpolation in Theorem P.6.1b.7 is additionally specified to be continuous in the finite-response topology, its scalar alternative and the exact finite-code envelope of P.6.1b.8a cannot jointly hold on a nontrivial finite-cost branch. The source does not explicitly impose that continuity, so this is an obstruction to the stated continuous-interpolation specialization, not an unconditional refutation of the owner theorem. The lexicographic and finite-gap alternatives remain available.

### Proof

The proposed inequality bounds every interpolated cost by $U=\max\{V(\gamma(0)),V(\gamma(1))\}<\infty$. By W4-P1, $\gamma([0,1])$ lies in the finite set $F_{\lfloor U/\alpha\rfloor}$. A continuous image of the connected interval is connected. A finite Hausdorff subspace is discrete, so its only connected nonempty subsets are singletons. This forces $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$, a contradiction. Strict convexity is stronger than the rejected non-strict inequality. ∎

No claim is made about an undefined, discontinuous notion of interpolation, a relaxed real-valued description surrogate, or a convexified randomized cost that replaces the owner's exact deterministic-code envelope. Those are different mathematical data. An affine mixture of finite outcome laws is continuous, so that standard interpretation is covered directly.

## 6. Fresh exhaustive dyadic sampler certificate

This section supplies a nonempty exact source family and a terminating checker. All choices below are mathematical source data, independent of observed physical constants.

### 6.1 Source language, coordinates and all admitted responses

For every $n\ge 0$ and every integer $0\le k\le 2^n$, use the word

$$
s(n,k)=1^n 0\, \mathrm{bin}_{n+1}(k).
$$

The first zero fixes $n$, then exactly $n+1$ payload bits are read. Thus the word length is $2n+2$, parsing is total on every finite input string, and no admitted word is a prefix of another: distinct $n$ first differ before either header ends, while equal $n$ have equal total length. The only admission test is the integer bound $k\le 2^n$.

The protocol category has the binary readout $P$, a ternary split refinement $Q$, and the one-outcome discard protocol $*$. There are protocol arrows $Q\to P$, $*\to Q$ and their composite $*\to P$. Contravariantly, the fixed response maps are the splitting kernel $T$ from binary to ternary outcomes and the two discard kernels, with

$$
T(0)=\delta_a,\qquad T(1)=(\delta_b+\delta_c)/2.
$$

The response is

$$
r(n,k)(P)=(1-p,p),\qquad r(n,k)(Q)=(1-p,p/2,p/2),\qquad r(n,k)(*)=(1),
$$

where $p=k/2^n$. Naturality is the equality $T\,r(P)=r(Q)$ and the normalization of both laws. Any natural isomorphism in finite probability spaces is an outcome permutation. A compatible pair $\sigma_P,\sigma_Q$ satisfies $\sigma_Q T=T\sigma_P$. Since the two columns of $T$ have support cardinalities one and two, $\sigma_{P}$ cannot interchange them. Thus $\sigma_{P}$ is the identity, $\sigma_{Q}$ fixes $a$ and may interchange $b,c$. This last permutation fixes every displayed $Q$-law, so natural-isomorphism classes are exactly the rational $p$, without any extra label-preservation axiom. The response closure is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$.

A stochastic finite-state realization draws $n$ independent uniform source bits, regards their concatenation as $R\in\{0,\dots,2^n-1\}$, and returns $Y=1$ iff $R<k$. Counting gives exactly $k$ successes, hence $\Pr(Y=1)=k/2^n$. An additional independent fair bit $Z$ implements the split protocol: output $a$ when $Y=0$, and output $b$ or $c$ according to $Z$ when $Y=1$. This gives the full ternary law above. The $n=0$ branch has one sample value $R=0$ and yields the deterministic binary responses $k=0$ or $k=1$ (the split response is still generated by its extra fair bit when $k=1$). The semantic decoder maps a code to this whole exact pair of $P$/$Q$ response laws and hence to one response class. A random sampler execution draws an individual outcome from that law; it does not change the semantic decoding. This is a finite source construction, not a call to a preexisting random program.

If $p$ has reduced dyadic denominator $2^j$, then $D(p)=2j+2$; the endpoints use $j=0$. Equality of fractions proves no code with smaller $n$ exists, and $s(j,k_{\mathrm{red}})$ attains the minimum.

### 6.2 Cost and exact global selector

Take $\alpha=1$, $L_{\mathrm{viol}}=0$ and $L_{\mathrm{regret}}=4p^{2}$, so $V(p)=D(p)+4p^{2}$ on decoded responses and $+\infty$ on uncoded responses. These are registered mathematical loss units; their common conversion is the identity.

Use the admitted incumbent $p=1/2$ with cost 5. W4-P1 gives $N=5$. The total parser examines at most $2^{N+1}-1$ strings at bound $N$ with $O(N)$ bit inspections per string; all fraction and cost comparisons in this source family are exact finite integer arithmetic. Exhaustive parsing of all 63 strings of length $\le 5$ admits exactly five codewords and exactly three response classes:

- $p=0$: $D=2$, $V=2$;
- $p=1/2$: $D=4$, $V=5$;
- $p=1$: $D=2$, $V=6$.

(The five words are $s(0,0)$, $s(0,1)$, $s(1,0)$, $s(1,1)$, $s(1,2)$.)

Every other class has reduced denominator at least 4 and $D\ge 6$, hence $V\ge 6>5$. Therefore $p=0$ is the unique global selector, and its exact gap is 3, attained by $p=1/2$. W4-P1's bound is $\min\{3,6-2\}=3$. A perturbation bounded by $\varepsilon<3/2$ preserves the unique selection on the same response domain.

With $L_{\mathrm{regret}}=0$ instead, exactly $p=0$ and $p=1$ minimize at cost 2, and the next response $p=1/2$ costs 4. This realizes finite degeneracy without pretending that an arbitrary two-point expansion satisfies all PU physical axioms.

### 6.3 Exact nonstationary completion and cost divergence

The rational response $p_*=1/3$ is in the closure but has no admitted exact dyadic code. For denominator $2^n$,

$$
\lvert 1/3-k/2^n\rvert=\lvert 2^n-3k\rvert/(3\cdot 2^n)\ge 1/(3\cdot 2^n),
$$

because 3 never divides $2^n$. Choosing the nearest integer $k$ to $2^n/3$ attains equality: $2^n$ is 1 or 2 modulo 3. For $n\ge 1$ that nearest numerator is odd, so its shortest code length is exactly $2n+2$. Hence along the best $n$-bit sampler approximants

$$
\varepsilon_n=1/(3\cdot 2^n),\qquad D_n=2n+2=2 \log_2(1/(3\varepsilon_n))+2.
$$

The responses converge in total variation to $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/3)$, but their complete description cost diverges. More generally any approximation with error $\varepsilon<1/(3\cdot 2^n)$ needs reduced denominator exponent greater than $n$. This is an exact all-precision lower bound, not a numerical grid observation.

### 6.4 Complete source, accounting, coordinate and clock maps

The fresh source DAG is:

syntax $(n,k)$ → finite uniform-bit carrier → threshold instrument → response $p$ → canonical quotient $j,k_{\mathrm{red}}$ → cost terms → exhaustive selector.

The random primitives are the $n$-bit source and the one-bit split source, with their explicit joint uniform law. The loss coefficient 4, $\alpha=1$, protocol alphabet, splitting kernel, code grammar and comparator are primitive registered inputs. The quotient normalization derives $j,k_{\mathrm{red}}$ from $p$ and never changes its marked outcome law. There is no empirical input leaf. Source ownership is separated as follows:

- grammar/parser owner: admitted descriptions and bit lengths;
- sampler owner: the joint uniform input law, threshold transition and split-bit refinement;
- protocol owner: response labels, splitting/discard maps and verification readout;
- cost owner: the already registered $\alpha$ and loss polynomial;
- selector owner: finite comparison and the proved outside-census inequality.

No statistical independence between derived cost and response is asserted; both descend from the same $p$. The recomposition map is exactly $V=\alpha D+0+4p^{2}$, with each summand appearing once. In particular raw redundant code length is not added again after minimizing to $D$.

For an explicit common finite execution schedule, use logical ticks $a=0,\dots,n+3$: initialize at 0; append one bit at ticks $1,\dots,n$; evaluate the threshold at $n+1$; draw the split bit and form $Q$ at $n+2$; emit/read the requested $P$ or $Q$ outcome and discard the working register at $n+3$. The state at tick $a\le n$ is $(n,k,a,R_a)$, with $R_{a+1}=2R_a+b_{a+1}$. The threshold equation and response formula above prove schedule-independent readout after the last bit. A unit conversion $t=t_0+a\tau$ would require an independently supplied physical $\tau>0$; none is inferred. No reset heat, gravitational source, biological clock or cosmic continuation is silently supplied by this logical schedule.

<a id="corollary-p61b8b-finite-response-representation-and-realization-boundary"></a>**Corollary P.6.1b.8b (Finite-Response Representation and Realization Boundary).** At each finite resolution, every PPI-admissible invariant has a response-presheaf image under
$$
\mathsf{Inv}_{\mathrm{PPI}}/{\sim_{\mathrm{op}}}
\hookrightarrow
[\mathsf P_{\mathrm{PU}}^{op},\mathsf{Prob}_{\mathrm{fin}}].
\tag{P.6.1b.8}
$$
The compact object closure of Theorem P.6.1b.8a may also contain formal limiting response objects. Such an object represents physical PPI content only if it lies in the essential image of the PPI representation, its required natural transformations are realized by admissible physical transformations, and it has a globally finite-cost representative. Response-null surplus is removed by Corollary P.6.1b.8. Equal-cost distinct quotient points are recorded as branch degeneracy; their number is finite only when the relevant quotient or minimizer set is finite or a finite-degeneracy certificate is supplied.

*Proof.* Theorem P.6.1b.3 gives the fully faithful embedding on the PPI-admissible domain. Operative Theorem P.6.1b.8a constructs a compact Hausdorff quotient of response objects, but object closure alone constructs neither all natural-transformation morphisms nor a physical realizing invariant. The essential-image, morphism-realization, and globally finite-cost hypotheses supply those three additional requirements. Corollary P.6.1b.8 removes response-null representatives. Operative Theorem P.6.1b.7 supplies scalar uniqueness only on its scalar strict-convexity branch and sequential uniqueness only on its lexicographic branch; without the relevant strictness condition, equal-cost quotient points remain a branch degeneracy. Compactness alone does not make that set finite. ∎

<a id="remark-p61b8e-finite-state-representations-of-an-infinite-carrier"></a>**Remark P.6.1b.8e (Finite State Representations of an Infinite Carrier).** Finite protocol and outcome sets in Theorem P.6.1b.8a coexist with a compact response space that can have infinitely many points: the laws of one binary protocol already form $\Delta(\{0,1\})\cong[0,1]$. Three useful finite representations of a state space $K$ with update $F:K\to K$ retain different data.

1. An exact finite quotient specifies a finite partition with quotient map $q$ satisfying
   $$
   q(x)=q(y)\ \Longrightarrow\ q(Fx)=q(Fy).
   $$
   Theorem K.10.25b then gives a deterministic descended update and its exact cell itineraries.
2. A finite invariant subset specifies $S\subseteq K$ with $|S|<\infty$ and $F(S)\subseteq S$. The bounded description-length sublevels of Theorem P.6.1b.8a are finite; using one as a state carrier additionally requires that the update preserve it.
3. A finite-horizon approximation on compact metric $K$ with continuous $F$ specifies its encoder, decoder, horizon $n$ and error $\varepsilon$. When every decoded history approximates the corresponding true history within $\varepsilon$ in the maximum history metric, its fixed-width binary budget satisfies
   $$
   B_n\ge\left\lceil\log_2s_n(K,2\varepsilon)\right\rceil
   $$
   by Theorem K.10.25a, where $s_n(K,2\varepsilon)$ is the maximum size of a set of histories pairwise more than $2\varepsilon$ apart.

Compactness alone does not make the response carrier finite or prove that an update preserves a chosen code sublevel. At a resolution where the separation entropy is positive, Theorem K.10.25b excludes exact deterministic descent to a finite partition whose cells have diameter at most $2\varepsilon$, and Theorem K.10.25a excludes a fixed tracking budget valid for every horizon. An approximation retains its declared horizon and error when used downstream.

<a id="theorem-p61b8c-affine-response-observable-duality"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8c (Affine Response-Observable Duality).** Fix a finite protocol budget $B$ and a sector $S$. Let $\mathsf P_B$ be the retained finite protocol family and let
$$
K_B(S)
=
\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\{R_B(q):q\in Q_B(S)\}
\subseteq
\prod_{P\in\mathsf P_B}\Delta(\Omega_P)
\tag{P.6.1b.9}
$$
be the finite response body after the PPI quotient. A retained real observable at budget $B$ is a continuous affine functional
$$
O:K_B(S)\longrightarrow\mathbb R
\tag{P.6.1b.10}
$$
that is invariant under response-null identifications. Equivalently, it is the restriction to $K_B(S)$ of a finite affine combination of retained protocol outcome-coordinate evaluations satisfying the naturality equalities of the protocol category.

Let $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_B/\mathcal N_B$ on a finite quantum branch. Restriction sends every effect $0\le E\le I$ in $\mathcal A$ to a positive normalized affine observable on the retained states. This restriction is injective when the retained states separate $\mathcal A$. It is surjective onto all positive normalized affine observables under the additional full-state hypothesis
$$
K_B(S)\cong\mathsf S(\mathcal A),
$$
where $\mathsf S(\mathcal A)$ is the complete state space of $\mathcal A$. Under that hypothesis, effects are precisely the affine functions $O:\mathsf S(\mathcal A)\to[0,1]$, and bounded real affine observables are precisely evaluations of self-adjoint elements. For a proper separating retained subset, the represented observables are exactly those affine functions lying in the image of the effect-restriction map; separation alone does not imply that every bounded affine function lies in this image.

If $S$ has an accepted strict certificate with selected quotient representative $q_S^*$, then every retained observable has the unique certified branch value
$$
O_{\mathrm{phys}}
=
O(R_B(q_S^*)).
\tag{P.6.1b.11}
$$

*Proof.* The response body lies in a finite-dimensional real affine space. Choose an affine basis of its affine hull. The value of an affine observable on that basis determines an affine extension to the hull, and the coordinate evaluations of the finite product span the affine dual of the hull. Imposing the finite naturality equalities restricts this dual to natural affine functionals. Response-null identifications are precisely the common kernel of the retained coordinate evaluations, so the functional descends to the quotient exactly when it is constant on each response-null class.

Put $\mathcal A=\mathcal A_B/\mathcal N_B$. If $E$ is an effect and $\rho\in\mathsf S(\mathcal A)$, positivity of $\rho$ gives
$$
0\le\rho(E)\le\rho(I)=1,
$$
so $E$ defines an affine function into $[0,1]$. Conversely, let $O:\mathsf S(\mathcal A)\to[0,1]$ be affine. For every nonzero positive functional $\phi$ on $\mathcal A$, define
$$
\widetilde O(\phi)
=
\phi(I)O\!\left(\frac{\phi}{\phi(I)}\right),
$$
and set $\widetilde O(0)=0$. Affineness of $O$ gives, for positive $\phi$ and $\psi$,
$$
\widetilde O(\phi+\psi)
=
\widetilde O(\phi)+\widetilde O(\psi),
$$
and positive homogeneity is immediate. Extending by differences defines a real linear functional on the Hermitian dual of $\mathcal A$. Finite dimensionality and the trace pairing therefore give a unique $E=E^*\in\mathcal A$ such that
$$
O(\rho)=\rho(E)
\qquad
(\rho\in\mathsf S(\mathcal A)).
$$
If $E$ had an eigenvalue below $0$ or above $1$, a vector state supported on the corresponding eigenspace would make $\rho(E)$ lie outside $[0,1]$. Hence $0\le E\le I$. States separate self-adjoint elements, so the representative is unique. Scaling and translating a bounded real affine function reduces it to the $[0,1]$ case, proving the self-adjoint representation. Restriction to a proper retained subset preserves injectivity when that subset separates $\mathcal A$, but the construction of $\widetilde O$ requires values on the full state space and therefore supplies no surjectivity claim for a proper subset. Finally, evaluation of a function at the selected point $R_B(q_S^*)$ is single-valued, proving (P.6.1b.11). ∎

<a id="theorem-p61b8f-shared-task-sufficient-records"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8f (Shared-Task Sufficient Records).** Fix a finite supported source law $p(x)$, a finite task set $\mathcal U$, positive weights $w_u$ summing to one, and finite outcome channels $T_u(y\mid x)$. A shared record is encoded before the independent task choice, with joint law
$$
p(x,m,u,y)=p(x)e(m\mid x)w_uT_u(y\mid x).
$$
Outcome alphabets may depend on $u$; $(u,y)$ is a tagged pair. Define $Z_*=z_*(X)$ by equality of every retained response row,
$$
z_*(x)=z_*(x')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
T_u(\cdot\mid x)=T_u(\cdot\mid x')\quad\text{for every }u,
$$
and let $Z_u$ be the corresponding quotient for task $u$ alone. With natural logarithms, write
$$
\Delta_u=I_u(X;Y\mid M),\qquad \Delta_w=\sum_u w_u\Delta_u.
$$
Here $I_u$ uses the law $p(x)e(m\mid x)T_u(y\mid x)$. Then
$$
\Delta_w=I(X;U,Y\mid M)=I(X;Y\mid M,U)
=\sum_{x,m,u}p(x)e(m\mid x)w_u
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(T_u(\cdot\mid x)\Vert p_u(\cdot\mid m)\right).
$$
Thus $\Delta_w=0$ exactly when every supported record label receives inputs from only one $Z_*$ class, equivalently $H(Z_*\mid M)=0$. Over all such lossless shared records,
$$
\min H(M)=\min I(X;M)=H(Z_*),\qquad
\min|\operatorname{supp}M|=|\operatorname{supp}Z_*|.
$$
If the task is instead revealed before encoding and retained as side information, the minimum conditional record entropy is $\sum_u w_uH(Z_u)$. The extra minimum entropy required by pre-task encoding is
$$
\mathcal P_w=H(Z_*)-\sum_u w_uH(Z_u)
=\sum_u w_uH(Z_*\mid Z_u)\ge0.
$$
It vanishes exactly when every positive-weight $Z_u$ determines $Z_*$ almost surely. Task-aware labels can be reused, giving minimum common label count $\max_u|\operatorname{supp}Z_u|$.

*Proof.* Independence gives $I(X;U\mid M)=0$. The chain rule and conditioning on $U$ give the first two equalities for $\Delta_w$; conditional independence of $M,Y$ given $X,U$ gives its KL expansion. Every summand is nonnegative. Their vanishing means that all rows entering any record label equal its posterior row for every positive-weight task, precisely recoverability of $Z_*$. If $Z_*$ is determined by $M$, then $H(M)\ge H(Z_*)$ and $I(X;M)\ge I(Z_*;M)=H(Z_*)$. A decoder onto every supported class requires at least that many labels. The choice $M=Z_*$ attains all three minima. Apply the same argument separately in every task branch to obtain $H(Z_u)$ and reuse its labels. Each $Z_u$ is a function of $Z_*$, so $H(Z_*)-H(Z_u)=H(Z_*\mid Z_u)$; positivity of the weights gives the equality criterion. ∎

This is a storage and statistical-sufficiency result for the specified source and task support. For two independent fair bits with tasks requesting either bit, each task needs one bit, while the shared record needs both: $\mathcal P_w=\ln2$. The tagged outcome represents the realized task; it requires no joint law of counterfactual outcomes. A source-dependent task choice carries its own information and obeys a different joint law.

On Theorem P.6.1b.8a's shared-arrow branch, equality of all fixed-label rows determines the entire response presheaf. Identifying $Z_*$ with the operational quotient additionally uses rigid retained labels or a registered protocol-compatible gauge fixing for which row equality is equivalent to natural isomorphism. When arrow maps vary between presentations, their conditioning and composition responses belong among the retained probes. Physical realization of the quotient and its transformations remains governed by Corollary P.6.1b.8b.

<a id="theorem-p61b8g-finite-response-loss-certificates"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8g (Finite Response-Loss Certificates).** On the datum of Theorem P.6.1b.8f, the following quantitative conclusions hold.

1. Keep the source law, encoder and channels fixed. For another task distribution $v$ supported on $w$, set $\kappa=\max_u(v_u/w_u)$. Then $\Delta_v\le\kappa\Delta_w$. For every decision problem with losses in $[0,1]$, its optimal Bayes risks satisfy
   $$
   0\le B_u(M)-B_u(X)\le\sqrt{\Delta_u/2}
   \le\sqrt{\Delta_w/(2w_u)}.
   $$

2. Suppose the encoder is deterministic, $M=g(X)$. If it merges supported inputs $x,x'$ of probabilities $a,b$, then
   $$
   \Delta_w\ge\frac{2ab}{a+b}\sum_u w_u
   \operatorname{TV}\!\left(T_u(\cdot\mid x),T_u(\cdot\mid x')\right)^2.
   $$
   If $Z_*$ has at least two supported classes, define
   $$
   p_{\min}=\min_xp(x)>0,\qquad
   \delta_w^2=\min_{z\ne z'}\sum_u w_u
   \operatorname{TV}\!\left(T_u(\cdot\mid z),T_u(\cdot\mid z')\right)^2>0.
   $$
   Every deterministic encoder failing to determine $Z_*$ obeys $\Delta_w\ge p_{\min}\delta_w^2$. Every same-record pair also satisfies
   $$
   \operatorname{TV}\!\left(T_u(\cdot\mid x),T_u(\cdot\mid x')\right)
   \le\sqrt{\Delta_w/(p_{\min}w_u)}.
   $$

3. On a fixed admissible branch with complete commensurate objective $V(e)=a\Delta_w(e)+C(e)$, $a>0$, suppose $C(e)\ge C_{\min}$ and an admissible sufficient comparator has complete cost $C_0<\infty$. Every $\eta$-near-minimizer satisfies
   $$
   \Delta_w(e)\le\frac{\eta+C_0-C_{\min}}{a}.
   $$
   If the sharper comparison $C(e_0)-C(e)\le b$ is supplied, replace $C_0-C_{\min}$ by $b$.

*Proof.* For part 1, the within-task laws are unchanged, so $\Delta_v=\sum_uv_u\Delta_u\le\kappa\Delta_w$. The optimal risk as a function of the outcome law is concave and 1-Lipschitz in total variation. Comparing each response row to the posterior row at $M$, then using Pinsker's inequality and Jensen's inequality, bounds the risk difference by $\sqrt{\Delta_u/2}$. Data processing gives its nonnegativity.

For part 2, let $Q_u$ be the posterior row at the merged record. The two inputs contribute at least $w_u[aD(P_u\Vert Q_u)+bD(P'_u\Vert Q_u)]$. Pinsker bounds this below by $2w_u(at^2+bs^2)$, where $t=\operatorname{TV}(P_u,Q_u)$, $s=\operatorname{TV}(P'_u,Q_u)$ and $t+s\ge d=\operatorname{TV}(P_u,P'_u)$. Minimization gives $at^2+bs^2\ge ab d^2/(a+b)$. Sum over tasks. Since $a,b\ge p_{\min}$, $2ab/(a+b)\ge p_{\min}$; any failure of quotient recovery merges two different classes, proving the threshold and same-record bounds. For part 3, $\inf V\le V(e_0)=C_0$ gives $a\Delta_w(e)+C(e)\le C_0+\eta$; rearrange. ∎

The deterministic restriction supplies the positive merge threshold. A stochastic encoder that emits $Z_*$ with probability $1-\epsilon$ and an independent erasure symbol otherwise has $\Delta_w=\epsilon I(X;Y\mid U)$ and $H(Z_*\mid M)=\epsilon H(Z_*)$: arbitrarily small positive loss permits incomplete recovery. Task-mixture transfer uses the same source and channels, and its factor grows when a deployment task had small training weight. The comparator term in part 3 records the complete cost of preserving predictive information.

### P.6.1c Primitive-Equivalence Normal Form

<a id="theorem-p61b8h"></a>

<a id="theorem-p61b8h-two-trial-identification-of-a-finite-predictive-service"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8h (Two-Trial Identification of a Finite Predictive Service).** Consider the binary predictive service with a fair initial tracked bit $B_1$, a fair independent setting $S_i$ and a fresh independent membership bit $M_i$ of probability $p\in(0,1/4)$. On each of two trials the fixed processor commits forecast $F_i$ before the membership result, updates the tracked bit to $Y_i=B_i\oplus(S_i\lor M_i)$, and records $E_i=F_i\oplus Y_i$. Thus $B_2=Y_1$. Fix a common input-dependent forecast kernel $x_{bs}=\Pr(F_i=1\mid B_i=b,S_i=s)$, using independent fresh selector randomness on the two trials. The retained labelled two-trial law of $(F_1,E_1,F_2,E_2)$ identifies $p$ and the whole kernel. For two such laws at the same $p$ their total variation distance $d$ gives $\|x-\tilde x\|_\infty\le 4d/(1-p)$. At potentially different $p,\tilde p$ it gives $|p-\tilde p|\le2d$ and $\|x-\tilde x\|_\infty\le8d$.

On the service with fixed additive resource entries for forecast workload and lost correctness reward, plus common initialized stock and maintained support, there are two finite dyadic kernels with identical one-trial $(F,E)$ laws and identical expected resource vectors. Their two-trial laws are distinct and neither policy minimizes the declared resource objective.

*Proof.* The output record recovers $Y_i=F_i\oplus E_i$. The tracked state stays fair since the update XORs it with independent noise. The probability of the observed transition $Y_2\ne Y_1$ is $(1+p)/2$. Put $w_{by}=\Pr(Y_1=b,F_2=1,Y_2=y)$. All these event probabilities are read from the full normalized two-trial law. Independence and $B_2=Y_1$ give
$$
4w_{00}=(1-p)x_{00},\qquad 4w_{01}=p x_{00}+x_{01},\qquad
4w_{11}=(1-p)x_{10},\qquad 4w_{10}=p x_{10}+x_{11}.
\tag{P.6.1b.8h.1}
$$
The first and third equations recover $x_{00},x_{10}$, and substitution recovers $x_{01},x_{11}$. Under a change in the retained law, each $w_{by}$ changes by at most $d$. The transition probability yields $|p-\tilde p|\le2d$. At fixed $p$ the first and third equations give errors at most $4d/(1-p)$. The other two errors are bounded by $4d+4pd/(1-p)=4d/(1-p)$. With variable $p$, use $0\le\tilde x_{bs}\le1$. The first and third errors are at most $(4d+|p-\tilde p|)/(1-p)$, and the second and fourth are bounded by the same expression after substitution. Since $p<1/4$, this is at most $8d$.

For one trial the joint law of $(F,E)$ is equivalent to the law of $(F,Y)$. In input order $(00,01,10,11)$ take
$$
x^A=(0,1,3/4,1/4),\qquad x^B=(1/8,7/8,7/8,1/8).
$$
They can be implemented by one common eight-valued fair selector per trial and a reversible controlled XOR into the forecast bit. For $A$ two selectors run $F=S$ and six run $F=B\oplus S$. For $B$ one selector runs each constant policy and six run $F=B\oplus S$. Keep the selector, settings, source records and both verification outcomes. All initial selector resources are common to the pair and to the XOR comparator. The candidate-specific lookup is a control in the same padded processor. The equality of resources below concerns the stipulated expected workload and reward accounts with common stock and support.

For both kernels $\Pr(F=1)=1/2$, and
$$
4\Pr(F=1,Y=1)=p x_{00}+x_{01}+(1-p)x_{10}=(7-3p)/4.
$$
Since $Y$ is fair, these two moments fix the entire one-trial $(F,E)$ law. In particular $\Pr(E=1)=1/8+3p/8$, so the workload and lost reward match on both trials. At two trials the probability $w_{00}$ differs by $(1-p)/32$. The one-trial law of $(B,S,F,Y,E)$ has distance $1/8$, since each conditional forecast law differs by $1/8$ and the conditional source law is common. If $r>0$ is the common calibrated resource rate, the forecast workload coefficient is $r(9+\log_2(5/4))$, and the mismatch reward coefficient is $100r$, the XOR policy has the same fair forecast and risk $p/2$. Each candidate then costs $\tfrac{25}{2}r(1-p)>0$ more than the admitted XOR policy. ∎

<a id="theorem-p61b8i"></a>

<a id="theorem-p61b8i-finite-physical-identification-with-opposed-strict-selectors"></a>**Theorem P.6.1b.8i (Finite Physical Identification with Opposed Strict Selectors).** Retain the two-trial binary predictive service of Theorem P.6.1b.8h at any fixed dyadic $0<p<1/4$. A fixed two-program physical candidate domain has an exact finite response realization, a separating empirical-input map, and a complete shortest-code ledger. A single symmetric positive tariff gives two distinct global minimizers on this finite domain. Two other positive tariffs on the same measured resources give opposed unique minimizers with strict gaps. The response records, physical cost inputs and fixed code are specified before a candidate is selected.

*Admissible finite programs.* Prepare the same fair tracked bit, setting and eight-word fair forecast selector of Theorem P.6.1b.8h. Generate each membership result from a fresh ready dyadic sampler of probability $p$. The selector words are finite binary registers and all controllers can be implemented by reversible copying into fresh targets. Use an immutable one-bit program selector with exactly the two compiled forecast tables
$$
x^{(0)}=(0,1,3/4,1/4),\qquad
x^{(1)}=(1/8,7/8,7/8,1/8).
$$
Each program implements the full two-trial service with fresh independent randomness on the second trial and the actual tracked update $B_2=F_1\oplus E_1$.
