The formal molecular input consists of the finite levels, their locations and the explicitly stated spin-coupling and reaction operators. Couplings are not inferred from the abstract Golay array.

### 2. Gates with a physical fuel and action record

Let $U$ be any of the involutive gates used here: CNOT, controlled-$X$, or an identity transfer used only when specified. A fresh fuel mode $F$ is in $|1\rangle$ and a fresh spent-energy mode $R$ in $|0\rangle$, with

$$
H_{\mathrm{FR}} = \Delta (n_F + n_R), \qquad \Delta > 0.
$$

On these modes and the degenerate memory, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_U = {}&|01\rangle\langle 10| \otimes U + |10\rangle\langle 01| \otimes U^{*} \\
&+ (|00\rangle\langle 00| + |11\rangle\langle 11|) \otimes I.
\end{aligned}
$$

$S_{U}$ is a Hermitian unitary, commutes with $H_{\mathrm{FR}}$, and exchanges one excitation from fuel to the retained spent-energy bank while implementing U. The actual controlled interaction is

$$
H_U = (\pi\hbar/(2t_g))(I - S_U).
$$

It commutes with $H_{\mathrm{FR}}$ and satisfies $\exp(-iH_Ut_g/\hbar)=S_U$. Consequently

$$
|1,0\rangle \otimes \psi \to |0,1\rangle \otimes U\psi.
$$

Each fueled gate transfers exactly $\Delta$ of energy to its own spent mode, uses one distinct fuel molecule, takes $t_{g}$, and has interaction norm-action $\pi\hbar$. On an empty pair $|0,0\rangle$ the same pulse is identity and transfers no energy. There is no assertion that this is a fundamental minimal gate cost. It is the exact cost of the registered mechanochemical implementation. The closed gate conserves total energy; the spent bank is not called heat or erased. The declared controls cannot reclaim its excitations during this cycle. Any later recycling would be a separately charged operation.

A finite, externally clocked controller applies this finite Hamiltonian schedule. Its program is one classical bit selecting two finite ROM words; there is no continuously programmable finite quantum register. The clock unit and allowed pulse amplitudes are registered branch inputs. The measured gate action, time and fuel transfer are retained in the response table. Clock/pulse costs are the same per scheduled gate and included in this gate implementation; no autonomous or energetically free clock theorem is claimed. Switching $H_{U}$ on supplies its initial interaction energy and switching it off recovers the same expectation, because that expectation is constant during its pulse. The ideal cyclic switch therefore has zero net work but a retained peak interaction-energy bound $\pi\hbar/t_g$ and the stated nonzero time/action budget. This is the admitted externally controlled branch; an irreversible autonomous clock would add its actual costs. Native enzyme coupling is enabled only in the exposure stage. Gate intervals have the declared Hamiltonians and the independent cell-death process, with no additional unlisted gate-noise channel.

All pure blank sites and fuel/spent pairs are supplied as part of the finite input resource bank. The model does not reset an unknown state. Syndrome outcomes and all discarded environments are retained, so no Landauer heat is silently assigned to parity bits or omitted by erasing a record. Installed memory, supplied blank states, ligand/environment preparations, daughter material and consumed fuel are separately counted. Only the last two and elapsed survival time affect the type ordering on this equal-hardware branch.

The generator $G=[I\mid A]$ is built from the marked cyclic Golay polynomial and row-reduced over $F_{2}$ from the marked polynomial and binary row reduction. #### 4.1 Asymmetric relaxation on a marked site

The exchange conserves the two-spin excitation energy when both have the same gap. This is a separate energetic site variant, with its bath preparation and any gate-frame energy conversion explicitly registered; the degenerate-gate cost numbers of §3 are not exported to it.

Golay syndrome recovery corrects whether site 0 flipped. On the encoded logical space its no-flip Kraus branches are diagonal in logical bit $m_{0}$ and its flip branches are restored by $X_{0}$. ### 5. Fuel loading and actual catalytic reproduction

#### 5.1 Finite fuel law

At cycle entry, the number $L$ of available gate-fuel excitations has support $0,\dots,L_{\max}$. It is prepared by the finite birth-death loading chain with upward rate $u$ for $L<L_{\max}$ and downward rate $v$ for $L>0$. With $r=u/v\in(0,1)$, detailed balance gives the unique stationary distribution

$$
\pi_l = (1-r) r^{l}/(1 - r^{L_{\max}+1}).
$$

This is a declared stationary preparation, not an assertion that a finite mixing time is exactly stationary. A finite source can prepare this distribution directly in its L register and fuel bank. A finite-time approximate loader has its own measured variation error, which propagates at most linearly to the success probabilities. The preparation cost and loader are common to both types.

The bank state with stock $L$ has its first $L$ fuel modes occupied and all later modes empty. The controller applies the $n_{i}$ prescribed pulses in order. On an empty fuel/spent pair a pulse acts as identity. The final spent bit $R_{n_i}$ is therefore one exactly when every required gate was fueled. The binding jump is gated by this actual completion bit; a cell with $L<n_i$ produces no viable daughter. No uncharged preflight measurement is used. Unused stock and partial computation records are retained. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(n_i) &= \Pr(L \ge n_i) \\
&= (r^{n_i} - r^{L_{\max}+1})/(1 - r^{L_{\max}+1}).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.1}
$$

The count is an actual resource threshold of the registered circuit, not an imposed price proportional to its coding success. Each attempt transfers $\Delta\min(L,n_i)$ to the spent bank, so its unconditional mean transferred energy is $\Delta\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}F(j)$. A completed circuit transfers $n_i\Delta$. Its whole programmed time and norm-action remain $n_it_g$ and $n_i\pi\hbar$, even if empty fuel modes prevent some gates from acting. These partial-failure resource costs are included in the retained raw ledger.

#### 5.2 Receptor chemistry, competing death and a division output

Let M be the isolated ligand pattern and D the decoded receptor-contact pattern. Native steric selectivity is represented by the contact projector

$$
\Pi_{\mathrm{match}} = \sum_m |m\rangle\langle m|_M \otimes |m\rangle\langle m|_D.
$$

The unbound receptor U binds the matching ligand at rate $k_{b}$ and no other ligand in this ideal-selectivity branch. A bound complex B catalyzes conversion of supplied nutrient/precursor material into two completed daughter aggregates at rate $k_{d}$. The finite Lindblad jump operators are, on the registered reaction states,

$$
\begin{aligned}
J_{\mathrm{bind}} &= \sqrt{k_b}\,|B\rangle\langle U| \otimes \Pi_{\mathrm{match}} \otimes |1\rangle\langle 1|_{R_n}, \\
J_{\mathrm{div}} &= \sqrt{k_d}\,|\mathrm{DaughterPair}\rangle\langle B| \otimes I_{\mathrm{type}},
\end{aligned}
$$

with the ligand and two precursor-token shifts included in the reaction kets. The daughter pair already contains the two faithfully copied type bits, the same molecular architecture and new blank memory/resource interfaces for the next cycle. The parent is consumed; its used registers enter a retained waste state. These are actual reaction maps on the finite carrier, not names assigned to successful decoding afterward.

The precursor stoichiometry and energies are owned separately. In units $E_{\mathrm{chem}}>0$, take parent energy $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$, two precursor tokens each $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$, two daughter assemblies each $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$, and retained waste energy $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$. Both sides of the division transition have energy $3E_{\mathrm{chem}}$. Binding may be taken resonant, or its independently fixed released energy is recorded in a separate bath mode. The chosen resonant branch has no hidden exergonic work credit. Fuel transfer $\Delta$, precursor energy $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$ and parity redundancy are different ledger coordinates.

An independent destructive reaction at rate $\delta$ kills the cell in either U or B, and during all preceding exposure/control stages. Its jump marks a retained nonviable state and produces no viable offspring. The viability flag is a separate molecular register: the external control program still finishes its scheduled pulses on the material, so loss of viability does not silently reduce the gate/fuel accounting. The binding and division jumps require the live flag. Successfully produced daughter pairs enter quiescent sealed compartments until the next registered generation boundary. Death acts on active parents; quiescent daughters have no active-parent hazard. All of these allowed reactions are exhaustive branch data. No undocumented viability filter or migration term is applied.

Before assay, active time is $\tau_i=T+n_it_g$. Conditional on correct contact, the density of a completed division at assay time $s$ is, for $k_b=k_d=k$,

$$
k^{2} s \exp[-(k+\delta)s].
$$

Indeed the binding time has density k exp[-(k+delta)t], and, after binding, successful division after delay s-t has density k exp[-(k+delta)(s-t)]. Integrating t from 0 to s gives the expression. Over assay window a,

$$
B_\delta(a) = k^{2}[1 - \exp(-(k+\delta)a)(1 + (k+\delta)a)]/(k+\delta)^{2}.
\tag{5.2}
$$

For unequal positive rates, the same convolution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^a k_b k_d [\exp(-(k_b+\delta)s) - \exp(-(k_d+\delta)s)] \\
&/(k_d - k_b)\, ds,
\end{aligned}
$$

with (5.2) its continuous equal-rate limit. The binding/commitment counters distinguish wrong receptor, fuel failure, pre-assay death, bound-but-uncommitted, assay death, and completed division. An assay deadline with no completed division produces no viable offspring. Thus neither death nor unsuccessful binding is removed by conditioning.

### 6. Fitness and predictive-score bridge derived from the cycle

The task $T_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is one-cycle reproduction of the sampled ligand-contact response. The evaluation window is the common bound $T+n_{\max}t_g+a$, and $q_{\mathrm{gen}}$ assigns one unit to each produced daughter aggregate whose parent receptor correctly matched that ligand. The biochemical selectivity theorem above implies that every counted daughter is correct and that no wrong response can produce a counted daughter. Conversely every completed matching division produces exactly two such daughters. Therefore the physically measured task-quality increment equals the viable-daughter count on this particular task. This is the required bridge; a generic quantum fidelity is not called biological fitness.

Independence of fuel loading, exposure collisions and destructive reactions, together with (5.1)-(5.2), gives the unconditional expected viable-descendant weight

$$
w_i = 2F(n_i) \exp(-\delta\tau_i) P_{c,i} B_\delta(a).
\tag{6.1}
$$

Each factor was derived from its source operator or native reaction law. All admission probabilities are strictly positive for the populated parameters. Define the dimensionless resource vector

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_i &= (-\ln F(n_i), \delta\tau_i, -\ln P_{c,i}, -\ln B_\delta(a)) \\
&\quad \in \mathbb{R}_+^{4}, \\
V_i &= (1,1,1,1) \cdot r_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $w_i=2\exp(-V_i)$ follows algebraically from the derived law, rather than supplying a fitted exponential fitness assumption. For the completed/live hard-report Brier window proved in the predictive-performance analysis below, $PP=1/(3-2P_c)$ and $B(PP)=\ln[(3-1/PP)/2]=\ln P_c$. In P.8.9a.6's notation use $R_{\mathrm{metabolic}}=-\ln F$, $R_{\mathrm{reproductive}}=-\ln B_\delta$, $V_{\mathrm{penalty}}=\delta\tau$, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{fitness}}=1$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}=1$. The benefit is strictly increasing on $1/3<PP\le 1$. A policy with $P_{c}=0$ is a sterile absorbing branch with $w=0$ and is not falsely assigned a finite logarithmic ledger.

The finite D.1f contract has configurations the two physical controllers with their complete declared inputs; protocol family comprising input/contact truth tables, syndrome records, gate/fuel counters, reaction/death outcomes, phase-sensitive channel tests and generation outputs; $K=\mathbb{R}_+^{4}$; resource map $r$ above; and $W=\{(1,1,1,1)\}$. Auxiliary changes are quotiented only when they preserve this entire retained response table, including resource and timing readouts. Thus all four coordinates descend. Fuel/action/time and assay records prevent a response-null control overhead from being compensated by an unrecorded improvement in another coordinate. Static hardware, input preparation and per-generation precursor stock are equal retained inputs, not erased cost variables.

This supplies a source-derived P10 resource/fitness functional on a complete declared comparison, without claiming a global quantum-circuit-complexity minimum or the more extensive P11 evolutionary mechanisms. For any enlarged finite controller list with actual circuits and the same exposure/assay rules, (6.1) still holds with the actual $n_i,\tau_i$ and $P_{c,i}$. One must count those circuits' resources before minimizing $V_{i}$; maximizing uncharged decoding probability is not the fitness optimization.

Faithful type copying and the finite branching reaction imply $\mathbb{E}[N_i(t+1)|N(t)]=w_iN_i(t)$. Hence $\mathbb{E}N_i(t)=N_i(0)w_i^{t}$ and normalized expected-count shares equal

$$
p_i(t) = p_i(0) \exp(-tV_i) / \sum_j p_j(0) \exp(-tV_j).
$$

They are not the expectation of random realized frequencies. For every finite horizon $H$, the full binary tree contains $N(0)(2^{H}-1)$ parent-cycle slots and $2N(0)(2^{H}-1)$ newly produced daughter-assembly slots. Supply one complete environment/blank/input bank and $L_{\max}$ fuel modes per parent-cycle slot, together with those daughter assemblies. The maximal simultaneous active population is $N(0)2^{H}$; that smaller bound is not used for cumulative material consumption. All consumed assemblies and records are retained in the corresponding finite waste banks. The resulting source is finite and realizes the formula for $0\le t\le H$. The familiar $t\to\infty$ selection statement belongs to the consistent family of increasing-$H$ experiments or a separately admitted infinite reservoir; it is not claimed for one finite bank.

For all $0<r<1$, $L_{\max}\ge305$, $\delta\ge 0$ and $t_{g}>0$, with the same burst law and common assay,

is greater than, equal to, or less than 3/4. This is the whole source-specific resource comparison, not one favorable parameter point. A union bound over the two policies gives a finite declared trial budget. Channel tomography, syndrome/fuel counters and contact-conditioned reaction counts distinguish an incorrect noise model from an incorrect reproductive bridge; one scalar aggregate cannot compensate for their disagreement.

### Binding proper-score performance and fitness bridge

### 1. Original definitions actually consumed

Definition 7 (Section 3.3.1) admits a point prediction or predictive distribution and a fixed finite nonnegative proper score, explicitly including Brier. Theorem 8 (Section 3.3.2) defines **window** performance from mean score and allows a registered positive-probability conditional evaluation law. P.8.9a.3 requires a separately proved predictive-quality/descendant bridge. P.8.9a.6 requires a fixed nondecreasing benefit of predictive performance and a complete source-derived ledger; it does not redefine PP to mean decoding accuracy.

The additive score normalization used here is the ordinary dimensionless categorical Brier score, without a factor one-half. The scale anchor is declared before comparing controllers: $\mathrm{PE}_*=1$ maps to $\mathrm{PP}_*=1/2$. Definition 7 therefore gives $k_{\mathrm{PP}}=(1/\mathrm{PP}_*-1)/\mathrm{PE}_*=1$. This is a score calibration, independent of native rates, offspring data, and the comparison's success probabilities.

### 2. Predictive object, task, and exact evaluation window

The fixed task is to preserve the original uniform ligand label $M$ in the 4096-element alphabet through the native exposure and report its value at the decoder output. The predictor's actual physical report is the classical receptor word $D$, represented by the probability vector $q=e_D$. The 12 receptor-contact bits already present in the source hold this report. The initially sampled ligand register holding $M$ remains isolated from the encoder, recovery controller, and decoder until the registered assay; it is the verification outcome, not side information available to the predictor.

For policy i, define the memory calibration window

$$
W_i = \{L \ge n_i \text{ and viability flag remains live through } \tau_i\}.
$$

Its probability is $q_{B,i}=F(n_i)\exp(-\delta\tau_i)>0$ at every populated policy. This is a **completed/live memory-port calibration task**, not the unconditional reproductive interface. The finite physical instruments already record both predicates: final spent-fuel bit and viability flag. The sampling rule is fixed for both policies; its duration and fuel count are the actual declared controller quantities.

The initial ligand, fuel-stock law, native noise processes, and viability-death process are independent source inputs. On $L\ge n_i$, every prescribed gate is executed exactly, and the resulting memory channel is the same native coding channel used to derive $P_{c,i}$. The event of survival through $\tau_i$ concerns only the independently driven viability flag. Hence for every message $m$ and native error $e$,

$$
\Pr(M = m, \mathrm{error} = e \mid W_i) = \Pr(M = m) \Pr(\mathrm{error} = e).
$$

This proves that the conditional decoder success is precisely the previously derived $P_{c,i}$; the window does not select a favorable error realization. Fuel insufficiency and death are not discarded from reproductive outcomes: their unconditional probabilities remain the separate factors in (A.2), and their failure flags remain retained observables. Applying the score to a different unconditional port would define a different PP and would require a different factorization; that alternative is not used here.

### 3. Properness, risk, and performance

For any probability vector q on the same alphabet and outcome m, set

$$
S(q,m) = \sum_x (q_x - 1_{x=m})^{2}.
$$

It is finite and nonnegative. If the true outcome law is p, direct expansion gives

$$
\mathbb{E}_p S(q,M) = \lVert q - p\rVert_2^{2} + 1 - \lVert p\rVert_2^{2}.
$$

Therefore its unique minimizer on the full probability simplex is $q=p$: this is a strictly proper scoring rule, even though the native admissible predictors output only point forecasts. For the actual report $q=e_D$,

$$
S(e_D, M) = 2\, 1_{D \ne M}.
$$

This identity is pointwise and holds for every deterministic or randomized hard decoder, every finite classical channel and every message prior. In the registered window,

$$
\operatorname{mean} \mathrm{PE}_i = \mathbb{E}[S(e_D, M) \mid W_i] = 2(1 - P_{c,i}).
$$

Definition 7/Theorem 8's window quantity is $\mathrm{PP}_i=1/(1+\operatorname{mean}\mathrm{PE}_i)$, which gives (A.1). It is **not** $\mathbb{E}[1/(1+S)\mid W_i]$: for the populated U policy these are respectively $2/3$ and $5/6$.

The populated values are

| Policy | $P_c$ | mean PE | window PP | $B(PP)$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| U | 3/4 | 1/2 | 2/3 | $\ln(3/4)$ |
| G | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |

The formula does not assert that arbitrary posterior proper-score risk determines hard-decision accuracy. For example the posterior laws `(1/2,1/2,0)` and `(2/3,1/6,1/6)` both have Bayes Brier risk 1/2 but have different optimal hard-decision success. The proved map uses the actual point-forecast task, not that broader class.

### 4. Benefit, ledger, and no double counting

On the positive-success domain $0<P_c\le 1$, (A.1) gives $1/3<\mathrm{PP}\le 1$. Its benefit is finite and strictly increasing:

$$
B'(\mathrm{PP}) = 1/[\mathrm{PP}(3\,\mathrm{PP} - 1)] > 0.
$$

Consequently set, exactly as the molecular source of Theorem P.8.9a.5e derives,

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_{\mathrm{metabolic}} &= -\ln F(n_i), \\
R_{\mathrm{reproductive}} &= -\ln B_\delta(a), \\
V_{\mathrm{penalty}} &= \delta\tau_i, \\
\Gamma_{\mathrm{fitness}} &= \lambda_{\mathrm{gen}} = 1, \\
V_{\mathrm{gen}} &= R_{\mathrm{metabolic}} + R_{\mathrm{reproductive}} + V_{\mathrm{penalty}} - B(\mathrm{PP}_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $B(\mathrm{PP}_i)=\ln P_{c,i}$ proves $w_i=2\exp(-V_{\mathrm{gen}})$ from (A.2). Each fuel, viability, coding and assay factor occurs once. In particular $\mathrm{PP}_i$ does not already contain $q_{B,i}$; charging $-\ln F+\delta\tau$ is therefore necessary and is not a second charge for the same failure. The original four-coordinate D.1f resource vector and complete retained response quotient are unchanged. All gate/fuel/clock/material costs remain the original physical observations, rather than being replaced by this dimensionless score.

For $P_c=0$, the policy is sterile with $w=0$ and $\mathrm{PP}=1/3$. It is excluded from P.8.9a.6's finite logarithmic-ledger subset, precisely as already stated in the molecular source. Both populated policies lie in the finite domain. The perfectly decoded finite task has $\mathrm{PP}_G=1$; Definition 7 explicitly permits this endpoint. This construction does not consume an additional theorem whose separate irreducible-error, strict-excitation, or open viability-band antecedents would exclude perfect prediction. P.8.9a.3 and P.8.9a.6 impose no such strict upper-endpoint premise.

### 5. The actual predictive-quality/offspring bridge

Define the bounded score-derived quality of a reported ligand prediction by

$$
Q(e_D, M) = 1 - S(e_D, M)/2 = 1_{D=M}.
$$

For one registered reproductive cycle, sum this quality over the daughters actually produced. If no daughter is produced the sum is zero. The contact-gated binding jump in the source acts only in $D=M$, and all subsequent division jumps preserve these classical registers. Hence every produced daughter is associated with the verified correct report, and the pointwise reproductive quality increment is

$$
\Delta Q_{\mathrm{reproductive}} = Y\, Q(e_D, M) = Y,
$$

where $Y$ is the actual 0-or-2 offspring count. This equality also holds on fuel/death/assay failures, for which $Y=0$. Thus $\mathbb{E}\,\Delta Q_{\mathrm{reproductive}}=w_i$ is derived from the score and the actual selective reaction operator, rather than identifying descendant count with PU quality by definition. The score, alphabet, truth register, contact predicate, assay window and implementation map are frozen across policies. A wrong-contact division channel would invalidate this bridge and remains an observable falsifier.

### Formal input, prediction, covariance and uncertainty extractor

### 1. Separate input and response records

The finite source is defined by the pulse and reaction operators in the molecular-source analysis. This protocol supplies its independently measurable input schema and complete retained prediction table. It is a formal experimental design; no organism data or observed offspring counts were used to select its parameters.

The input record contains: marked site/ligand labels, the two fixed controller words, the initial ligand prior, the two enzyme rates $\gamma_B,\gamma_Z$, exposure $T$, gate duration $t_{g}$, viability-loss rate $\delta$, binding/division rates $k_b,k_d$, assay time $a$, $L_{\max}$, loading ratio $r$, fuel gap $\Delta$, precursor energy $E_{\mathrm{chem}}$, the action unit $\hbar$, and the initial type counts. Every clock quantity carries the same time unit. Energy/action calibrations are carried separately from coding success.

The response record contains: programmed pulse count and completion bit, initial and spent fuel counts, viability flags, the input and decoded contact labels on the completed branch, syndrome bits, the coherent-port channel test probabilities, binding/commitment/death outputs, offspring count and inherited type bits. Incomplete circuits have a retained failure tag; their partial quantum material is outside the recovery port but remains in the waste/resource ledger. The complete source map predicts every retained output rather than fitting a scalar reproduction score.

### 2. Independent finite calibration protocols

1. **Burst enzyme.** Prepare the three marked sites in $|000\rangle$, expose them for $T$, and read the computational bits. The triple-flip frequency is $p_B=(1-\exp(-2\gamma_BT))/2$. This calibrates $\gamma_B=-\ln(1-2p_B)/(2T)$ on $0\le p_B<1/2$, without any encoder or division assay.
2. **Phase enzyme.** Prepare the marked phase site in $|+\rangle$ and the other burst sites in $X$ eigenstates; $X$-burst conjugation is invisible to the $X$ readout, whereas $Z$ changes its sign. The minus probability is $p_{Z}$ and gives the analogous independent rate calibration.
3. **Viability loss.** Read the separate viability register after a known duration $t$, without binding ligand. Its survival probability is $s=\exp(-\delta t)$, giving $\delta=-\ln s/t$.
4. **Binding and commitment.** Supply a known matched receptor with its completion bit set and inhibit commitment by omitting precursor. The probability that binding occurs before the independent viability loss by time $a$ is $h(k_b)=k_b[1-\exp(-(k_b+\delta)a)]/(k_b+\delta)$. Record the first binding event. In a separate supplied bound-state preparation with precursor, the analogous first commitment probability is $h(k_d)$. Each map is strictly increasing from zero to one: its derivative is $\delta[1-\exp(-(k+\delta)a)]/(k+\delta)^{2}+ka\exp(-(k+\delta)a)/(k+\delta)>0$. Thus exact data determine the rate uniquely, and interval data give a unique rate interval by monotone inversion. These protocols use the same native jump operators and owned preparation; no reproduction advantage enters the calibration.
5. **Fuel and units.** Read the finite stock register. Its adjacent stationary masses obey $\pi_1/\pi_0=r$. The time, interaction pulse and energy-gap records fix $T,t_g,a,\hbar,\Delta,E_{\mathrm{chem}}$ in their registered units. Clock and energy spectroscopy are independent input protocols; the finite code has no authority to set these units. The equal hardware and precursor inventories are checked directly.

A finite empirical input consists of raw integer counts for these finite-outcome protocols, their trial totals, the marked clock/energy calibration values and uncertainty intervals, and a declared common experimental identifier. Estimated rates without those raw records are insufficient. A proposed rate calibration outside the admitted positive/survival domain rejects this branch rather than being clipped to improve the output fit.

### 3. Exact joint source law and observable extraction

For every positive parameter point, the encoder/noise/recovery outputs are computed from the actual fixed circuits. On a completed classical $G$ circuit $P_{c,G}=1$ for all rates in the registered $B/Z$ family; on $U$, $P_{c,U}=1-p_B$. The coherent completed-port identity weights are $f_G=1-p_Z$ and $f_U=(1-p_B)(1-p_Z)$, because finite nonnegative Poisson rates give $p_B,p_Z\le 1/2$. The all-CPTP Pauli theorem supplies their corresponding optimum errors. The resource-flagged channel error is the separate formula in the molecular-source analysis §3.1.

The initial stock $L$ has the finite geometric law. Completion equals $\mathbf{1}_{L\ge n_i}$; spent fuel is $\min(L,n_i)$. Pre-assay survival is independent Bernoulli $\exp(-\delta\tau_i)$. Conditional on a completed live circuit, correct contact is the Bernoulli variable given by the actual noise/decoder truth table, independent of fuel and survival. Conditional on a live matching receptor, the assay has four mutually exclusive outputs:

$$
U\ (\text{unbound}), \quad B\ (\text{bound, uncommitted}), \quad D\ (\text{two daughters}), \quad X\ (\text{nonviable}).
$$

For equal rates k,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_U &= \exp(-(k+\delta)a), \\
P_B &= k a \exp(-(k+\delta)a), \\
P_D &= B_\delta(a), \\
P_X &= 1 - P_U - P_B - P_D.
\end{aligned}
$$

For unequal rates, $P_{B}$ is the binding-to-bound convolution and $P_{D}$ the binding-to-commitment convolution in the source proof. All are nonnegative because they are probabilities of the same finite-state absorbing Markov generator. For a wrong-contact or incomplete live cell, binding and division are absent, with $P_U=\exp(-\delta a)$, $P_X=1-P_U$. A pre-assay nonviable cell stays $X$. $D$ produces the counted variable $Y=2$ and all other outcomes $Y=0$. The daughter type is the original type with probability one.

These rules give an explicit finite joint distribution by summing $L=0,\dots,L_{\max}$, the four enzyme parities and the finite survival/reaction states. Template labels remain in the truth-table protocol. General variants use their explicitly supplied finite channel matrices/Kraus operators, not the $B/Z$ formula. This finite joint table is the total prediction functional. Means and covariances of every retained bounded output vector $Z$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}
m(\theta) &= \sum_z P_\theta(z)\, z, \\
\Sigma(\theta) &= \sum_z P_\theta(z)(z - m)(z - m)^{T}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is an exact covariance map, retaining correlations caused by shared fuel, survival and binding. It does not falsely treat those final counters as independent. In particular, with $w_i=\mathbb{E}Y$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(Y) &= 2w_i - w_i^{2}, \\
\operatorname{Cov}(Y, C_{\mathrm{fuel}}) &= w_i[1 - F(n_i)], \\
\operatorname{Cov}(Y, U_{\mathrm{spent}}) &= w_i[n_i - \mathbb{E} \min(L, n_i)].
\end{aligned}
$$

The last identity follows because every division occurs at full completion, hence $YU_{\mathrm{spent}}=n_iY$. For $N$ independent trials, the covariance of the sample mean is $\Sigma/N$. Independent policy trial sets have zero cross-covariance; shared calibration uncertainty is retained separately.

### 4. Finite uncertainty and total falsification rule

For each calibration indicator in $[0,1]$, Hoeffding gives $\Pr(|\hat{p}-p|\ge\epsilon)\le 2\exp(-2N\epsilon^{2})$. For $J$ such indicators, choose their trial budgets so the sum of these bounds is at most $\alpha_{\mathrm{cal}}$. Apply the monotone inversions in §2 and interval clock/energy calibrations to obtain a simultaneous parameter box $\Theta_{\mathrm{cal}}$. If a needed denominator, such as $1-2p$ or $\pi_{0}$, has an interval including zero, report the input as unresolved; do not manufacture a finite rate.

The full prediction set is $\{m(\theta),\Sigma(\theta):\theta\in\Theta_{\mathrm{cal}}\}$, computed by the exact finite law above. Compact positive boxes permit rigorous interval/Taylor bounds and interval subdivision to any requested tolerance. No delta-method approximation is required. Where an approximate Gaussian calibration is separately justified, the linear propagated covariance is $J_m\Sigma_{\mathrm{cal}}J_m^{T}$, with $J_{m}$ the derivative of the same exact forward map; it is explicitly an approximation and does not replace the interval certificate.

For the two offspring means, each Y lies in [0,2]. Thus

$$
\Pr(|\hat{w}_i - w_i| \ge \epsilon) \le 2\exp(-N\epsilon^{2}/2).
$$

At the populated point, the exact source intervals give $w_G-w_U>0.1969$. To resolve each mean within $\epsilon=1/20$ with joint failure probability at most $1/100$, $N=4800$ independent trials per policy suffices, because $4\exp(-4800/800)=4\exp(-6)<1/100$. Calibration error, if present, is added through $\Theta_{\mathrm{cal}}$ and an independently allocated failure budget. The symbolic exact-input branch does not pretend that 4800 trials also calibrate every source parameter.

A total falsification test accepts only if every retained input calibration is in domain, every normalized channel/source probability is valid, every type/clock/fuel overlap is compatible, and the vector of observed output means lies in its simultaneous prediction enclosure. Any wrong-contact committed division directly rejects the ideal-selectivity model. Channel, fuel and reaction residuals are tested separately, so an improved offspring count cannot compensate for a violated quantum-channel or resource record. The formal construction fixes this extractor before outcome data; actual experimental execution is a separate empirical task.

## P.8.9a.5 Conditional Generational-PCE Representation of Normalized Selection

This section proves an equation-level representation on a declared finite-type biological branch. The representation is non-teleological: conditional on the stated biological branch contract, it describes a normalized frequency update and no foresight, intention, or universal evolutionary objective is inferred.

The PU framework supplies a conditional bridge between biological selection and PCE. On a declared generational model whose heritable types carry a generational PCE ledger and whose relative viable-descendant weights are exponential in the negative ledger value, normalized selection is exactly multiplicative PCE reweighting. The result is a non-teleological frequency-update theorem on that branch.

### P.8.9a.5.1 The Evolutionary POP

<a id="definition-p89a3-generational-pop"></a>**Definition P.8.9a.3 (Generational POP).** Fix a biological prediction task $T_{\mathrm{gen}}$, score $q_{\mathrm{gen}}$, evaluation window $W_{\mathrm{gen}}$, and a nonempty admissible class $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{gen}}$ of heritable transition or variation policies.

Fix a registered implementation map
$$
\iota_{\mathrm{gen}}:
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{gen}}
\to
\mathcal S_{\mathrm{phys}}.
$$
For each $\mu\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{gen}}$, let $\mathbb P_{\mu}$ be the declared one-generation outcome law and let $\Delta Q_{\mathrm{reproductive}}$ be an integrable registered PU predictive-quality increment for $(T_{\mathrm{gen}},q_{\mathrm{gen}},W_{\mathrm{gen}})$ under $\mathbb P_{\mu}$. Define the implementation complexity
$$
C_{\mathrm{gen}}(\mu)
:=
C_P\!\left(\iota_{\mathrm{gen}}(\mu)\right).
$$
For a finite available budget $C_{\mathrm{available}}$, define

$$
\operatorname{POP}_{\mathrm{gen}}
=
\sup_{\substack{\mu\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{gen}}\\
C_{\mathrm{gen}}(\mu)\le C_{\mathrm{available}}}}
\mathbb E_{\mu}\!\left[\Delta Q_{\mathrm{reproductive}}\right],
$$

provided the feasible set is nonempty.

The quantity $\Delta Q_{\mathrm{reproductive}}$ is a registered PU predictive-quality increment for the fixed task, score, and window; it is not identified with raw descendant count unless a separate bridge establishes that identification. A maximizing policy exists only when the displayed supremum is attained.

*Interpretation.* Developmental trajectories, behavioral responses, and viable-descendant outcomes may serve as retained response variables only through the fixed task, score, window, and biological-to-PU implementation map. Selection changes heritable-type frequencies according to a separately declared viable-descendant law. Proposition P.8.9a.6 states the additional branch contract required to compare reproductive success with predictive performance.

<a id="proposition-p89a6-conditional-generational-pce-representation-of-fixed-weight-selection"></a>**Proposition P.8.9a.6 (Conditional Generational-PCE Representation of Fixed-Weight Selection).** Let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be a nonempty finite set of heritable types and let $p(0)\in\Delta(\mathcal I)$ be their initial frequency vector. For each $i\in\mathcal I$, define the generational PCE ledger

$$
V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)
=
R_{\mathrm{metabolic}}(i)
+
R_{\mathrm{reproductive}}(i)
+
V_{\mathrm{penalty}}^{\mathrm{gen}}(i)
-
\Gamma_{\mathrm{fitness}}
B\!\left(PP_{\mathrm{survival}}(i)\right),
$$

where all terms are finite, $B$ is a fixed nondecreasing benefit map, and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{fitness}}$ converts the benefit to the same units as the cost terms. Assume:

0. There is a registered biological PCE branch contract $\mathfrak B$ in the sense of Definition D.1f, and $\mathcal I$ indexes a finite retained subset of $\mathcal X_{\mathfrak B}/\!\sim_{\mathfrak B}$. For some registered $\vartheta\in W_{\mathfrak B}$, $V_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is the descended scalar certificate $V_{\mathfrak B,\vartheta}$ on that subset. The branch ledger includes every admitted term whose omission could change the ordering of retained types.
1. $V_{\mathrm{gen}}$ is time-independent over the comparison window.
2. There are branch-specific constitutive parameters $a>0$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}>0$, neither a universal PU constant, with $\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}V_{\mathrm{gen}}$ dimensionless, such that the expected viable-descendant weight of type $i$ is
   $$
   w_i
   =
   a\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)\right].
   $$
3. Inheritance is faithful and generations do not overlap on the retained type coordinate: there is no mutation, recombination, migration, or other type flux. For some $N(0)>0$, let $N_i(0)=N(0)p_i(0)$ and assume the deterministic expected-count or infinite-population update
   $$
   N_i(t+1)=w_iN_i(t).
   $$

For every $t\ge0$, let
$$
N(t):=\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}N_j(t)
$$
and define
$$
p_i(t):=\frac{N_i(t)}{N(t)}.
$$
On the deterministic expected-count branch these are normalized expected-count shares; they are not expected realized finite-population frequencies, which require a separate stochastic population model.

Let

$$
\mathcal I_0
=
\{i\in\mathcal I:p_i(0)>0\},
\qquad
V_*
=
\min_{i\in\mathcal I_0}V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i),
$$

and

$$
\mathcal M_*
=
\{i\in\mathcal I_0:V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)=V_*\}.
$$

Then, for every integer $t\ge0$,

$$
p_i(t)
=
\frac{
p_i(0)\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}tV_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)\right]
}{
\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}
p_j(0)\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}tV_{\mathrm{gen}}(j)\right]
},
$$

and

$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}p_i(t)
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{p_i(0)}
{\sum_{j\in\mathcal M_*}p_j(0)},
&
i\in\mathcal M_*,
\\[10pt]
0,
&
i\notin\mathcal M_*.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus the normalized expected-count shares, or the frequencies on the deterministic infinite-population reading, concentrate exactly on the global minimizers of $V_{\mathrm{gen}}$ within the initial support. If $\mathcal M_*=\{i_*\}$, then $p(t)\to e_{i_*}$.

*Proof.* Since $w_i>0$ and $\sum_iN_i(0)=N(0)>0$, the total expected count remains positive. Normalizing the count update gives

$$
p_i(t+1)
=
\frac{p_i(t)w_i}
{\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}p_j(t)w_j}.
$$

The common factor $a$ cancels. Iterating the count equation gives

$$
N_i(t)
=
N_i(0)a^t
\exp\!\left[-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}tV_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)\right].
$$

Division by $\sum_jN_j(t)$ and $N_i(0)=N(0)p_i(0)$ proves the displayed frequency formula.

For convergence, put

$$
\delta_i
=
V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)-V_*
\ge0
\qquad
(i\in\mathcal I_0)
$$

and

$$
q_*
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal M_*}p_j(0)>0.
$$

After multiplying numerator and denominator by
$\exp(\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}tV_*)$, the frequency formula becomes, for every $i\in\mathcal I_0$,

$$
p_i(t)
=
\frac{p_i(0)e^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}t\delta_i}}
{\sum_{j\in\mathcal I_0}
p_j(0)e^{-\lambda_{\mathrm{gen}}t\delta_j}}.
$$

The denominator is at least $q_*$ for every $t$. If $i\notin\mathcal I_0$, the original frequency formula gives $p_i(t)=0$ for every $t$. If $i\in\mathcal I_0\setminus\mathcal M_*$, then $\delta_i>0$, so the numerator tends to zero and hence $p_i(t)\to0$. If $i\in\mathcal M_*$, then $\delta_i=0$. Every term with positive $\delta_j$ tends to zero, while the terms with $j\in\mathcal M_*$ sum to $q_*$. Therefore $p_i(t)\to p_i(0)/q_*$. The finite type set makes these limits exhaustive and proves concentration on $\mathcal M_*$. The singleton case follows immediately. ∎

<a id="theorem-p89a6a-exact-normalized-selection-bayes-multiplicative-weights-correspondence"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6a (Exact Normalized-Selection–Bayes–Multiplicative-Weights Correspondence).** Let

$$
\Delta(\mathcal I)
=
\left\{
p\in[0,1]^m:
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}p_i=1
\right\},
$$

let $p\in\Delta(\mathcal I)$, let $w\in[0,\infty)^{\mathcal I}$, and define

$$
Z(p,w)
=
\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}p_jw_j.
$$

On the exact domain

$$
\mathcal D
=
\left\{
(p,w)\in\Delta(\mathcal I)\times[0,\infty)^{\mathcal I}:
Z(p,w)>0
\right\},
$$

define the normalized-selection map

$$
\bigl[\mathsf S_w(p)\bigr]_i
=
\frac{p_iw_i}{Z(p,w)}.
$$

Then the following statements hold.

1. **Bayesian form.** Choose any
   $$
   0<c\le\frac{1}{\max_{j\in\mathcal I}w_j}.
   $$
   This interval is nonempty because $Z(p,w)>0$ implies $\max_jw_j>0$. Let $\{H_i\}_{i\in\mathcal I}$ be hypotheses with prior $\mathbb P(H_i)=p_i$, and let $Y\in\{0,1\}$ satisfy
   $$
   \mathbb P(Y=1\mid H_i)=cw_i.
   $$
   Then $\mathbb P(Y=1)=cZ(p,w)>0$ and
   $$
   \mathbb P(H_i\mid Y=1)
   =
   \bigl[\mathsf S_w(p)\bigr]_i.
   $$

2. **Exponential- or multiplicative-weights form.** Fix any learning rate $\eta>0$ and define the extended loss
   $$
   \ell_i
   =
   \begin{cases}
   -\eta^{-1}\ln w_i,
   &
   w_i>0,
   \\[4pt]
   +\infty,
   &
   w_i=0.
   \end{cases}
   $$
   With the convention $e^{-\eta(+\infty)}=0$, the multiplicative-weights update is
   $$
   \frac{p_ie^{-\eta\ell_i}}
   {\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}p_je^{-\eta\ell_j}}
   =
   \bigl[\mathsf S_w(p)\bigr]_i.
   $$
   If every $w_i>0$, all losses are finite. In the Bayesian realization of part 1, unit-rate log loss
   $$
   \ell_i^{\log}
   =
   -\ln(cw_i)
   $$
   gives the same normalized update.

   For $w_i>0$ this is the ordinary finite-loss exponential-weights update. Allowing $w_i=0$ uses the declared $+\infty$ boundary extension and does not invoke any standard bounded-loss regret theorem.

3. **Support and zero boundary.** On $\mathcal D$,
   $$
   \operatorname{supp}\mathsf S_w(p)
   =
   \operatorname{supp}(p)\cap\operatorname{supp}(w).
   $$
   Hence $p_i=0$ is preserved in the absence of type flux, and a type with $p_i>0$ and $w_i=0$ is removed in one step. Moreover,
   $$
   Z(p,w)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   w_i=0
   \text{ for every }i\in\operatorname{supp}(p).
   $$
   At that boundary the normalized-selection update is undefined, the Bayesian event $Y=1$ has prior-predictive probability zero, and the multiplicative-weights denominator is zero. None of the three formalisms supplies a normalized posterior or successor state there without an additional rule.

4. **Common-scale invariance.** For every $r>0$,
   $$
   \mathsf S_{rw}(p)=\mathsf S_w(p).
   $$
   Thus only relative fitness, relative likelihood, or loss differences enter the normalized map.

5. **Constant-relative-fitness iteration.** Suppose a sequence of raw generational weights has the form
   $$
   w_i(t)=a_t w_i,
   \qquad
   a_t>0,
   $$
   for one fixed $w$, and suppose $Z(p(0),w)>0$. Then for every integer $t\ge1$,
   $$
   p_i(t)
   =
   \frac{p_i(0)w_i^t}
   {\sum_{j\in\mathcal I}p_j(0)w_j^t}.
   $$
   In particular, whenever
   $p_i(0)p_j(0)w_iw_j>0$,
   $$
   \frac{p_i(t)}{p_j(t)}
   =
   \frac{p_i(0)}{p_j(0)}
   \left(\frac{w_i}{w_j}\right)^t.
   $$

6. **Mutation and frequency-dependent boundaries.** Let $M=(M_{ij})$ be a column-stochastic parent-to-descendant mutation kernel,
   $$
   M_{ij}\ge0,
   \qquad
   \sum_{i\in\mathcal I}M_{ij}=1
   \quad
   \text{for every }j.
   $$
   Selection followed by mutation is
   $$
   p_i^+
   =
   \sum_{j\in\mathcal I}
   M_{ij}
   \frac{p_jw_j}{Z(p,w)}
   =
   \bigl[M\mathsf S_w(p)\bigr]_i.
   $$
   This update coincides with the unmutated map $\mathsf S_w(p)$ for every $(p,w)\in\mathcal D$ if and only if $M=I$. If instead $w=w(p,t)$ is frequency- or time-dependent, parts 1–4 remain valid pointwise at every step for which $Z(p,w(p,t))>0$. Part 5 applies when the weights along the retained trajectory are proportional to one fixed vector by a common positive factor; no fixed-weight multi-step formula follows in general.

*Proof.* For part 1, the law of total probability gives

$$
\mathbb P(Y=1)
=
\sum_j\mathbb P(H_j)\mathbb P(Y=1\mid H_j)
=
c\sum_jp_jw_j
=
cZ(p,w)>0.
$$

Bayes' rule therefore gives

$$
\mathbb P(H_i\mid Y=1)
=
\frac{p_i(cw_i)}{cZ(p,w)}
=
\frac{p_iw_i}{Z(p,w)}.
$$

For part 2, the definition of $\ell_i$ gives $e^{-\eta\ell_i}=w_i$ for $w_i>0$, while the stated convention gives the same equality when $w_i=0$. Substitution into the multiplicative-weights normalization gives $\mathsf S_w(p)$. Replacing $w_i$ by $cw_i$ multiplies every unnormalized weight by the same positive constant and therefore leaves the normalized vector unchanged.

For part 3, $Z(p,w)>0$ and nonnegativity imply

$$
\bigl[\mathsf S_w(p)\bigr]_i>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_iw_i>0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
p_i>0\text{ and }w_i>0,
$$

which proves the support identity. Because every summand $p_iw_i$ is nonnegative, their sum is zero exactly when every summand is zero. For $i\in\operatorname{supp}(p)$ this is equivalent to $w_i=0$. The three zero-denominator statements then follow directly from their displayed normalizations.

For part 4,

$$
\bigl[\mathsf S_{rw}(p)\bigr]_i
=
\frac{p_i(rw_i)}{\sum_jp_j(rw_j)}
=
\frac{p_iw_i}{\sum_jp_jw_j}.
$$

For part 5, every common factor $a_t$ cancels by part 4, so the update at every step is $\mathsf S_w$. The formula holds for $t=1$ by definition. If it holds at $t$, then

$$
p_i(t+1)
=
\frac{
\left(
p_i(0)w_i^t/
\sum_kp_k(0)w_k^t
\right)w_i
}{
\sum_j
\left(
p_j(0)w_j^t/
\sum_kp_k(0)w_k^t
\right)w_j
}
=
\frac{p_i(0)w_i^{t+1}}
{\sum_jp_j(0)w_j^{t+1}}.
$$

Induction proves the formula for every $t\ge1$. Dividing the formulas for $i$ and $j$ proves the ratio identity under the stated positivity condition.

For part 6, a parent of type $j$ contributes its selected frequency $p_jw_j/Z(p,w)$, and $M_{ij}$ is the conditional fraction assigned to descendant type $i$; summing over parents gives $M\mathsf S_w(p)$. If $M=I$, equality with the unmutated map is immediate. Conversely, suppose

$$
M\mathsf S_w(p)=\mathsf S_w(p)
$$

for every $(p,w)\in\mathcal D$. For each $j$, choose $p=e_j$ and any $w$ with $w_j>0$. Then $\mathsf S_w(e_j)=e_j$, so $Me_j=e_j$. Thus every column of $M$ is the corresponding standard basis vector and $M=I$. Finally, replacing $w$ by the declared $w(p,t)$ in the proofs of parts 1–4 proves their pointwise forms. The induction in part 5 uses one fixed normalized map and therefore applies under the stated common-proportionality condition, while no such induction is asserted outside it. ∎

<a id="remark-p89a6b-mechanism-mutation-and-reflexive-boundaries"></a>**Remark P.8.9a.6b (Mechanism, Mutation, and Reflexive Boundaries).** Theorem P.8.9a.6a is an exact equality of normalized equations on one finite type simplex. It does not by itself identify the causal mechanisms, state spaces, or PU functional roles of selection, Bayesian inference, and a learning algorithm. A claim that a biological process instantiates forecast generation, verification, or model update requires separate retained biological protocol maps establishing those roles. Mutation is the additional kernel $M$, recombination requires its own parent-to-descendant kernel, and neither is supplied by the normalized-selection identity. A diffusion or stochastic-gradient representation of those mechanisms requires an independently derived scaling limit and the regularity, drift, covariance, and boundary data of Appendix D; it does not follow from the presence of variation alone. The theorem concerns the discrete generational map and does not identify it with a continuous-time replicator differential equation without a separate continuous-time limit.

The normalized-selection, Bayesian, and exponential-weights equality is an elementary equation correspondence. No novelty is claimed for that algebraic identity, and no Bayesian consistency theorem, evolutionary stochastic-process theorem, or online-learning regret bound is imported by it.

Frequency dependence $w=w(p,t)$ establishes only that the selection weights depend on the current population state. By itself it supplies neither a model representing the system to itself in the sense of Definition 9 nor the coded evaluator, simulation, predicate evaluation, Boolean post-processing, logical memory, and uniform diagonal closure required by Theorems 10–11. Frequency-dependent selection therefore does not by itself engage SPAP, Reflexive Undecidability, or the horizon-constant construction.

<a id="theorem-p89a6c-replicator-mutator-scaling-limit-of-normalized-mutation-selection"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6c (Replicator–Mutator Scaling Limit of Normalized Mutation–Selection).** Let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,m\}$, let $V_{\mathrm{gen}}:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R$ be a fixed generational ledger with oscillation $\operatorname{osc}V:=\max V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\min V_{\mathrm{gen}}$, let $\lambda\ge0$, and let $G$ be a mutation generator: $G_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_iG_{ij}=0$ for every $j$, with $g:=\max_j|G_{jj}|$. For a generation length $h>0$ with $hg\le1$, the normalized mutation–selection map of part 6 of Theorem P.8.9a.6a,
$$
\Psi_h(p):=(I+hG)\,\mathsf S_{w(h)}(p),
\qquad
w_i(h)=e^{-\lambda hV_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)},
$$
maps the type simplex $\Delta(\mathcal I)$ into itself. Let $p_h(n+1)=\Psi_h(p_h(n))$, and let $p(t)$ solve the replicator–mutator equation
$$
\dot p=F(p):=Gp-\lambda\bigl(V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_p\bigr)\odot p,
\qquad
\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_p:=\sum_jp_jV_{\mathrm{gen}}(j),
$$
with $p(0)=p_h(0)\in\Delta(\mathcal I)$. Then:

1. The flow of $F$ leaves $\Delta(\mathcal I)$ invariant, and for every $T>0$,
$$
\max_{0\le nh\le T}\bigl\|p_h(n)-p(nh)\bigr\|_1\le C_T\,h,
\qquad
C_T=\Bigl(\tfrac14\lambda^2(\operatorname{osc}V)^2+2g\lambda\operatorname{osc}V+\tfrac12\bigl(2g+\tfrac32\lambda\operatorname{osc}V\bigr)\bigl(2g+\lambda\operatorname{osc}V\bigr)\Bigr)\,T\,e^{\frac32\lambda\operatorname{osc}V\,T}.
\tag{P.8.9a.6c.1}
$$
2. For fixed $h$, if $A_h:=(I+hG)\operatorname{diag}(w(h))$ is primitive, then $p_h(n)$ converges from every initial frequency vector to the normalized Perron vector of $A_h$.
3. The limit equation depends on $G$ beyond $V_{\mathrm{gen}}$. For $m=2$, $V_{\mathrm{gen}}\equiv0$ and $G=\begin{pmatrix}-a&b\\a&-b\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,b\ge0$ and $a+b>0$, the unique stationary frequency is $(b,a)/(a+b)$, so equal ledgers with different rate ratios give different stationary laws. The fixed-weight form $p_i(t)\propto p_i(0)e^{-\lambda tV_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)}$ solves the limit equation for every initial frequency if and only if $G=0$.

*Proof.* The matrix $I+hG$ is nonnegative and column-stochastic when $hg\le1$, and $\mathsf S_{w(h)}$ maps $\Delta(\mathcal I)$ into itself, so $\Psi_h$ does too; column-stochasticity also gives $\|(I+hG)x\|_1\le\|x\|_1$. Along a solution of $\dot p=F(p)$, $p$ solves the linear equation $\dot x=B(t)x$ with $B(t)=G-\lambda\operatorname{diag}(V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_{p(t)})$, whose off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, so its propagator is entrywise nonnegative and $p(t)\ge0$. The columns of $G$ sum to zero and $\sum_i(V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_p)p_i=0$, so $\sum_iF_i=0$ and $\sum_ip_i=1$ is conserved. Compactness of $\Delta(\mathcal I)$ gives global existence.

*Consistency.* For fixed $p$, put $\varphi(s):=\mathsf S_{w(s)}(p)$. Then $\varphi'=-\lambda\varphi\odot(V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_\varphi)$ and $\varphi_i''=\lambda^2\varphi_i\bigl[(V_{\mathrm{gen}}(i)-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_\varphi)^2-\operatorname{Var}_\varphi V_{\mathrm{gen}}\bigr]$, so $\|\varphi'\|_1\le\lambda\operatorname{osc}V$ and $\|\varphi''\|_1\le2\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}_\varphi V_{\mathrm{gen}}\le\tfrac12\lambda^2(\operatorname{osc}V)^2$ by Popoviciu's inequality. With $f(p):=-\lambda(V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_p)\odot p$, Taylor's formula gives $\|\mathsf S_{w(h)}(p)-p-hf(p)\|_1\le\tfrac14\lambda^2(\operatorname{osc}V)^2h^2$ and $\|\mathsf S_{w(h)}(p)-p\|_1\le\lambda h\operatorname{osc}V$. Since $\Psi_h(p)-p-hF(p)=[\mathsf S_{w(h)}(p)-p-hf(p)]+hG(\mathsf S_{w(h)}(p)-p)$ and the $\ell^1$ operator norm of $G$ is $2g$,
$$
\|\Psi_h(p)-p-hF(p)\|_1\le Kh^2,
\qquad
K:=\tfrac14\lambda^2(\operatorname{osc}V)^2+2g\lambda\operatorname{osc}V.
$$

*Stability.* Let $u=w(h)$, $r=\max u/\min u=e^{\lambda h\operatorname{osc}V}$ and $\delta=p-q$ for $p,q\in\Delta(\mathcal I)$. Then
$$
\mathsf S_u(p)-\mathsf S_u(q)=\frac{u\odot\delta-\mathsf S_u(q)\langle u,\delta\rangle}{\langle u,p\rangle},
$$
and $\sum_i\delta_i=0$ gives $|\langle u,\delta\rangle|\le\tfrac12(\max u-\min u)\|\delta\|_1$. Hence $\|\mathsf S_u(p)-\mathsf S_u(q)\|_1\le\tfrac12(3r-1)\|\delta\|_1\le e^{Lh}\|\delta\|_1$ with $L:=\tfrac32\lambda\operatorname{osc}V$, and the same bound holds for $\Psi_h$.

*Local error of the flow.* On $\Delta(\mathcal I)$, $\|F(p)\|_1\le2g+\lambda\operatorname{osc}V$. For $\sum_i\delta_i=0$, $DF(p)\delta=G\delta-\lambda(V_{\mathrm{gen}}-\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}}\rangle_p)\odot\delta+\lambda\langle V_{\mathrm{gen}},\delta\rangle p$ has norm at most $(2g+\tfrac32\lambda\operatorname{osc}V)\|\delta\|_1$. Since $\ddot p=DF(p)\dot p$, $\|p(t+h)-p(t)-hF(p(t))\|_1\le\tfrac12(2g+\tfrac32\lambda\operatorname{osc}V)(2g+\lambda\operatorname{osc}V)h^2$.

*Accumulation.* Let $e_n=\|p_h(n)-p(nh)\|_1$ and let $K'h^2$ be the sum of the two local bounds. Then $e_0=0$ and $e_{n+1}\le e^{Lh}e_n+K'h^2$, so $e_n\le K'h^2ne^{\mathrm{Lnh}}\le C_Th$ whenever $nh\le T$, which is (P.8.9a.6c.1).

For item 2, $\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}(I+hG)=\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}$ gives $\Psi_h(p)=A_hp/\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}A_hp$, hence $p_h(n)=A_h^np_h(0)/\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}A_h^np_h(0)$. For primitive $A_h$ with Perron root $r_h$, the Perron–Frobenius theorem gives $r_h^{-n}A_h^n\to vu^{\mathsf T}$ with strictly positive right and left Perron vectors $v,u$; since $u^{\mathsf T}p_h(0)>0$, $p_h(n)\to v/\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}v$.

For item 3, the two-type equation is $\dot p_1=-ap_1+bp_2$ on $p_1+p_2=1$, whose unique rest point is $p_1=b/(a+b)$. If $G=0$, the fixed-weight form solves $\dot p=f(p)$ by direct differentiation. Conversely, its derivative at $t=0$ is $f(p(0))$, whereas the equation requires $F(p(0))=Gp(0)+f(p(0))$; agreement for every $p(0)\in\Delta(\mathcal I)$ forces $Gp(0)=0$ on a spanning set, so $G=0$. ∎

<a id="definition-p89a6d-finite-parental-stochastic-tensor-branch"></a>**Definition P.8.9a.6d (Finite Parental Stochastic-Tensor Branch).** The following fixed data define the common finite-parent branch. Section and equation numbers in each native module are local. No physical/biological law is inferred merely from the tensor representation.

## 2. Frozen kernel class and classification

Let $I=\{1,\dots,m\}$, $\Delta=\{x_i\ge 0,\ \sum_i x_i=1\}$, and $\Delta_N=\Delta\cap N^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{m}$. $N$ counts the independently sampled units: individuals for genotype sampling, gene copies for haploid sampling. It must not silently be changed from $N$ individuals to $2N$ gene copies.

Choose an integer $r\ge 1$ and a parental tensor

$$
T_{i;j_1,\ldots,j_r}(x) \ge 0, \qquad \sum_i T_{i;j_1,\ldots,j_r}(x) = 1.
$$

At state $x$, parent slots are drawn independently with replacement with probabilities $q(x)$. Given those slots, the offspring type has the displayed law. Different offspring repeat the entire experiment independently, conditional on $x$. For selection followed by inheritance set

$$
\begin{aligned}
Z(x) &= \sum_j x_j w_j(x) > 0, \\
q_j(x) &= x_j w_j(x)/Z(x), \\
F_i(x) &= \sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_r} T_{i;j_1,\ldots,j_r}(x) \prod_{a=1}^{r} q_{j_a}(x).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

Weights are nonnegative. For global statements assume they and $T$ are continuous and $Z\ge z_*>0$ on $\Delta$. For the fluctuation theorem use $C^{2}$ extensions to a neighborhood in the affine hyperplane $\sum x_i=1$, with $Z$ positive there near $\Delta$. Strictly positive smooth weights, in particular finite smooth exponential ledgers, satisfy the denominator condition by compactness. The values of an extension outside $\Delta$ carry no biological interpretation.

Constant T belongs to the product of $m^{r}$ copies of the output simplex $\Delta$. Thus nonnegativity and the column-sum equations classify exactly every conditional offspring law in this frozen finite-parent protocol. Conversely any such protocol determines those conditional probabilities, up to choices on parental tuples never visited. Permutation-invariant parent roles impose corresponding linear tensor symmetries. Given gamete alphabets and meiosis matrices, Mendelian restrictions are additional explicit factorization equations, as in §5; being stochastic alone does not certify Mendelian biology.

For constant $T$, write $R_T(q)$ for the last line of (1). Product-measure telescoping and contraction by a stochastic kernel give

$$
\lVert R_T(q) - R_T(q')\rVert_1 \le r\lVert q - q'\rVert_1.
\tag{2}
$$

If $\max_j\lVert T_{\cdot;j}(x)-T_{\cdot;j}(y)\rVert_1\le L_T\lVert x-y\rVert_1$ and $q$ is $L_q$-Lipschitz, $F$ is $(L_T+rL_q)$-Lipschitz. Here $j$ abbreviates the parental tuple. A concrete bound for $q$ follows if $0\le w_j\le W$ and $|w_j(x)-w_j(y)|\le K\lVert x-y\rVert_1$: the unnormalized vector has Lipschitz constant $W+K$ and normalization gives $L_q\le 2(W+K)/z_*$. These are upper bounds, not optimal constants.

Finite compositions of selection, mutation and tensor reproduction maps obey all results below whenever the composite F has the stated regularity and the final offspring are sampled independently. The order of composition is retained data. An intermediate finite random sample cannot be replaced by its mean without changing the exact kernel.

<a id="theorem-p89a6e-finite-population-kernel-and-fixed-generation-limits"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6e (Finite Population Kernel and Fixed-Generation Limits).** Theorems P.8.9a.6e.1 and P.8.9a.6e.2 below carry their displayed independence, regularity and fixed-window hypotheses.

## 3. The finite-population theorem

<a id="theorem-p89a6e1-exact-kernel-boundary-concentration-lln"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6e.1 (exact kernel, boundary, concentration, LLN).** Let $F$ be a map as above that is $L$-Lipschitz, or more generally any $L$-Lipschitz $F:\Delta\to\Delta$. Define

$$
P_N(x,y) = N! / \prod_i (Ny_i)! \times \prod_i F_i(x)^{Ny_i}, \qquad x, y \in \Delta_N,
\tag{3}
$$

with $0^{0}=1$. This is the transition kernel of $X^N_{n+1}=N^{-1}\operatorname{Multinomial}(N,F(X^N_n))$. Put $C(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{T}$. Exactly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[X^N_{n+1} - X^N_n \mid X^N_n = x] &= F(x) - x, \\
\operatorname{Cov}(X^N_{n+1} - X^N_n \mid X^N_n = x) &= C(F(x))/N,
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(X^N_{n+1} - x)(X^N_{n+1} - x)^{T} \mid x] \\
&= C(F(x))/N + (F(x) - x)(F(x) - x)^{T}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x_{n+1}=F(x_n)$. If $\lVert X^N_0-x_0\rVert_1\le\varepsilon_0$ surely, then for every integer $K\ge 1$ and $a>0$, with probability at least $1-\min\{1,2mK\exp(-2Na^{2}/m^{2})\}$, simultaneously for $0\le n\le K$,

$$
\lVert X^N_n - x_n\rVert_1 \le L^{n} \varepsilon_0 + a \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} L^{j}.
\tag{5}
$$

The empty sum is zero and $L^{0}=1$, also when $L=0$. If $X^N_0\to x_0$ in probability, then $\max_{n\le K}\lVert X^N_n-x_n\rVert_1\to 0$ in probability for every fixed $K$. In (5), the same conclusion with a random initial error holds on the event that this error is $\le\varepsilon_0$, subtracting its failure probability.

The face $\Delta_S=\{x:\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq S\}$ is invariant for every population size and every initial point in that face if $F_i(x)=0$ for all $x\in\Delta_S$ and $i\notin S$. Conversely invariance for all $N$ implies that identity by continuity and density of rational points. For tensor (1), $F_i(x)>0$ exactly when some parental tuple has $T_{i;j}(x)>0$ and every $q_{j_a}(x)>0$. Thus a missing type can be recreated by recombination or mutation; the support formula for selection alone is not inherited by the composite map.

**Proof.** Conditional independence gives (3) by counting offspring sequences. The multinomial theorem proves row normalization, including zero probabilities. Write offspring as independent one-hot random vectors $Y_{l}$. Their conditional mean is $F(x)$, and covariance is $C(F(x))$; averaging gives (4). The covariance is positive semidefinite since $v^{T}C(p)v=\sum p_iv_i^{2}-(\sum p_iv_i)^{2}$, and $C(p)\mathbf{1}=0$.

For each coordinate, Hoeffding's bound for $N$ independent $[0,1]$-valued indicators gives $P(|X^N_{n+1,i}-F_i(X^N_n)|>a/m\mid\text{history})\le 2\exp(-2Na^{2}/m^{2})$. A union bound over coordinates and $K$ generations proves the probability bound without assuming independence between generations. On the complementary good event the pathwise error obeys $e_{n+1}\le Le_n+a$; iteration gives (5). Choose $a\to 0$ with $Na^{2}\to\infty$ and use initial convergence to obtain the LLN. Finally, an output type has positive probability exactly when its conditional marginal is positive, proving the support and face assertions. ∎

The finite-generation qualification matters: an exponentially amplifying deterministic orbit or rare fixation event is not controlled for arbitrary growing K by a fixed-K LLN. Equation (5), rather than an unsupported uniform-in-time claim, supplies any permitted growing-window condition.

<a id="theorem-p89a6e2-joint-finite-generation-fluctuations"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6e.2 (joint finite-generation fluctuations).** Suppose $F$ has the $C^{2}$ regularity above and $U^N_0=\sqrt{N}(X^N_0-x_0)$ converges in law to $U_{0}$. For each fixed $K$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\sqrt{N}(X^N_n - x_n))_{n=0}^{K} &\Rightarrow (U_n)_{n=0}^{K}, \\
U_{n+1} &= A_n U_n + \xi_{n+1}, \qquad A_n = DF(x_n)|_{1^{\perp}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
$$

where $\xi_1,\dots,\xi_K$ are independent centered Gaussian vectors, independent of $U_{0}$, with $\operatorname{Cov}\xi_{n+1}=C(x_{n+1})$. If $U_{0}$ is Gaussian (a constant vector is allowed), the whole limit is jointly Gaussian; otherwise it is an affine propagation of $U_{0}$ plus Gaussian innovations and need not be Gaussian. For Gaussian $U_{0}$ with mean $\mu_{0}$ and covariance $\Sigma_{0}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{n+1} &= A_n \mu_n, \\
\Sigma_{n+1} &= A_n \Sigma_n A_n^{T} + C(x_{n+1}),
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(U_{n+1}, U_k) = A_n \operatorname{Cov}(U_n, U_k), \qquad k \le n.
$$

The covariance statements describe the limiting law. Convergence of finite-N covariances additionally needs uniform integrability of the squared fluctuations; convergence in distribution alone does not supply it.

**Proof.** Set $\xi^N_{n+1}=\sqrt{N}(X^N_{n+1}-F(X^N_n))$. Conditional on history with $p=F(X^N_n)$, its characteristic function is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\exp(-i\sqrt{N}\,\theta\cdot p)\Bigl[\sum_i p_i \exp(i\theta_i/\sqrt{N})\Bigr]^{N} \\
&= \exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2}\theta^{T} C(p)\theta + O_\theta(N^{-1/2})\Bigr),
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
$$

uniformly for $p\in\Delta$, by Taylor expansion of the exponential and logarithm around 1. By Theorem P.8.9a.6e.1, $p\to x_{n+1}$. Conditional characteristic functions and induction establish joint convergence to independent innovations, independent also of the limiting initial variable. Tightness at each finite $n$ follows by induction; Taylor expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{N}(F(X^N_n) - F(x_n)) &= A_n U^N_n + O(\lVert U^N_n\rVert^{2}/\sqrt{N}) \\
&= A_n U^N_n + o_P(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

This proves (6); (7) follows from independence. All arguments hold on simplex faces. Zero coordinates of $x_{n+1}$ have zero innovation variance, and all vectors lie in $\mathbf{1}^{\perp}$. At $x_{0,i}=0$, a Gaussian limiting $U_{0,i}$ must have zero variance because finite-$N$ $U^N_{0,i}\ge 0$, but may have a nonnegative deterministic mean. No reflecting Gaussian surrogate or clipping rule is introduced. ∎

For explicit computation with constant T,

$$
\begin{aligned}
DF_i(x)[v] &= \sum_j T_{i;j} \sum_{a=1}^{r} Dq_{j_a}(x)[v] \prod_{b \ne a} q_{j_b}(x), \\
Dq_i[v] &= (v_i w_i + x_i\, Dw_i[v])/Z - q_i\, DZ[v]/Z, \\
DZ[v] &= \sum_j (v_j w_j + x_j\, Dw_j[v]).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
$$

For state-dependent $T$ add $\sum_j DT_{i;j}(x)[v]\prod_a q_{j_a}$. Formula (9) has no division by $q_{i}$, so it remains valid at zero frequencies.

<a id="theorem-p89a6f-separately-scaled-diffusion-branch"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6f (Separately Scaled Diffusion Branch).** The generic uniqueness premise below remains in place; the later fixed-parent and selection modules discharge it exactly on their named subfamilies.

## 4. Independent weak-effect diffusion theorem

Theorems P.8.9a.6e.1–P.8.9a.6e.2 concern generation number $n$, not continuous time. Now retain a different family $F_N:\Delta\to\Delta$ satisfying, uniformly on $\Delta$,

$$
F_N(x) = x + b(x)/N + o(1/N),
\tag{10}
$$

with continuous bounded $b$. Let $X^N$ use kernel (3) with $F_{N}$ and let $Y^N(t)=X^N_{\lfloor Nt\rfloor}$. Suppose $X^N_0\Rightarrow X_0$. Then $Y^N$ is tight on each finite interval in the Skorokhod space, every subsequential limit has continuous paths and solves the martingale problem on $\Delta$ for

$$
Lf(x) = b(x)\cdot\nabla f(x) + \frac{1}{2} C(x) : \nabla^{2} f(x),
\tag{11}
$$

for $C^{3}$ test functions defined near $\Delta$. If that martingale problem is unique in law for the retained initial distribution, the whole sequence converges. Uniqueness is an explicit hypothesis here, not a consequence asserted for arbitrary continuous $b$. The coordinate representation is independent of the chosen smooth extension because $\mathbf{1}^{T}b=0$ and $C\mathbf{1}=0$. At $x_{i}=0$, (10) forces $b_i(x)\ge 0$. There is no arbitrary reflecting boundary condition.

**Proof.** Put $d_N=F_N(x)-x$ and $\delta=X^N_{n+1}-x$. Uniformly,

$$
N \mathbb{E}\delta \to b, \qquad N \mathbb{E}\delta\delta^{T} = C(F_N(x)) + N d_N d_N^{T} \to C(x).
$$

For centered multinomial averages $\mathbb{E}\lVert X^N_{n+1}-F_N(x)\rVert^{4}=O_m(N^{-2})$, uniformly, by expanding sums of centered independent bounded variables; only index patterns with no singleton survive. Hence $\mathbb{E}\lVert\delta\rVert^{4}=O(N^{-2})$ and $\mathbb{E}\lVert\delta\rVert^{3}=O(N^{-3/2})$. Taylor's theorem now gives uniform convergence of the accelerated generators $N\,\mathbb{E}[f(x+\delta)-f(x)]$ to (11), with the cubic remainder $O(N^{-1/2})$ for bounded $C^{3}$ norm. Over $\lfloor NT\rfloor$ steps, the probability of any jump exceeding $\varepsilon$ is $O(T/(N\varepsilon^{4}))$, hence vanishes.

Decompose $Y^N$ into an initial state, a predictable drift bounded by a constant per unit accelerated time, and a martingale with conditional coordinate variances bounded by a $\text{constant}/N$ per step. The stopped increment second-moment bound is $O(\delta+1/N)$, and the drift increment bound is $O(\delta+1/N)$, so the stopping-time tightness criterion applies; compactness of $\Delta$ gives compact containment. Vanishing jumps give continuous limits. The discrete generator martingales, bounded coefficients, and uniform generator convergence identify every limit with (11). Uniqueness, when established, identifies the entire sequence. This is the standard martingale-problem diffusion approximation with its needed moment and boundary data checked for this family. ∎

### A concrete family that produces the drift

Let $s_{i}$ be bounded $C^{2}$ functions, $G$ a column-conservative mutation generator, $R:\Delta\to\Delta$ a $C^{2}$ parental map, and $\rho\ge 0$. For $N\ge\max\{\rho,\max_j|G_{jj}|\}$, use the successive operations

$$
\begin{aligned}
q &= S_{\exp(s/N)}(x), \\
q' &= q + (\rho/N)(R(q) - q), \\
F_N(x) &= (I + G/N)\,q'.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$

Each map preserves $\Delta$. Uniform Taylor expansion on the compact simplex proves (10), with an $O(N^{-2})$ remainder, and

$$
b_i(x) = (Gx)_i + x_i\Bigl(s_i(x) - \sum_j x_j s_j(x)\Bigr) + \rho(R_i(x) - x_i).
\tag{13}
$$

This proves generator identification for every such family. Full diffusion convergence follows whenever well-posedness of its particular (11) is supplied. For the PU exponential branch $s_i=-\lambda V_i(x)$, the selection term is $-\lambda x_i(V_i(x)-\sum_jx_jV_j(x))$; $G$ and $R$ remain separate data.

### Fully verified two-allele diffusion subclass

For $m=2$, $\rho=0$, $G=\begin{bmatrix} -u & v \\ u & -v \end{bmatrix}$, $u,v\ge 0$, let $x=x_1$ and $s_1-s_2=a(x)$, a bounded $C^{1}$ function on $[0,1]$. Then (11) has the unique solution in law on $[0,1]$ of

$$
dX = [v(1-X) - uX + X(1-X)a(X)]\,dt + \sqrt{X(1-X)}\,dW.
\tag{14}
$$

Existence follows from the preceding compactness construction. For uniqueness, extend the drift outside $[0,1]$ by its endpoint values and $\sigma(x)=\sqrt{\pi(x)(1-\pi(x))}$, where $\pi$ clips to $[0,1]$. The drift extension is globally Lipschitz, and $|\sigma(x)-\sigma(y)|^{2}\le|x-y|$. The one-dimensional Yamada–Watanabe criterion applies with modulus $\sqrt{u}$ (the reciprocal squared-modulus integral $\int_0 du/u$ diverges), yielding pathwise uniqueness and therefore uniqueness in law. Concretely, smooth convex approximations $\varphi_{k}$ to $|\cdot|$ with $\varphi_{k}''$ supported in shrinking annuli and $\varphi_k''(z)\le 2/(k|z|)$ give $\mathbb{E}\varphi_k(X_t-Y_t)\le L\int_0^t\mathbb{E}|X_s-Y_s|\,ds+t/k$ for solutions driven by the same Brownian motion. Taking $k\to\infty$ and applying Grönwall proves pathwise uniqueness. The classical weak-existence/pathwise-uniqueness implication then gives uniqueness in law. The existence already constructed stays in $[0,1]$. Thus the entire chain (12) converges to (14), including boundary-starting initial laws. If $u=v=0$ the endpoints absorb. Positive inward mutation drift changes this behavior; reflection is not imposed.

A diploid weak-selection allele-sampling model can be specified independently: let symmetric genotype coefficients $\sigma_{\mathrm{AA}},\sigma_{\mathrm{Aa}},\sigma_{\mathrm{aa}}$, Hardy–Weinberg frequencies imposed at the allele-pool stage, and genotype fitnesses $1+\sigma/N$, with $N$ large enough that all three fitnesses are strictly positive (for example $N>\max\{0,-\sigma_{\mathrm{AA}},-\sigma_{\mathrm{Aa}},-\sigma_{\mathrm{aa}}\}$). The marginal allele selection drift is $x(1-x)[x(\sigma_{\mathrm{AA}}-\sigma_{\mathrm{Aa}})+(1-x)(\sigma_{\mathrm{Aa}}-\sigma_{\mathrm{aa}})]$. Substituting this affine $a(x)$ in (14) gives a genuine diploid-selection diffusion for that stated gene-copy sampling model. It is not a proof that the full genotype-state chain is already one-dimensional or near identity.

### Fixed reproduction is not weak reproduction

If $F$ is independent of $N$ and $F(x)\ne x$ for some $x$, $N(F(x)-x)$ diverges. Starting at lattice points $x_N\to x$, the first generation tends to $F(x)$ while its accelerated time is $1/N$. This cannot converge to a continuous diffusion starting at $x$. Fast equilibration and an allele-frequency or slow-manifold projection can sometimes yield a different diffusion, but require a separate two-time-scale theorem and closure certificate. Increasing $N$ alone does not supply them.

<a id="remark-p89a6g-mendelian-examples-state-closure-and-source-transfer"></a>**Remark P.8.9a.6g (Mendelian Examples, State Closure and Source Transfer).** The examples and nonentailments below retain the stated genotype/census/clock and source boundaries.

## 5. Explicit covered examples and obstruction checks

### 5.1 Mendelian diploid genotype kernel

Let the individual types be AA,Aa,aa and let $h=(1,1/2,0)$ give the probability of an A gamete from each genotype. With two independently selected parent slots $j,k$, set

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{AA;jk} &= h_j h_k, \\
T_{Aa;jk} &= h_j(1 - h_k) + (1 - h_j)h_k, \\
T_{aa;jk} &= (1 - h_j)(1 - h_k).
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
$$

Every tensor column is a probability vector and is symmetric in $j,k$. If $g=\sum_jq_jh_j$, then $F(x)=(g^{2},2g(1-g),(1-g)^{2})$. Equations (3)–(9) apply to $N$ independently formed diploid individuals. In the neutral case $g=x_{\mathrm{AA}}+x_{\mathrm{Aa}}/2$. At $x=(0,1,0)$, $F=(1/4,1/2,1/4)$, so $\lVert F-x\rVert_1=1$: the full genotype map is not near identity even without selection.

For the allele observable $\ell=(1,1/2,0)$, exactly $\operatorname{Var}(\ell\cdot X^N_{n+1}|x)=\ell^{T}C(F(x))\ell/N=g(1-g)/(2N)$. This factor is derived from the genotype tensor; it must not be guessed. Conditional on $x$, $2N$ offspring alleles are independent in this particular random-parent/random-gamete construction. A different within-offspring joint law changes the result.

Full genotype states can be indispensable. With weights $(2,1,1)$, both $x=(1/2,0,1/2)$ and $x'=(0,1,0)$ have allele frequency $1/2$, but selected gamete probabilities are respectively $2/3$ and $1/2$. Their next allele expectations differ. Therefore the allele-frequency projection is not a Markov lumping valid for all genotype states in this model. Hardy–Weinberg substitution without a protocol or limit would erase required state data.

For multiple loci, replace $h$ by a declared stochastic meiosis matrix $H_{a;j}$ from parental genotypes to gamete haplotypes, incorporating phased chromosomes and recombination probabilities. Ordered offspring genotype $(a,b)$ has $T_{(a,b);jk}=H_{a;j}H_{b;k}$; for unordered $a\ne b$ add the two orders. Nonnegative unit column sums of $H$ prove the tensor conditions. This covers every specified finite meiosis matrix, not an inference of that matrix from a ledger.

### 5.2 Two-locus recombination tensor

For haplotypes $j=(j_1,j_2)\in\{0,1\}^{2}$ and $c\in[0,1]$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{i;jk} = {}&(1-c)/2\, [1_{i=j} + 1_{i=k}] \\
&+ c/2\, [1_{i=(j_1,k_2)} + 1_{i=(k_1,j_2)}].
\end{aligned}
\tag{16}
$$

Duplicate outcomes add their probabilities. Every column sums to 1. Its map is $R_c(q)=(1-c)q+c(q_{\mathrm{first}}\otimes q_{\mathrm{second}})$. The conventional two-locus Mendelian recombination-fraction range $c\le 1/2$ is a subfamily; $c$ up to 1 is a valid mathematical crossover tensor without that biological interpretation. If $q=(1/2,0,0,1/2)$ in order 00,01,10,11, then

$$
R_c(q) = (1/2 - c/4, c/4, c/4, 1/2 - c/4), \qquad \lVert R_c(q) - q\rVert_1 = c.
$$

Missing recombinant types appear despite a constant zero ledger. At $c=1/2$ the one-step displacement is 1/2 for every N. This verifies both ledger nonidentifiability and the failure of automatic continuous-time scaling. For the same neutral ledger, $c=0$ and $c=1/2$ give different deterministic maps and different finite-N kernels.

### 5.3 Smooth frequency dependence

For any $C^{2}$ payoff matrix or ledger field, $w_i(x)=\exp(s_i(x))>0$ gives a smooth global normalized map. In two types, $s_1(x)=a(1-x_1)$, $s_2(x)=ax_1$ produces state-dependent selection, with (3)–(9) valid for every finite $a$. Replacing $s$ by $s/N$, not merely increasing population size at fixed $s$, gives the weak-selection scaling (12). Frequency dependence supplies no coded evaluator, self-model, diagonalization closure, or SPAP premise.

### 5.4 Exact sampling counterexample

The same deterministic neutral map $F(x)=x$ can be realized either by multinomial offspring or by selecting one parent and assigning its type to every offspring. The latter has $\operatorname{Cov}(X^N_{n+1}|x)=C(x)$, not $C(x)/N$. Thus neither the mean update nor a ledger determines genetic-drift covariance; independent offspring sampling is indispensable. Exchangeable offspring alone is insufficient.

### 5.5 Boundary singularity

Allowing $w=(1,0)$ at $x=(0,1)$ makes $Z=0$, so neither selection nor a Markov kernel is defined by (1). One must specify an extinction/cemetery or replacement rule, or restrict the domain and stop before exiting it. No continuous extension of $x_iw_i/Z$ is presumed. Exponential finite ledgers avoid this singularity on the finite simplex.

## 6. PU transfer and boundaries of Appendix D

<a id="proposition-p89a6g1-conditional-transfer-and-nonidentifiability"></a>**Proposition P.8.9a.6g.1 (conditional transfer and nonidentifiability).** Suppose the registered biological branch identifies retained types with a finite response quotient, certifies the complete descended ledger $V_i(x)$, and independently certifies the constitutive selected-parent weights $w_i(x)=a(x)\exp(-\lambda V_i(x))$, $a(x)>0$. Suppose it further certifies the actual inheritance tensor, the order of population regulation and reproduction, the independently sampled unit, and offspring independence. Then cancellation of $a(x)$ gives exactly (1), and Theorems P.8.9a.6e.1–P.8.9a.6e.2 apply when their denominator/regularity assumptions hold. If the separately retained family uses weak effects as in (12), its scaled moments are (11)–(13), and the diffusion conclusions apply with the stated well-posedness condition or the proved subclass (14).

**Proof.** The branch identification transports the biological selected-parent and conditional offspring probabilities onto the finite state space. Multiplying the conditional probabilities and summing over parental tuples gives (1); conditional independence gives (3). Theorems P.8.9a.6e.1–P.8.9a.6e.2 and the weak-effect theorem are then literal substitutions, not analogies. Conversely, (16) with $c=0$ and $c=1/2$ has identical zero ledger and different expected successor laws; §5.4 has identical mean laws and different covariances. Neither the inheritance map nor stochastic sampling follows from the ledger. ∎

For Appendix D's convention $\sigma\sigma^{T}=2D$, the Wright–Fisher covariance gives $D=C/2$, not $C$. The simplex has boundary and $C$ degenerates there; even on the interior the ambient normal direction is null. Its usual square-root noise is not globally Lipschitz at boundary faces. Therefore Appendix D's compact boundaryless uniformly elliptic branch (A3)–(A5), its heat-kernel minorization, and its Gibbs conclusions do not apply. Mutation and recombination drift are not automatically a gradient of the ledger. For fixed $V$ the selection-only drift equals $-\lambda C(x)V$, but this degenerate simplex mobility is not Appendix D's uniformly positive metric mobility; adding state-dependent $V$ does not even identify $V_i(x)$ with a gradient of a scalar population potential. No stochastic-gradient, Gibbs, universal optimizer, or biological-realization conclusion is claimed.

<a id="theorem-p89a6h-finite-exchangeable-counts-cannings-families-and-distinct-stochastic-limits"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6h (Finite Exchangeable Counts, Cannings Families and Distinct Stochastic Limits).** The complete argument follows. Equation and section numbers refer only to this native module; every stated mechanism, boundary, independence and scaling premise is retained.

### 2 Every finite exchangeable offspring law is a count kernel

Let $I=\{1,\dots,m\}$, $\Delta=\{x\ge 0:\sum_i x_i=1\}$, $\Delta_N=\Delta\cap N^{-1}\mathbb{Z}^{m}$, and let $Z_1,\dots,Z_N$ take values in the unit vectors $e_{i}$. Conditional on the retained population state $x$, assume their joint law is invariant under permutations of the $N$ offspring labels. Write $Y=N^{-1}\sum_a Z_a$ and let $K_N(x,y)=P(Y=y|x)$.

<a id="theorem-p89a6h1-finite-representation-and-moments"></a>**Theorem P.8.9a.6h.1 (finite representation and moments).** For each $x$, exchangeable offspring laws are in one-to-one correspondence with probability vectors $(K_N(x,k/N))$ over integer $k_i\ge 0$, $\sum_i k_i=N$. Given counts $k$, the labeled offspring sequence is uniform over its $N!/\prod_i k_i!$ distinct arrangements. In particular,

$$
P(Z_1 = z_1, \ldots, Z_N = z_N \mid x) = K_N(x, k/N)/(N!/\prod_i k_i!).
\tag{1}
$$

For $N\ge 2$, put $p_N(x)=\mathbb{E}[Z_1|x]$ and $H_N(x)=\mathbb{E}[Z_1Z_2^{T}|x]$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y \mid x] &= p_N(x), \\
\operatorname{Cov}(Y \mid x) &= C(p_N)/N + (N-1)(H_N - p_N p_N^{\mathsf T})/N, \\
C(p) &= \operatorname{diag}(p) - p p^{\mathsf T}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

For distinct specified offspring labels with prescribed type multiplicities $r_{i}$ and $r=\sum_i r_i\le N$, their joint probability is

$$
