# Part IV: PCE Selection of the Moonshine Module

## P.13.7 The Precision Cost Principle

### Theorem P.13.18 (Conditional Precision-Dependent Symmetry Cost)

Let $K$ be a nonempty compact smooth embedded $m$-dimensional manifold in a Lie group $G$, with smooth boundary allowed, and use the distance induced by a smooth ambient Riemannian metric. Let $N_K(\delta)$ be the least number of radius-$\delta$ metric balls with centers in $K$ that cover $K$. Assume that a physical controller stores one of $N_K(\delta)$ equiprobable resolution labels, resets that label once per control cycle, has no retained side information, and incurs a registered operational cost $c_0>0$ per nat. Then
$$
V_{\mathrm{op}}(K;\delta)
=
c_0m\ln(1/\delta)+O(1)
$$
as $\delta\downarrow0$.

*Proof.* For $m>0$, finitely many interior and boundary charts give constants $a,b,r_0>0$ for which the induced $m$-volume of $K\cap B(x,r)$ lies between $ar^m$ and $br^m$, uniformly in $x\in K$ and $0<r<r_0$. A cover therefore needs at least $\operatorname{vol}_m(K)/(b\delta^m)$ balls. A maximal $\delta$-separated set covers $K$ by radius-$\delta$ balls, while its radius-$\delta/2$ balls are disjoint; their volume lower bound bounds the set's cardinality above by $\operatorname{vol}_m(K)/(a(\delta/2)^m)$. If $m=0$, compactness makes $K$ a nonempty finite set, and sufficiently small balls each cover one point. Thus in either case positive constants $c_-,c_+$ satisfy
$$
c_-\delta^{-m}\le N_K(\delta)\le c_+\delta^{-m}
$$
for all sufficiently small $\delta$. Hence
$$
\ln N_K(\delta)=m\ln(1/\delta)+O(1).
$$
The equiprobable label has entropy $\ln N_K(\delta)$ nats. Under the declared reset and per-nat cost model,
$$
V_{\mathrm{op}}(K;\delta)
=
c_0\ln N_K(\delta)
=
c_0m\ln(1/\delta)+O(1).
$$
Without the coding and reset hypotheses, the covering-number identity alone is not a physical cost equality. ∎

---

<a id="corollary-p1318a-precision-labels-and-retained-access"></a>**Corollary P.13.18a (Precision Labels and Retained Access).** Fix $T>0$. Suppose the finite classical controller label $L_\delta$ is uniform on $N(\delta)$ resolution cells, with $\ln N(\delta)=m\ln(1/\delta)+O(1)$. Reset this label while the unchanged finite classical side record $R_\delta$ remains accessible under the ideal conditional thermal-control contract of Theorem P.15.2a. Then
$$
\inf\frac{Q_\delta}{k_BT}=H(L_\delta\mid R_\delta)
=\ln N(\delta)-I(L_\delta;R_\delta).
$$
Every actual exact reset in this physical class obeys
$$
\frac{Q_\delta}{k_BT}+H(R_\delta)\ge\ln N(\delta).
$$
Consequently bounded side-record entropy preserves the logarithmically divergent heat lower bound when $m>0$. Bounded ideal reset heat requires
$$
I(L_\delta;R_\delta)\ge m\ln(1/\delta)-O(1).
$$
*Proof.* The conditional-reset infimum follows from Theorem P.15.2a's conditional state-transformation contract. Use $H(L_\delta\mid R_\delta)=H(L_\delta)-I(L_\delta;R_\delta)$ and $H(L_\delta)=\ln N(\delta)$. The inequality $I(L_\delta;R_\delta)\le H(R_\delta)$ gives the actual-reset bound. Substituting the covering-number asymptotic proves both scaling conclusions. ∎

The controller architecture and access schedule are the specified ones. Acquisition, maintenance and eventual reset of $R_\delta$ retain their separate entries in the complete cost ledger.

**Preservation of a registered comparison gap.** Suppose a frozen finite comparison has nominated winner $a_*$ and baseline differences $C_0(a)-C_0(a_*)\ge g>0$ for every competitor. If its remaining complete-cost differences satisfy $C_1(a)-C_1(a_*)>-g$, the winner remains strict for $C_0+C_1$. Indeed adding the two inequalities gives $(C_0+C_1)(a)-(C_0+C_1)(a_*)>0$. This preserves an established gap and does not supply the physical objective or baseline winner.

### Definition P.13.2 (Precision-Independent Effective Operational Symmetry-Family Cost)

For a symmetry group $G$ whose full action family must be represented by MPUs through a finite-precision control specification at resolution $\delta>0$, let $V_{\text{op}}(G;\delta)$ denote the operational cost required to maintain that representation at precision $\delta$ (Theorem P.13.18). The precision-independent effective symmetry cost is defined by
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(G) := \lim_{\delta \to 0} V_{\text{op}}(G;\delta),
$$
when the limit exists in $[0,\infty]$.

Operational predictions are expressed in terms of configurations sampled from the relevant stationary regime of the dynamics (Theorem D.5, Appendix D); in low-noise detailed-balance regimes this stationary measure is concentrated near the low-potential sector. When a full symmetry action family must be instantiated uniformly along the operational refinement $\delta\to 0$, it is compatible with a resolution-independent PU description only if $V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(G) < \infty$; if $V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(G) = \infty$, the action family cannot be implemented as an exact uniformly refinable operational symmetry (though it may still appear as an effective symmetry at finite $\delta$).

### Theorem P.13.19 (Conditional Operational Symmetry-Family Penalty)

Let $K$ be a compact $m$-dimensional control region in a Lie group. Assume that, at every sufficiently small resolution $\delta$, a controller stores one of $N_K(\delta)$ equiprobable labels, resets that label once per control cycle, retains no side information, and incurs registered operational cost $c_0>0$ per nat. Then
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(K):=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}V_{\mathrm{op}}(K;\delta)
=+\infty
\qquad\text{if }m>0.
$$
For a finite group $G$, under the analogous equiprobable-label/reset model,
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(G)=c_0\ln|G|<\infty.
$$

*Proof.* A positive-dimensional compact metric space $K$ is infinite. For each integer $n\ge2$, choose $n$ distinct points of $K$ and let $d_n>0$ be their minimum pairwise distance. If $\delta<d_n/2$, one radius-$\delta$ ball contains at most one of these points, so $N_K(\delta)\ge n$. Consequently $N_K(\delta)\to\infty$ as $\delta\downarrow0$. The declared label/reset model gives $V_{\mathrm{op}}(K;\delta)=c_0\ln N_K(\delta)$, which tends to $+\infty$ because $c_0>0$. This divergence requires no particular logarithmic growth coefficient. If $G$ is finite, sufficiently small balls separate all its elements, so $N_G(\delta)=|G|$ and the same model gives $V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{sym}(G)=c_0\ln|G|<\infty$. ∎

The divergent branch is equivalently the budget-indexed statement
$$
\forall B\in\mathbb R\ \exists\delta_B>0\ \forall\delta\in(0,\delta_B),
\qquad
V_{\mathrm{op}}(K;\delta)>B.
$$
Each fixed-resolution cycle retains a finite label record and a finite registered cost under the theorem's hypotheses. The $+\infty$ limit is therefore a family of finite-budget exclusions and assigns no infinite heat or cost to one finite-resolution cycle.

### Corollary P.13.19a (Conditional $U(1)^{24}$ Controller Cost)

If the full $U(1)^{24}$ action is implemented by the equiprobable-label, once-per-cycle reset, no-side-information, positive-per-nat controller architecture of Theorem P.13.19 at every resolution $\delta$, then
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{sym}}(U(1)^{24})=+\infty.
$$

*Proof.* Under those hypotheses the control region has positive dimension $24$, so Theorem P.13.19 applies. ∎

### Corollary P.13.19b (Continuous Symmetry on the Registered Uniform-Controller Branch)

Assume the full action family of a positive-dimensional compact symmetry region must, at every refinement scale $\delta$, be represented by one of $N_K(\delta)$ equiprobable stored labels, reset once per cycle with no retained side information and charged $c_0>0$ per nat. Then Theorem P.13.19 gives
$$
V_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\mathrm{sym}}(K)=+\infty,
$$
so that particular uniformly refinable controller architecture cannot realize the exact action at finite asymptotic cost. This does not exclude exact continuous symmetry on branches with relational, gauge-redundant, analog, nonuniform, side-information-assisted, or otherwise differently encoded realizations.

For the separately registered electromagnetic phase branch, Appendix Q proves that
$$
G_L=\{e^{iN\ln2}:N\in\mathbb Z\}
$$
is dense in $U(1)$. Hence its closure reproduces $U(1)$ at finite phase tolerance. Density supplies one effective-closure realization; it does not prove that every physical $U(1)$ must arise this way.

*Proof.* The first statement is exactly Theorem P.13.19 with its hypotheses retained. The density statement is Appendix Q. Neither theorem classifies controller architectures outside its stated domain. ∎

### Theorem P.13.19c (Program-Processor Symmetry Cost)

Let $\mathcal H$ be the Hilbert completion of an orthogonal sum $\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathcal H_n$ of finite-dimensional grades, let $\Omega\in\mathcal H_0$ be a unit vector, and write $D_n=\bigoplus_{k\le n}\mathcal H_k$ with orthogonal projector $P_n$. Let $G$ be a compact metrizable group with Haar probability measure $\mu$ and a faithful strongly continuous unitary representation $g\mapsto U_g$ on $\mathcal H$ such that every $U_g$ preserves each $\mathcal H_n$ and fixes $\Omega$. The **program-processor controller branch** registers the following data before any group is compared.

1. *Program carrier.* One carrier $\mathcal P=\ell^2(\mathbb N_0)$ with program Hamiltonian $H_{\mathcal P}=\epsilon\sum_{m\ge0}m\,|m\rangle\langle m|$, $\epsilon>0$. Every action-dependent control resource (labels, timing choices, reference states, Hamiltonian selections and side information) is part of the program state.
2. *Processors.* At resolution $\delta>0$, a processor is one completely positive trace-preserving map $\Phi_\delta$ from the trace class of $\mathcal H\otimes\mathcal P$ to that of $\mathcal H$, together with a measurable assignment $g\mapsto\sigma_{g,\delta}$ of normal program states of finite energy $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_{g,\delta})$.
3. *Accuracy.* With $C_n(\rho)=P_n\rho P_n+\operatorname{Tr}[(I-P_n)\rho]\,|\Omega\rangle\langle\Omega|$, the processor has accuracy $\delta$ when, for every $n\le1/\delta$,
$$
\sup_{g\in G}\bigl\|C_n\circ\Phi_\delta(\,\cdot\otimes\sigma_{g,\delta})-\operatorname{Ad}U_g\bigr\|_{\diamond,D_n}\le\delta,
\tag{P.13.19c.1}
$$
where $\|\cdot\|_{\diamond,D_n}$ is the diamond norm of maps on the trace class of $D_n$.
4. *Delivered-work boundary.* Each call starts the program in $|0\rangle$, charges the preparation of $\sigma_{g,\delta}$ to its energy supply, runs a processor whose Stinespring unitary commutes with $H_{\mathcal P}\otimes I$, and ends by exchanging the spent program with a ground-state load cell carrying the same ladder; the load is not returned. The cost of a call is the energy delivered to that load, and calls have a common period $T_{\mathrm{call}}>0$.

Write
$$
\bar c(\delta)=\int_G\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_{g,\delta})\,d\mu(g),
\qquad
V^{\mathrm{prog}}_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)=\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\ \inf\frac{\bar c(\delta)}{T_{\mathrm{call}}},
\tag{P.13.19c.2}
$$
the infimum running over the processors of accuracy $\delta$. A processor of accuracy $\delta'<\delta$ also has accuracy $\delta$, so the infimum is nondecreasing as $\delta\downarrow0$ and the limit exists in $[0,\infty]$. Then the following hold.

1. **Delivered work.** On the boundary of item 4 a call with program $\sigma_{g,\delta}$ delivers the energy $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_{g,\delta})$, so $\bar c(\delta)$ is the Haar-mean delivered work per call.
2. **Exact programs are orthogonal.** Let $D$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let one completely positive trace-preserving map $\Psi$ from the trace class of $D\otimes\mathcal P$ to that of $D$ satisfy $\Psi(\rho\otimes\sigma_i)=U_i\rho U_i^*$ for every state $\rho$ on $D$ and $i=1,\dots,N$, where the unitaries $U_i$ are pairwise not proportional. Then the supports of $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_N$ are pairwise orthogonal and
$$
\sum_{i=1}^N\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_i)\ge\epsilon\,\frac{N(N-1)}2.
\tag{P.13.19c.3}
$$
3. **Continuous families.** If $G$ is infinite, then for every $E<\infty$ there is $\delta_E>0$ such that every processor of accuracy $\delta<\delta_E$ has $\bar c(\delta)>E$. Hence $V^{\mathrm{prog}}_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)=+\infty$. This applies to every $G$ that contains a nontrivial strongly continuous one-parameter subgroup.
4. **Finite groups.** If $G=\{g_0,\dots,g_{N-1}\}$ is finite, the processor with programs $|k\rangle\langle k|$ and Stinespring unitary
$$
W=\sum_{k<N}|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes U_{g_k}+\sum_{k\ge N}|k\rangle\langle k|\otimes I
$$
implements every $\operatorname{Ad}U_g$ exactly, commutes with $H_{\mathcal P}\otimes I$ and with every $P_n$, and has $\bar c(\delta)=\epsilon(N-1)/2$ at every resolution. Hence $V^{\mathrm{prog}}_{\mathrm{eff}}(G)\le\epsilon(N-1)/(2T_{\mathrm{call}})<\infty$.

*Proof.* (1) The processor's Stinespring unitary commutes with $H_{\mathcal P}\otimes I$, so the spent program has the mean energy $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_{g,\delta})$ of the prepared one, and the exchange with a ground-state load cell transfers exactly that energy to the load.

(2) For pure programs this is the no-programming theorem (Nielsen and Chuang 1997); the argument below includes mixed programs. Let $\Psi(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}[VXV^*]$ with an isometry $V:D\otimes\mathcal P\to D\otimes\mathcal E$. If $\dim D=1$, any two unitaries are proportional; let $\dim D\ge2$. Say that a unit vector $a\in\mathcal P$ implements $U_i$ if $\Psi(\rho\otimes|a\rangle\langle a|)=U_i\rho U_i^*$ for all $\rho$. For each unit $\psi\in D$ the output $U_i|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|U_i^*$ is then pure, so $V(\psi\otimes a)=U_i\psi\otimes e(\psi)$ with a unit vector $e(\psi)\in\mathcal E$. For linearly independent $\psi,\phi$, linearity gives $U_i(\psi+\phi)\otimes e(\psi+\phi)=U_i\psi\otimes e(\psi)+U_i\phi\otimes e(\phi)$, and independence of $U_i\psi,U_i\phi$ forces $e(\psi)=e(\phi)$; hence $V(\psi\otimes a)=U_i\psi\otimes e_a$ with $e_a$ independent of $\psi$. If $a,b$ implement $U_i$, then $V(\psi\otimes(\alpha a+\beta b))=U_i\psi\otimes(\alpha e_a+\beta e_b)$, so the vectors implementing $U_i$, together with $0$, form a closed linear subspace. Write $\sigma_i=\sum_k\lambda_k|a_k\rangle\langle a_k|$ with $\lambda_k>0$. Then $\operatorname{Ad}U_i=\sum_k\lambda_k\Psi(\,\cdot\otimes|a_k\rangle\langle a_k|)$ decomposes a unitary channel into channels; its normalized Choi operator is a pure state, an extreme point, so every summand equals $\operatorname{Ad}U_i$ and every vector of the support of $\sigma_i$ implements $U_i$. For $a$ in the support of $\sigma_i$ and $b$ in that of $\sigma_j$, isometry of $V$ gives
$$
\langle a,b\rangle\langle\psi,\phi\rangle=\langle e_a,e_b\rangle\langle\psi,U_i^*U_j\phi\rangle
\qquad(\psi,\phi\in D),
$$
so $\langle a,b\rangle I_D=\langle e_a,e_b\rangle U_i^*U_j$. For $i\ne j$ the operator $U_i^*U_j$ is not a scalar, hence $\langle a,b\rangle=0$. With $Q_i$ the support projectors, $\sigma_i\le Q_i$ and $\sum_iQ_i\le I$, so $Q=\sum_i\sigma_i$ obeys $0\le Q\le I$ and $\operatorname{Tr}Q=N$. The numbers $q_m=\langle m|Q|m\rangle\in[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_mq_m=N$, and
$$
\sum_m mq_m-\sum_{m<N}m=\sum_{m\ge N}mq_m-\sum_{m<N}m(1-q_m)\ge N\sum_{m\ge N}q_m-N\sum_{m<N}(1-q_m)=0,
$$
which is (P.13.19c.3).

(3) Suppose the claim fails. Then there are $E<\infty$, $\delta_k\downarrow0$ and processors $(\Phi_k,\sigma_{g,k})$ of accuracy $\delta_k$ with $\bar c(\delta_k)\le E$. Haar measure of an infinite compact group has no atoms, since translation invariance would give every point the same positive mass. Fix a compatible metric $d$ on $G$. Then $\sup_g\mu(B(g,r))\to0$ as $r\downarrow0$: otherwise points $g_l$ and radii $r_l\to0$ with $\mu(B(g_l,r_l))\ge\eta>0$ would have a convergent subsequence $g_l\to g$, and $\mu(B(g,s))\ge\eta$ for every $s>0$ would give $\mu(\{g\})\ge\eta$. Fix an integer $N>1+4E/\epsilon$ and $r>0$ with $\mu(B(g,r))<1/(2N)$ for all $g$. Markov's inequality gives $\mu(A_k)\ge\frac12$ for $A_k=\{g:\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_{g,k})\le2E\}$. Choose $g_{1,k},\dots,g_{N,k}\in A_k$ successively outside the radius-$r$ balls about the points already chosen; the removed balls have total measure below $\frac{N-1}{2N}<\frac12$. Passing to a subsequence, $g_{i,k}\to g_i$ with $d(g_i,g_j)\ge r$ for $i\ne j$, so the $g_i$ are distinct.

Faithfulness gives, for $i\ne j$, a vector $x$ with $U_{g_i}x\ne U_{g_j}x$; because every $U_g$ commutes with $P_n$ and $P_nx\to x$, some $D_n$ separates each pair, and we fix one $n$ that separates all pairs. Since $\Omega\in D_n$ is fixed by every $U_g$, the restrictions $U_{g_i}|_{D_n}$ are pairwise not proportional. On $D_n$ strong continuity is norm continuity, so $\operatorname{Ad}U_{g_{i,k}}\to\operatorname{Ad}U_{g_i}$ in $\|\cdot\|_{\diamond,D_n}$. For $k$ so large that $n\le1/\delta_k$, (P.13.19c.1) applies, and with $\Psi_k=C_n\circ\Phi_k$ restricted to the trace class of $D_n\otimes\mathcal P$ and $\sigma_{i,k}=\sigma_{g_{i,k},k}$,
$$
\Psi_k(\,\cdot\otimes\sigma_{i,k})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ad}U_{g_i}\quad\text{on }D_n .
$$

*Compact programs.* Put $\Pi_m=\sum_{l\le m}|l\rangle\langle l|$. A state $\tau$ with $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\tau)\le2E$ has $\operatorname{Tr}[(I-\Pi_m)\tau]\le2E/(\epsilon(m+1))$, and the gentle-measurement bound gives $\|\tau-\Pi_m\tau\Pi_m\|_1\le2\sqrt{2E/(\epsilon(m+1))}$. The set of such states is therefore totally bounded in trace norm; it is closed, because the energy is the supremum of the trace-norm continuous truncated energies. After a further subsequence, $\sigma_{i,k}\to\sigma_i$ in trace norm with $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_i)\le2E$ for every $i$.

*Compact processors.* For each $m$, the restrictions of $\Psi_k$ to the trace class of $D_n\otimes\Pi_m\mathcal P$ are completely positive trace-preserving maps between finite-dimensional spaces, a compact set. A diagonal subsequence converges for every $m$; the limits are compatible under the inclusions, define a completely positive trace-preserving map on the union of these finite-program trace classes, and extend by trace-norm contractivity to such a map $\Psi$ on the trace class of $D_n\otimes\mathcal P$.

For a state $\rho$ on $D_n$, contractivity bounds the contribution of the tails $\sigma_{i,k}-\Pi_m\sigma_{i,k}\Pi_m$ and $\sigma_i-\Pi_m\sigma_i\Pi_m$ by $4\sqrt{2E/(\epsilon(m+1))}$, uniformly in $k$, while $\Psi_k(\rho\otimes\Pi_m\sigma_{i,k}\Pi_m)\to\Psi(\rho\otimes\Pi_m\sigma_i\Pi_m)$. Letting $k\to\infty$ and then $m\to\infty$ gives $\Psi(\rho\otimes\sigma_i)=U_{g_i}\rho U_{g_i}^*$ for every $\rho$ and $i$. Part (2) then gives $\epsilon N(N-1)/2\le\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathcal P}\sigma_i)\le2EN$, so $N\le1+4E/\epsilon$, contrary to the choice of $N$. A nontrivial strongly continuous one-parameter subgroup has infinitely many elements.

(4) $W$ is unitary and block diagonal in the program basis, so it commutes with $H_{\mathcal P}\otimes I$; it commutes with every $P_n$ because each $U_g$ preserves the grades. For the program $|k\rangle$ the output is $U_{g_k}\rho U_{g_k}^*$ exactly, and the delivered energy is $\epsilon k$, whose uniform mean is $\epsilon(N-1)/2$. ∎

Theorem P.13.19c supplies, on the program-processor controller branch, the exclusion of positive-dimensional compact symmetry families used in hypothesis (ii) of Theorem P.13.24 and in assumption 2 of Theorem P.13.27. It uses no equiprobable-label, reset or per-nat model. A controller that selects an action through a parameter outside the program carrier belongs to a different branch.

## P.13.8 The Canonical Orbifold Construction

### <a id="theorem-p1320-canonical-1-involution"></a>Theorem P.13.20 (Canonical (-1) Involution)

The map $(-1): \Lambda_{24} \to \Lambda_{24}$ given by $v \mapsto -v$ is:
1. An automorphism of $\Lambda_{24}$
2. Central in $\text{Aut}(\Lambda_{24}) = \text{Co}_0$
3. Of order 2

*Proof.* Because $\Lambda_{24}$ is an additive subgroup of its real span, $v\in\Lambda_{24}$ implies $-v\in\Lambda_{24}$. Thus $-I$ maps the lattice to itself, and its inverse is itself. For all $v,w\in\Lambda_{24}$,
$$
\langle-v,-w\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle,
$$
so $-I$ is a lattice isometry and hence an element of $\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})$.

For every $h\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})$ and $v\in\Lambda_{24}$, linearity gives
$$
(-I)h(v)=-h(v)=h(-v)=h(-I)(v),
$$
so $-I$ is central. Finally,
$$
(-I)^2=I.
$$
The Leech lattice contains nonzero vectors, so $-I\ne I$; consequently its order is exactly two. ∎

<a id="proposition-p1320a-canonicity-of-1-for-the-leech-lattice"></a>**Proposition P.13.20a (Canonicity of (-1) for the Leech Lattice).** For the Leech lattice $\Lambda_{24}$, the involution $(-1)$ is the unique nontrivial central element of order 2 in $\text{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})=\text{Co}_0$.

*Proof.* By Theorem P.13.20, the map $v\mapsto -v$ is a central automorphism of $\Lambda_{24}$ of order 2. Conway's description of the full automorphism group gives
$$
Z(\text{Co}_0)=\{\pm1\}
$$
(Conway 1969b). Hence the only central elements are $\pm1$, and the unique non-identity central involution is $(-1)$. ∎

---

### Theorem P.13.21 (Lift to VOA)

**Reference:** Borcherds (1986, §§2–4), together with the explicit inversion-cocycle calculation in the proof.

The $(-1)$ involution on $\Lambda_{24}$ lifts to an involution $\theta$ on $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ with:

1. **Action on Heisenberg:** $\theta(\alpha^i_{-n}|0\rangle) = -\,\alpha^i_{-n}|0\rangle$
2. **Action on lattice vectors:** $\theta(e_v) = e_{-v}$

More generally, for a pure Heisenberg monomial one has
$$
\theta\!\left(\alpha^{i_1}_{-n_1}\cdots \alpha^{i_m}_{-n_m}|0\rangle\right)
=
(-1)^m\alpha^{i_1}_{-n_1}\cdots \alpha^{i_m}_{-n_m}|0\rangle.
$$

In particular, on weight-one currents:
$$
\theta(\alpha^i_{-1}|0\rangle) = -\alpha^i_{-1}|0\rangle
$$
so the weight-one currents are $\theta$-odd, and $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^\theta$ has $\dim((V_{\Lambda_{24}})^\theta_1) = 0$.

*Proof.* Choose an ordered integral basis $b_i$ of the even lattice and a bimultiplicative sign cocycle $\epsilon$ with commutator $\epsilon(v,w)/\epsilon(w,v)=(-1)^{\langle v,w\rangle}$. Such a cocycle is obtained for $v=\sum_i m_i b_i$ and $w=\sum_i n_i b_i$ by taking the sign with exponent
$$
\sum_{i>j}m_i n_j\langle b_i,b_j\rangle
+\sum_i m_i n_i\frac{\langle b_i,b_i\rangle}{2}.
$$
Bimultiplicativity gives $\epsilon(-v,-w)=\epsilon(v,w)$. Hence the map $e_v\mapsto e_{-v}$ preserves the twisted group-algebra product $e_ve_w=\epsilon(v,w)e_{v+w}$ and squares to the identity. Combined with negation on the Heisenberg generators, it preserves the lattice vertex-operator formula: the oscillator factors and lattice exponent are carried to those indexed by $-v$, with their cocycle coefficients preserved. This defines the chosen phase-normalized inversion lift in the lattice-VOA construction, consistent with Borcherds (1986, §§2–4). An arbitrary lattice isometry may require additional cocycle phases. For this inversion lift one obtains
$$
\theta(\alpha^i_{-n}|0\rangle)=(-\alpha^i)_{-n}|0\rangle=-\alpha^i_{-n}|0\rangle
$$
for every mode number $n$, and
$$
\theta(e_v)=e_{-v}.
$$
Applying $\theta$ multiplicatively to a monomial with $m$ Heisenberg creation operators yields the factor $(-1)^m$. The weight-one space of $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ is spanned by the vectors $\alpha^i_{-1}|0\rangle$, so every weight-one current is odd and no nonzero weight-one vector survives in the fixed-point subspace. ∎

<a id="corollary-p1321a-canonical-properties-of-theta"></a>**Corollary P.13.21a (Canonical Properties of $\theta$).** The chosen $(-1)$ lift $\theta$ is characterized by:
1. its underlying lattice isometry $-I$, which is central in $\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})$;
2. its action by $-1$ on each Heisenberg creation operator, equivalently by $(-1)^m$ on a state with $m$ Heisenberg factors; and
3. its action $e_v\mapsto e_{-v}$ on lattice vertex operators.

These properties specify the chosen lift. They do not make $\theta$ central in the full VOA automorphism group: for a torus automorphism $A_h=\exp(2\pi i h_0)$, one has $\theta A_h\theta^{-1}=A_h^{-1}$.

---

### Theorem P.13.22 (The FLM Orbifold Construction)

**Reference:** (Carnahan 2023, Definition 4.1; Miyamoto 2004a, §9)

The $\theta$-orbifold of $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ is the Moonshine module:
$$(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\text{orb}} = (V_{\Lambda_{24}})^\theta \oplus (V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{tw,\theta} = V^\natural$$

where $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^\theta$ is the $\theta$-fixed subspace and $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{tw,\theta}$ is the $\theta$-twisted sector.

**Epistemic Status:** Established mathematical orbifold construction on the stated Leech-lattice and order-two-lift branch. The modern sources identify the resulting VOA with the historical FLM Moonshine module; the original FLM book proof was not inspected.

---

## P.13.9 The Z₂ Structure from PCE

### Theorem P.13.23 (Canonical $\mathbb{Z}_2$ from the PCE-Attractor)

Assume the PCE-attractor branch carries the registered two-label fixed-ready-state quotient of Definition J.1 and retains its two labels as a logical subspace. The automorphism group of that quotient is $\mathbb Z_2$, and its nonidentity element lifts to an order-two unitary on the registered logical subspace.

*Proof.* Let
$$
r:\{0,1\}\to\{\mathrm{ready}\}
$$
be the registered constant quotient. Exactly two permutations of $\{0,1\}$ satisfy $r\circ s=r$: the identity and the bit flip. They form $S_2\cong\mathbb Z_2$. On a Hilbert realization with the two labels represented by an orthonormal basis, the bit flip lifts to a unitary $S$ with $S^2=I$; its $\pm1$ eigenspaces give the corresponding grading. SPAP and PCE alone do not supply the quotient or Hilbert realization. $\square$

---

### Theorem P.13.24 (Canonical Involution from Weight-One Rigidity)

Let $g \in \mathrm{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})$ satisfy $g^2 = I$, and let $\hat g$ be a standard lift of $g$ to $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$. Then
$$
\dim\big((V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1\big)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
g=-1.
$$
In particular, among standard lifts of lattice involutions on the Leech branch, vanishing fixed weight-one space singles out $g=-1$; no centrality assumption is required.

For the orbifold consequence, assume additionally that (i) the selected extension $\mathcal V$ contains $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}$ as its untwisted subVOA with the same conformal vector, is of CFT type with finite-dimensional graded subspaces, and carries a semisimple real-charge action of the specified Heisenberg zero modes, and (ii) the operational controller criterion excludes every nontrivial positive-dimensional compact automorphism family of $\mathcal V$. Then $g=-1$, the standard lift $\hat g$ is conjugate to the chosen phase-normalized lift $\theta$, and conjugation transports the corresponding orbifold extension data to an isomorphic extension.

*Proof.*

1. By Theorem P.13.14, because the Leech lattice is rootless,
$$
(V_{\Lambda_{24}})_1=\mathfrak h(-1)|0\rangle \cong \mathfrak h:=\Lambda_{24}\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb C,
$$
and there are no lattice-vector contributions in weight one.

2. For a standard lift of a lattice isometry, the action on the Heisenberg creation operators is the linear action of the underlying lattice automorphism. Therefore $\hat g$ acts on $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})_1$ exactly as $g$ acts on $\mathfrak h$, and
$$
(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1 \cong \mathfrak h^g.
$$
Hence
$$
\dim\big((V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1\big)=\dim(\mathfrak h^g).
$$

3. Since $g^2=I$, the minimal polynomial of $g$ divides $x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$, whose roots are distinct. Thus $g$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb C$ with eigenvalues contained in $\{+1,-1\}$.

4. If $\dim((V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1)=0$, then $\mathfrak h^g=0$. So $g$ has no $+1$-eigenvectors. By Step 3, all eigenvalues are therefore $-1$, which implies $g=-I$ on $\mathfrak h$. Since $\Lambda_{24}$ spans $\mathfrak h$, this means $g(v)=-v$ for every $v\in\Lambda_{24}$, i.e. $g=-1$.

5. Conversely, if $g=-1$, every standard lift is conjugate to the phase-normalized lift $\theta$ of Theorem P.13.21. Conjugation preserves fixed-space dimensions, and
$$
\theta(\alpha^i_{-1}|0\rangle)=-\alpha^i_{-1}|0\rangle
$$
for every weight-one Heisenberg current. Hence $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1=0$, proving the converse implication without identifying an arbitrary standard lift literally with $\theta$.

6. For the final claim, suppose $\mathfrak h^g\ne0$. Because $g$ is an integral involution, $\ker(g-I)$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$; hence the fixed lattice $\Lambda_{24}^g=\Lambda_{24}\cap\ker(g-I)$ contains a nonzero vector $u$. By Steps 1--2 the current $u(-1)\mathbf1$ lies in $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1$, and by hypothesis (i) it lies in $\mathcal V_1$. It is primary of weight one, so $u_0$ commutes with $L_0$, annihilates the conformal vector, preserves every graded subspace of $\mathcal V$, and is a derivation of the vertex-operator product. Those subspaces are finite dimensional and $u_0$ acts on them semisimply with real charges, so
$$
U_t:=\exp(2\pi i t u_0),\qquad t\in\mathbb R,
$$
is a one-parameter group of automorphisms of $\mathcal V$ whose closure is a positive-dimensional compact abelian subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal V)$. It is nontrivial already on the untwisted sector: nondegeneracy supplies $\alpha\in\Lambda_{24}$ with $\langle u,\alpha\rangle\ne0$, and the $\hat g$-symmetrization $w$ of $e^{2\alpha}$ is a nonzero vector of $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}$, because $\hat g$ acts on $e^{2\alpha}$ by the square of its sign on $e^{\alpha}$ when $g\alpha=\alpha$ and permutes $e^{2\alpha}$ with $e^{2g\alpha}$ otherwise. Since $gu=u$ gives $\langle u,g\alpha\rangle=\langle u,\alpha\rangle$, one has $u_0w=2\langle u,\alpha\rangle w\ne0$. This contradicts hypothesis (ii). Thus $\mathfrak h^g=0$, and Steps 4--5 give $g=-1$ and conjugacy of $\hat g$ with $\theta$. Conjugating the untwisted fixed-point subVOA and the associated twisted-module action transports the standard orbifold extension data, so the corresponding extensions are isomorphic. No separate certificate that the circle extends from the invariant subVOA to the orbifold is required, because $u(-1)\mathbf1$ is a weight-one vector of $\mathcal V$ itself. ∎

### Proposition P.13.24a (Invariant Weight-One Census on the Niemeier Class)

Let $L$ represent a class of $\mathfrak N_{24}$ in the fixed normalization of Selection Principles P.13.7–P.13.8, write $\Phi(L)=\{v\in L:q_0(v)=2\}$ and $\mathfrak h=L\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb C$, let $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(L)$ satisfy $g^2=I$, and let $\hat g$ be a standard lift of $g$ to $V_L$ with $\hat g^2=1$.

1. If $g\ne-1$, then $(V_L^{\hat g})_1\supseteq\mathfrak h^g(-1)\mathbf1\ne0$. If $g=-1$, then $\dim(V_L^{\hat g})_1=N_{\mathrm{root}}(L)/2$. Consequently $(V_L^{\hat g})_1=0$ if and only if $L\cong\Lambda_{24}$ and $g=-1$.
2. Let $\mathcal V$ be a unitary vertex operator algebra of CFT type with finite-dimensional graded subspaces that contains $V_L^{\hat g}$ as a subalgebra with the same conformal vector. If $(V_L^{\hat g})_1\ne0$, there is $x\in\mathcal V_1$ with $x_0$ self-adjoint and nonzero, and $t\mapsto\exp(itx_0)$ is a nontrivial strongly continuous one-parameter group of vertex-algebra automorphisms of $\mathcal V$ that preserve the scalar product, fix $\mathbf1$ and the conformal vector, and commute with $L_0$.
3. Among the involutive standard-lift orbifold packages over the twenty-four classes of $\mathfrak N_{24}$, the only one with vanishing invariant weight-one space is $(\Lambda_{24},-1)$; its orbifold extension is $V^\natural$.

For $g=-1$ the values of $N_{\mathrm{root}}(L)/2$ over the twenty-four classes are $0$ for $\Lambda_{24}$ and $12h$ otherwise, where $h\in\{2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,12,13,14,16,18,22,25,30,46\}$ is the common Coxeter number of the root system; the smallest positive value is $24$, for $A_1^{24}$.

*Proof.* (1) The weight-one space of $V_L$ is $\mathfrak h(-1)\mathbf1\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi(L)}\mathbb Ce^\alpha$, because $e^\beta$ has weight $q_0(\beta)/2$. A standard lift acts on $\mathfrak h(-1)\mathbf1$ by $g$ and sends $e^\alpha$ to a nonzero multiple of $e^{g\alpha}$. Since $g^2=I$, $g$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\pm1$, and if $g\ne-1$ its fixed space $\mathfrak h^g$ is nonzero. If $g=-1$, then $\mathfrak h^g=0$; writing $\hat ge^\alpha=c_\alpha e^{-\alpha}$, the relation $\hat g^2=1$ gives $\hat ge^{-\alpha}=c_\alpha^{-1}e^\alpha$, so the invariant vectors of $\mathbb Ce^\alpha\oplus\mathbb Ce^{-\alpha}$ form the line spanned by $e^\alpha+c_\alpha e^{-\alpha}$, and $\dim(V_L^{\hat g})_1=N_{\mathrm{root}}(L)/2$. By Theorem P.13.10, Step 2, $\Lambda_{24}$ is the only rootless class.

(2) *A nonzero zero mode.* If $g\ne-1$, the space $\ker(g-I)$ is defined over $\mathbb Q$, so it contains a nonzero $u\in L$; choose $\beta\in L$ with $\langle u,\beta\rangle\ne0$ and put $y=u(-1)\mathbf1$. If $g\beta\ne\beta$, let $w=e^{2\beta}+\hat ge^{2\beta}$. If $g\beta=\beta$, then $\hat ge^\beta=\pm e^\beta$; since $e^{2\beta}$ is a nonzero multiple of $e^\beta_{-q_0(\beta)-1}e^\beta$, $\hat ge^{2\beta}=e^{2\beta}$, and we let $w=e^{2\beta}$. In both cases $w\ne0$ is invariant and $y_0w=2\langle u,\beta\rangle w\ne0$, because $\langle u,g\beta\rangle=\langle gu,g\beta\rangle=\langle u,\beta\rangle$. If $g=-1$ and $\alpha\in\Phi(L)$, put $y=e^\alpha+c_\alpha e^{-\alpha}$ and $w=e^{2\alpha}+\hat ge^{2\alpha}$. The lattice vertex operator gives
$$
Y(e^\beta,z)e^\gamma=\pm z^{\langle\beta,\gamma\rangle}\exp\Bigl(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{\beta(-n)}n\,z^n\Bigr)e^{\beta+\gamma}.
$$
Since $\langle\alpha,2\alpha\rangle=\langle-\alpha,-2\alpha\rangle=4$, the zero modes $e^\alpha_0e^{2\alpha}$ and $e^{-\alpha}_0e^{-2\alpha}$ vanish. Since $\langle-\alpha,2\alpha\rangle=-4$, the vector $e^{-\alpha}_0e^{2\alpha}$ is $\pm$ the coefficient of $z^3$ in $\exp(-\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha(-n)z^n/n)$ applied to $e^\alpha$, which contains the nonzero term $-\frac13\alpha(-3)e^\alpha$; symmetrically $e^\alpha_0e^{-2\alpha}$ is a nonzero vector of charge $-\alpha$. Thus $y_0w$ has nonzero components of charges $\alpha$ and $-\alpha$, and $y_0w\ne0$. In all cases $y\in(V_L^{\hat g})_1\subseteq\mathcal V_1$ and $y_0\ne0$ on $\mathcal V$.

*A self-adjoint choice.* The unitary structure of $\mathcal V$ includes its PCT operator $\phi$, an antilinear involutive automorphism fixing $\mathbf1$ and the conformal vector, and invariance of the scalar product gives $a_n^\dagger=-(\phi a)_{-n}$ for every quasi-primary $a$ of weight one (Carpi et al. 2015, definition of a unitary vertex operator algebra). Every $a\in\mathcal V_1$ is primary: $L_1a\in\mathcal V_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$ with $\langle L_1a,\mathbf1\rangle=\langle a,L_{-1}\mathbf1\rangle=0$, and $L_na=0$ for $n\ge2$ because $\mathcal V$ has no negative weights. Because $\phi$ fixes the conformal vector, it commutes with $L_0$ and preserves $\mathcal V_1$, which is therefore $W\oplus iW$ with $W=\{a\in\mathcal V_1:\phi a=-a\}$. As $a\mapsto a_0$ is complex linear and $y_0\ne0$, some $x\in W$ has $x_0\ne0$, and $x_0^\dagger=-(\phi x)_0=x_0$.

*The automorphisms.* The zero mode $x_0$ is a derivation of $\mathcal V$, $[x_0,Y(b,z)]=Y(x_0b,z)$. For a primary vector of weight one $[L_m,x_n]=-nx_{m+n}$, so $x_0$ commutes with every $L_m$; it annihilates $\mathbf1$ and therefore the conformal vector $L_{-2}\mathbf1$, preserves every finite-dimensional $\mathcal V_n$ and is self-adjoint there. Hence $\exp(itx_0)$ is, for each real $t$, an automorphism of $\mathcal V$ that preserves the scalar product, fixes $\mathbf1$ and the conformal vector, and commutes with $L_0$; on the Hilbert completion these operators form a strongly continuous unitary group, nontrivial because $x_0\ne0$.

(3) follows from (1): for $g=-1$ every standard lift is conjugate to the lift $\theta$ of Theorem P.13.21 (Theorem P.13.24, Step 5), and Theorem P.13.22 identifies the $\theta$-orbifold of $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ with $V^\natural$. The values of $N_{\mathrm{root}}/2$ follow from the twenty-four Niemeier root systems, each of rank $24$ with $N_{\mathrm{root}}=24h$ (Conway and Sloane 1999). ∎

## P.13.10 Weight-2 Structure and the Griess Algebra

### Theorem P.13.25 (Weight-2 Counting)

**Reference:** (Frenkel, Lepowsky and Meurman 1988)

For the Leech lattice VOA $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$, the weight-2 space has dimension:
$$\dim(V_{\Lambda_{24}})_2 = 324 + 196560 = 196884$$

*Proof.*

**Step 1 (Heisenberg contribution).** For rank $r = 24$, weight-2 oscillator states include:
- $\alpha^i_{-2}|0\rangle$: dimension $r = 24$
- $\alpha^i_{-1}\alpha^j_{-1}|0\rangle$: dimension $r(r+1)/2 = 300$

Total Heisenberg contribution: $24 + 300 = 324$.

**Step 2 (Lattice vector contribution).** Vectors of norm 4 in the Leech lattice contribute $e_v$ states. The number of norm-4 vectors is the kissing number: 196,560.

**Step 3 (Total).** $\dim(V_{\Lambda_{24}})_2 = 324 + 196560 = 196884$. $\square$

### Theorem P.13.26 (Moonshine Module Weight-2 Structure)

**Reference:** Dong et al. (2007, §1) for the weight-two identification and dimension; Höhn (2010, §1) for the full automorphism group of the Griess algebra and the historical division of results. The FLM orbifold-character premise is retained separately in Theorem P.13.22 and its source ledger.

The orbifold procedure preserves the weight-2 dimension:
$$\dim(V^\natural_2) = 196884$$

The space $V^\natural_2$ carries the structure of the Griess algebra, a commutative non-associative algebra with the Monster as its automorphism group.

*Proof.* Theorem P.13.22 identifies the object under consideration with the Frenkel--Lepowsky--Meurman $\theta$-orbifold
$$
V^\natural=V_{\Lambda_{24}}^+\oplus V_{\Lambda_{24}}^{T,+}.
$$
The graded-character theorem for this orbifold (Carnahan 2023, Lemma 4.2) states
$$
\operatorname{Tr}_{V^\natural}q^{L_0-1}
=
J(q)
=
q^{-1}+196884q+21493760q^2+\cdots.
$$
The central charge is $24$, so a vector of conformal weight $n$ contributes to the coefficient of $q^{n-1}$. The coefficient of $q$ is therefore
$$
\dim V^\natural_2=196884.
$$
The absence of a constant term also gives $V^\natural_1=0$.

For $u,v\in V^\natural_2$, define
$$
u\cdot v=u_1v.
$$
This product remains in weight two because the mode $u_1$ changes weight by $\operatorname{wt}(u)-1-1=0$. VOA skew-symmetry gives
$$
u_1v
=
v_1u-L_{-1}(v_2u)+\frac12L_{-1}^2(v_3u).
$$
Here $v_2u\in V^\natural_1=0$, while $v_3u\in V^\natural_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$ and $L_{-1}\mathbf1=0$. Hence $u\cdot v=v\cdot u$. For the specific FLM Moonshine module $V^\natural$ identified in Theorem P.13.22, Dong et al. (2007, §1) identify the first-product algebra $(V^\natural_2,u_1v)$ with the 196884-dimensional Griess algebra $\mathcal B$. The conditions $V_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$ and $V_1=0$ establish the elementary commutativity calculation above; by themselves they do not establish this identification. Höhn (2010, §1) records the full algebra-automorphism result $\operatorname{Aut}(\mathcal B)=\mathbb M$ and attributes its fullness to Tits (1984). Transporting automorphisms across the stated algebra isomorphism gives
$$
\operatorname{Aut}(V^\natural_2,\cdot)\cong\mathbb M.
$$
This conclusion is conditional on the separately stated identification of the underlying VOA with $V^\natural$.
Thus the weight-two dimension, product structure, and automorphism group have the asserted values. ∎

## P.13.11 Main Selection Theorem

### Theorem P.13.27 (Moonshine-Module Identification on the Leech Branch)

Assume:
1. the Leech-lattice branch of Theorem P.13.10,
2. the operational exact-symmetry criterion of Definition P.13.2 and Theorem P.13.19, together with the exclusion of every nontrivial positive-dimensional compact automorphism family required by hypothesis (ii) of Theorem P.13.24; Theorem P.13.19 supplies this exclusion only for families satisfying its complete controller/reset and cost hypotheses, while exclusion beyond that class is an independent premise, and
3. the selected vacuum is realized as an orbifold extension of $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ by an involutive standard lift $\hat g$ of an involution $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(\Lambda_{24})$, realizes the canonical $\mathbb Z_2$ of Theorem P.13.23, and satisfies the untwisted-subVOA hypotheses in the final clause of Theorem P.13.24.

Then the resulting holomorphic $c = 24$ vacuum VOA is the Moonshine module:
$$
\mathcal{V}_{\text{PCE}}\cong V^\natural.
$$

*Proof.*

**Step 1 (Lattice selection).** By Theorem P.13.10, the branch lattice is $\Lambda_{24}$.

**Step 2 (Lattice VOA).** By Theorem P.13.14, $\Lambda_{24}$ admits a VOA structure $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ with $c = 24$ and $\dim(V_1) = 24$.

**Step 3 (Orbifold branch and weight-one exclusion).** Assumptions 2--3 supply the final-clause hypotheses of Theorem P.13.24. If $(V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1\ne0$, that theorem produces a nontrivial positive-dimensional compact automorphism family of the selected orbifold, contradicting the controller criterion. Therefore
$$
\dim\big((V_{\Lambda_{24}})^{\hat g}_1\big)=0.
$$

**Step 4 (Weight-one rigidity).** By Theorem P.13.24, the vanishing of the invariant weight-one subspace forces the underlying lattice involution to be $g=-1$. The standard lift $\hat g$ is conjugate to the chosen lift $\theta$ of Theorem P.13.21, so their orbifold extensions are isomorphic.

**Step 5 (FLM construction).** By Theorem P.13.22, the $\theta$-orbifold of $V_{\Lambda_{24}}$ is the Moonshine module $V^\natural$. Therefore the $\hat g$-orbifold is isomorphic to $V^\natural$.

**Step 6 (Uniqueness verification).** By Theorem P.13.16, among holomorphic $c = 24$ VOAs with $\dim(V_1) = 0$ and Griess algebra on $V_2$, exactly one exists: $V^\natural$.

**Step 7 (Conclusion).** On this branch,
$$\mathcal{V}_{\text{PCE}} = V^\natural \quad \square$$

**Epistemic Status:** Conditional framework-to-mathematics identification. The framework fixes the Leech branch and excludes surviving positive-dimensional weight-one symmetry families; once the selected branch is realized as an orbifold by an involutive standard lift, Theorem P.13.24 forces $g=-1$, and the FLM orbifold theorem then identifies $V^\natural$.

### Theorem P.13.28 (Conditional Modular and Weight-One Selection)

Assume the torus, mapping-class, and scalar-partition-function hypotheses of Proposition P.13.6.5. For the VOA-character conclusion, assume additionally that every candidate is a nonnegatively graded, rational, $C_2$-cofinite, holomorphic $c=24$ VOA with trivial modular multiplier. Suppose the admissible class contains at least one candidate $V_0$ with $\dim((V_0)_1)=0$ and finite PCE potential. Suppose also that each candidate $V$ with $\dim(V_1)>0$ carries a positive-dimensional compact operational symmetry region satisfying the controller/reset hypotheses of Theorem P.13.19, and that its remaining PCE terms are finite. Then the scalar character is modular invariant and every finite-potential PCE minimizer satisfies $\dim(V_1)=0$.

*Proof.* Proposition P.13.6.5 gives scalar $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$ invariance under the stated modular hypotheses. Miyamoto's modular-invariance theorem (Miyamoto 2004b, Theorem 5.5) applies on this branch; rationality reduces the modular action to ordinary characters and holomorphicity makes their span one-dimensional, and the trivial-multiplier hypothesis makes it invariant. For a holomorphic $c=24$ candidate,
$$
\chi_V(\tau)=j(\tau)+C,
\qquad
744+C=\dim(V_1).
$$
If $\dim(V_1)>0$, the declared controller branch and Theorem P.13.19 give $V_{\mathrm{op}}(V)=+\infty$. The other PCE terms are finite, so $V_{\mathrm{PCE}}(V)=+\infty$. The candidate $V_0$ has finite potential; hence no infinite-potential candidate can minimize. Therefore every finite-potential minimizer has $\dim(V_1)=0$. This argument does not distinguish among multiple admissible zero-weight-one candidates. ∎

**Epistemic Status:** Conditional framework-to-mathematics selection on the stated modular, admissibility, and registered-controller branch.

### Theorem P.13.28a (Modular Polar Rigidity of the Vacuum Spectrum)

Let $f(\tau)$ and $g(\tau)$ be weakly holomorphic modular functions of weight zero for $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$, with no poles away from the cusp. Suppose their principal parts at $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}=0$ agree:
$$
f(\tau)-g(\tau)=O(q^0).
$$
Then $f-g$ is constant. If their constant terms also agree, then
$$
f(\tau)=g(\tau).
$$
Consequently, on the Moonshine branch, the vacuum character with principal part $q^{-1}$ and vanishing constant term is uniquely
$$
J(\tau)=j(\tau)-744
=
q^{-1}+196884q+21493760q^2+\cdots.
$$

*Proof.* The compactified modular curve
$$
X(1)=SL_2(\mathbb Z)\backslash\mathbb H^*
$$
is compact. Since $f$ and $g$ are weakly holomorphic modular functions with no poles away from the cusp and have the same principal part at the cusp, the difference
$$
h=f-g
$$
has no pole at the cusp and no pole anywhere else on $X(1)$. Thus $h$ is a holomorphic function on the compact Riemann surface $X(1)$. Every holomorphic function on a compact connected Riemann surface is constant, so $f-g$ is constant. If the constant terms also agree, that constant is zero, hence $f=g$.

For the Moonshine branch, the character is a weight-zero modular function with a single pole $q^{-1}$ at the cusp and no other pole. The normalization $\dim(V_1)=0$ from Theorem P.13.28 fixes the constant term to zero. Therefore the preceding uniqueness result identifies the character with $j(\tau)-744=J(\tau)$. ∎

<a id="corollary-p1328b-finite-polar-data-determine-the-infinite-vacuum-tower"></a>**Corollary P.13.28b (Finite Polar Data Determine the Infinite Vacuum Tower).** On the Moonshine branch, once the modular group, weight, pole order $q^{-1}$, and constant term are fixed, all positive Fourier coefficients of the vacuum character are forced.

*Proof.* Theorem P.13.28a proves uniqueness of the modular function with those data. If any positive coefficient differed, the resulting function would be a distinct modular function with the same principal part and constant term, contradicting uniqueness. ∎

### Theorem P.13.28c (Common-Clock Spectral Costs and Finite Package Selection)

Assume the nonnegative integral CFT-type grading, rationality, $C_2$-cofiniteness, holomorphicity, central charge $24$, and trivial scalar modular multiplier of Proposition P.13.6.5. Write $a_P=\dim V(P)_1$ for an admitted package $P$. Theorem P.13.28a gives
$$
Z_P(q)=\operatorname{Tr}_{V(P)}q^{L_0-1}=J(q)+a_P,
\qquad
J(q)=q^{-1}+196884q+21493760q^2+\cdots.
\tag{P.13.28c.1}
$$
Here $q$ denotes the common character coordinate. The vacuum coefficient and all coefficients at conformal weights $n\ge2$ are common to the compared packages.

#### 1. Linear spectral objectives

For an absolutely convergent objective
$$
C_w(P)=\sum_{n\ge0}w_n\dim V(P)_n,
$$
its entire discriminating part is
$$
C_w(P)-C_w(Q)=w_1(a_P-a_Q).
\tag{P.13.28c.2}
$$
Thus $w_1>0$ favors fewer weight-one currents, $w_1<0$ favors more, and $w_1=0$ gives equality. A nonlinear function of the complete scalar spectrum is likewise a function of $a_P$ once the common spectral coefficients are fixed.

*Proof.* The vacuum is $q^{-1}$ because $c/24=1$ and $V_0=\mathbb C\mathbf1$. Subtracting $J$ removes the only principal part; Theorem P.13.28a makes the difference constant, and that constant is $a_P$. Absolute convergence permits subtraction of the linear series, in which every term except $n=1$ cancels. The final assertion follows because the complete coefficient sequence is determined by $a_P$. ∎

#### 2. Canonical free energy has a definite comparison sign

Suppose each nominated package has the same calibrated cylinder convention
$$
H_P=\epsilon(L_0-1)+E_{\mathrm{common}}I,
\qquad
\epsilon=\frac{2\pi\hbar v}{L}>0,
\qquad
q=e^{-\beta\epsilon},
\qquad
\beta=(k_BT)^{-1},\quad T>0.
\tag{P.13.28c.3}
$$
The velocity $v$, circumference $L$, temperature, and additive energy are common to the comparison. Then
$$
F_P=E_{\mathrm{common}}-k_BT\ln\bigl(J(q)+a_P\bigr).
\tag{P.13.28c.4}
$$
For a nominated Moonshine package $P_0$ with $a_{P_0}=0$,
$$
F_P-F_{P_0}
=-k_BT\ln\!\left(1+\frac{a_P}{J(q)}\right).
\tag{P.13.28c.5}
$$
In particular, $F_{744}<F_{24}<F_0$. At $\tau=i$, where $q=e^{-2\pi}$ and $J(i)=984$, the free-energy advantages of the $a=24$ and $a=744$ spectra relative to $a=0$, divided by $k_BT$, are exactly $\ln(42/41)$ and $\ln(72/41)$.

*Proof.* Taking the trace of $e^{-\beta H_P}$ in (P.13.28c.3) gives $e^{-\beta E_{\mathrm{common}}}(J(q)+a_P)$. The definition $F=-k_BT\ln\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}$ proves (P.13.28c.4). Subtraction gives (P.13.28c.5). The positive-coefficient expansion in (P.13.28c.1) gives $J(q)>0$ for $0<q<1$, so every $a_P>0$ strictly lowers this free energy. The two rational ratios follow by substituting $J(i)=984$. ∎

#### 3. Complete finite-cost selector and error margin

Let $\mathfrak P$ be a specified class of admitted realized packages, with its specified package equivalence $\sim$. Suppose the complete descended comparison cost, in a common energy unit, is
$$
\mathcal C(P)=\Gamma(P)-k_BT\ln\bigl(J(q)+a_P\bigr).
\tag{P.13.28c.6}
$$
The function $\Gamma$ contains every remaining candidate-dependent completion, bulk, boundary, apparatus, normalization, control, and cost term; any omitted term must be proved common before it cancels. The common additive energy in (P.13.28c.3) may be absorbed into a common term in $\Gamma$.

For an admitted $P_0$ with $a_{P_0}=0$, strict selection of $P_0$ over every inequivalent admitted package is equivalent to
$$
\Gamma(P)-\Gamma(P_0) >k_BT\ln\!\left(1+\frac{a_P}{J(q)}\right)
\quad\text{for every }P\in\mathfrak P,\ P\not\sim P_0.
\tag{P.13.28c.7}
$$
If $|\widehat\Gamma(P)-\Gamma(P)|\le e_P$, with $e_P\ge0$, a sufficient certified comparison is
$$
\widehat\Gamma(P)-\widehat\Gamma(P_0) >k_BT\ln\!\left(1+\frac{a_P}{J(q)}\right)+e_P+e_{P_0}.
\tag{P.13.28c.8}
$$
For positive-current competitors, the independently derived inequality
$$
\Gamma(P)-\Gamma(P_0)\ge\lambda a_P,
\qquad
\lambda\ge\frac{k_BT}{J(q)}
\tag{P.13.28c.9}
$$
is sufficient. An inequivalent zero-current package instead requires $\Gamma(P)>\Gamma(P_0)$.

*Proof.* Subtract (P.13.28c.6) at $P_0$ from its value at $P$. Positivity of the difference is exactly (P.13.28c.7), for each inequivalent competitor. The error inequalities bound the true difference of $\Gamma$ below by the estimated difference minus $e_P+e_{P_0}$, proving (P.13.28c.8). For $x>0$, $\ln(1+x)<x$, so (P.13.28c.9) is strictly stronger than the required threshold when $a_P>0$. When $a_P=0$, the spectral term cancels and (P.13.28c.7) reduces to the stated strict comparison of $\Gamma$. ∎

Theorem P.13.28 retains its exact registered-controller selection on its own branch. The finite inequalities above apply to the specified complete cost (P.13.28c.6); the character identity supplies neither that physical cost equality nor a choice of $\Gamma$. The admitted chiral functor and response separation of Proposition P.13.30b remain available on their stated source domain. Complete scalar spectra alone do not supply package equivalence or the vertex products already distinguished there.

### <a id="corollary-p1328d-exact-thermal-gaussian-niemeier-threshold"></a>Corollary P.13.28d (Exact Thermal–Gaussian Niemeier Threshold)

Fix the root-length normalization, the complete twenty-four-class Niemeier comparison, and $t>0$ of Selection Principle P.13.9. Write $q=e^{-2\pi t}$, $\Lambda$ for the Leech lattice, and $N_L$ for a competitor's root count. On the explicitly specified combined-cost model
$$
\mathcal C(L)-\mathcal C(\Lambda)
=\kappa_{\mathrm{lat}}N_L\Delta(it)
-k_BT\ln\!\left(1+\frac{N_L}{J(it)+24}\right),
\quad \kappa_{\mathrm{lat}}>0,\quad T>0,
\tag{P.13.28d.1}
$$
Leech strictly beats every rootful Niemeier competitor if and only if
$$
\kappa_{\mathrm{lat}}\Delta(it) >\frac{k_BT}{48}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{48}{J(it)+24}\right).
\tag{P.13.28d.2}
$$
The Gaussian and thermal moduli in this model are the same registered $it$; on the cylinder branch this means $\beta\epsilon=2\pi t$. All other candidate-dependent terms are included in the specified cost or proved to cancel.

*Proof.* The $\theta$ identity of Selection Principle P.13.9 and $\eta^{24}=\Delta$ give
$$
\Theta_L-\Theta_\Lambda=N_L\Delta,
\qquad
Z_L-Z_\Lambda=N_L,
\qquad
Z_\Lambda=J+24.
\tag{P.13.28d.3}
$$
Thus (P.13.28d.1) is exactly the sum of the Gaussian difference and the common-clock canonical thermal difference. Put $A=J(it)+24>0$. For $N>0$,
$$
\frac{d}{dN}\frac{\ln(1+N/A)}{N}
=\frac{N/(A+N)-\ln(1+N/A)}{N^2}<0.
\tag{P.13.28d.4}
$$
Indeed, $g(x)=\ln(1+x)-x/(1+x)$ has $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=x/(1+x)^2>0$ for $x>0$. The smallest nonzero Niemeier root count is $48$, attained by $A_1^{24}$. Dividing (P.13.28d.1) by $N_L$ therefore makes that lattice the largest required threshold. This proves sufficiency of (P.13.28d.2), and the $A_1^{24}$ competitor proves necessity. ∎

Selection Principle P.13.9 specifies the pure Gaussian restriction. Equation (P.13.28d.1) is an additional complete-cost model with a retained thermal term. Its positive net margin selects the lattice isometry class in this model; a same-realization dynamical gap or stability theorem remains a separate claim.

### Theorem P.13.28e (Package Classification on the Program-Processor Controller Branch)

Let $\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{orb}}$ be the class of packages $P=(L,g,\hat g,\mathcal V,\Phi)$ in which $[L]\in\mathfrak N_{24}$ carries the fixed normalization of Selection Principles P.13.7–P.13.8; $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(L)$ satisfies $g^2=I$; $\hat g$ is an involutive standard lift of $g$ to $V_L$; $\mathcal V$ is the orbifold extension of $V_L^{\hat g}$ by its $\hat g$-twisted sector ($\mathcal V=V_L$ when $g=I$), realized as a unitary vertex operator algebra of CFT type with finite-dimensional graded subspaces that contains $V_L^{\hat g}$ with the same conformal vector; and $\Phi$ is a controller of the program-processor branch of Theorem P.13.19c for the group $\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)$ of automorphisms of $\mathcal V$ preserving its scalar product, with common $\epsilon$ and $T_{\mathrm{call}}$. Packages are equivalent when their algebras $\mathcal V$ are isomorphic, the controller being transported. Let the complete descended cost be
$$
\mathcal C(P)=V^{\mathrm{prog}}_{\mathrm{eff}}\bigl(\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)\bigr)+\mathcal R(P),
\tag{P.13.28e.1}
$$
where $\mathcal R(P)$ contains every other candidate-dependent term of the complete descended cost, with $\mathcal R(P)>-\infty$ for every package and $\mathcal R(P)<\infty$ for the package $(\Lambda_{24},-1)$. Then:

1. if $(L,g)$ is not isomorphic to $(\Lambda_{24},-1)$, the group $\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)$ is infinite and $\mathcal C(P)=+\infty$;
2. if $(L,g)\cong(\Lambda_{24},-1)$, then $\mathcal V\cong V^\natural$, $\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)=\mathbb M$ and
$$
\mathcal C(P)\le\frac{\epsilon(|\mathbb M|-1)}{2T_{\mathrm{call}}}+\mathcal R(P)<\infty;
$$
3. hence $V^\natural$ is the unique class minimizing $\mathcal C$ on $\mathfrak P_{\mathrm{orb}}$, every inequivalent package has infinite cost, and a package is excluded exactly when $\dim(V_L^{\hat g})_1>0$, with $\dim(V_L^{\hat g})_1=N_{\mathrm{root}}(L)/2$ for $g=-1$ (Proposition P.13.24a).

*Proof.* $\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)$ acts on the Hilbert completion by unitaries that fix $\mathbf1$ and preserve every $\mathcal V_n$. It is a closed subgroup of the compact metrizable group $\prod_nU(\mathcal V_n)$, because preserving each finite-grade product $\mathcal V_k\otimes\mathcal V_l\to\mathcal V_m$, $a\otimes b\mapsto a_jb$, is a closed condition; on it the product topology is the strong topology, and the action is faithful. Theorem P.13.19c therefore applies to $G=\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)$.

(1) Proposition P.13.24a(1) gives $(V_L^{\hat g})_1\ne0$, and Proposition P.13.24a(2) gives a nontrivial strongly continuous one-parameter subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_u(\mathcal V)$. Theorem P.13.19c(3) gives $V^{\mathrm{prog}}_{\mathrm{eff}}=+\infty$, and $\mathcal R(P)>-\infty$ gives $\mathcal C(P)=+\infty$.

(2) Every standard lift of $-1$ is conjugate to $\theta$, and conjugation transports the orbifold extension data (Theorem P.13.24, Steps 5–6); Theorem P.13.22 identifies the $\theta$-orbifold with $V^\natural$. Theorem P.13.29 gives $\operatorname{Aut}(V^\natural)=\mathbb M$, and the Monster preserves the positive invariant scalar product of $V^\natural$ (Proposition P.13.30b), so $\operatorname{Aut}_u(V^\natural)=\mathbb M$. Theorem P.13.19c(4) bounds the controller term.

(3) follows from (1), (2) and Proposition P.13.24a. ∎

The classification uses no lattice-sector cost; on its own certified Gaussian branch, Theorem P.13.10 selects the same lattice $\Lambda_{24}$.

# Part V: The Monster Group

## P.13.12 Main Results

### Theorem P.13.29 (Moonshine Automorphism Theorem)

**Reference:** (Miyamoto 2004a, §9) (an independent full-group proof identifying the VOA with the FLM Moonshine module).

$$\text{Aut}(V^\natural) = \mathbb{M}$$

The Monster group $\mathbb{M}$ is the largest sporadic simple group. Its order has the factorization recorded in the ATLAS Monster entry (Wilson et al. n.d.):

$$\approx 8.08 \times 10^{53}$$

### P.13.19.3 What the Monster Represents

The Monster group $\mathbb M=\operatorname{Aut}(V^\natural)$ is the complete automorphism group of the Moonshine VOA on the P.13.27 branch. Its elements preserve the vacuum vector, conformal vector, grading, and vertex-operator product of $V^\natural$, and therefore preserve the graded character and the associated Moonshine-module structure.

Proposition P.13.19.3a proves that a fixed positive trace-preserving map sending every state of the orbit of the matrix attractor $\rho_0=\frac12I_2\oplus0_6$ to a pure state is constant; Theorem P.13.30c realizes the QFI responses of $\rho_0$ instead by a coupling to grade-two vectors of $V^\natural$. Deriving $\mathbb M$ as a stabilizer of predictive data, or making $\mathbb M$ a spacetime symmetry, requires an explicit realization homomorphism and a proof that it preserves the retained response algebra.

<a id="proposition-p13193a-pure-output-realization-obstruction"></a>**Proposition P.13.19.3a (Pure-Output Realization Obstruction).** Let $E$ be a positive trace-preserving linear map from the operators on $\mathbb C^{d}$, $d\ge3$, to the trace-class operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$.

1. If $E(P/2)$ is pure for every rank-two orthogonal projector $P$, there is a pure state $\sigma$ with $E(X)=\operatorname{Tr}(X)\,\sigma$ for every $X$. Such a map sends the whole orbit $\mathcal O_{\rho_0}$ of Theorem P.13.5a to one state, so the output quantum Fisher information vanishes and every output response is constant on the orbit.
2. Let $\rho_t=\frac12(|1\rangle\langle1|+|v_t\rangle\langle v_t|)$ with $v_t=\cos t\,|2\rangle+\sin t\,|3\rangle$. Its quantum Fisher information is $2$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_t|2\rangle\langle2|)=\frac12\cos^2t$. If $E(\rho_t)$ is pure for every $t$ in an interval of positive length, then $E(\rho_t)$ is constant on that interval.
3. Put $\rho_{12}=\frac12(|1\rangle\langle1|+|2\rangle\langle2|)$ and $\rho_{13}=\frac12(|1\rangle\langle1|+|3\rangle\langle3|)$, at trace distance $\frac12$. If $E$ preserves this trace distance, then $\operatorname{Tr}E(\rho_{12})^2+\operatorname{Tr}E(\rho_{13})^2\le\frac32$, so one of the two outputs has purity at most $\frac34$. The bound is attained by the measure-and-prepare map $E(X)=\sum_k\langle k|X|k\rangle\tau_k$ with $\tau_1=|+\rangle\langle+|$, $\tau_2=|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $\tau_3=|1\rangle\langle1|$ on a qubit: both outputs have purity $\frac34$ and trace distance $\frac12$.

*Proof.* (1) For orthonormal $u,w$ and $P=|u\rangle\langle u|+|w\rangle\langle w|$, positivity and trace preservation make $E(|u\rangle\langle u|)$ and $E(|w\rangle\langle w|)$ density operators whose equal mixture is the pure state $E(P/2)$; a pure state is an extreme point, so both equal $E(P/2)$. Any two unit vectors $x,y$ lie in a common two-dimensional subspace $S$, and applying this to orthonormal bases of $S$ containing $x$ and $y$ gives $E(|x\rangle\langle x|)=E(P_S/2)=E(|y\rangle\langle y|)=:\sigma$. Rank-one projectors span all operators, so linearity gives $E(X)=\operatorname{Tr}(X)\sigma$.

(2) The state $\rho_t$ has eigenvalue $\frac12$ on $|1\rangle$ and on $v_t$ and eigenvalue $0$ elsewhere, and $\partial_t\rho_t=\frac12(|\dot v_t\rangle\langle v_t|+|v_t\rangle\langle\dot v_t|)$ with $\dot v_t=-\sin t\,|2\rangle+\cos t\,|3\rangle$ orthogonal to $|1\rangle$ and $v_t$. The only nonzero matrix elements of $\partial_t\rho_t$ in this eigenbasis are $\langle v_t|\partial_t\rho_t|\dot v_t\rangle=\langle\dot v_t|\partial_t\rho_t|v_t\rangle=\frac12$, so
$$
F_Q(\rho_t)=2\sum_{p_i+p_k>0}\frac{|\langle i|\partial_t\rho_t|k\rangle|^2}{p_i+p_k}=2\Bigl(\frac{1/4}{1/2}+\frac{1/4}{1/2}\Bigr)=2 .
$$
If $E(\rho_t)$ is pure, the argument of (1) gives $E(|1\rangle\langle1|)=E(|v_t\rangle\langle v_t|)=E(\rho_t)$, so $E(\rho_t)=E(|1\rangle\langle1|)$ throughout the interval.

(3) Write $\tau_k=E(|k\rangle\langle k|)$. Since $E(\rho_{12})-E(\rho_{13})=\frac12(\tau_2-\tau_3)$, preservation of the distance gives $\frac12\|\tau_2-\tau_3\|_1=1$, so $\tau_2$ and $\tau_3$ have orthogonal supports and $\tau_2+\tau_3\le I$. Then
$$
\operatorname{Tr}E(\rho_{12})^2+\operatorname{Tr}E(\rho_{13})^2
=\tfrac14\bigl(2\operatorname{Tr}\tau_1^2+\operatorname{Tr}\tau_2^2+\operatorname{Tr}\tau_3^2+2\operatorname{Tr}\tau_1(\tau_2+\tau_3)\bigr)\le\tfrac14(2+1+1+2)=\tfrac32 .
$$
In the example, $E(\rho_{12})=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\1/4&1/4\end{pmatrix}$ and $E(\rho_{13})=\begin{pmatrix}1/4&1/4\\1/4&3/4\end{pmatrix}$ have purity $\frac34$, and their difference is $\operatorname{diag}(\frac12,-\frac12)$. ∎

Let $P_{N}$ be the spectral projection of $L_{0}$ through grade $N$, and $Q_N=I-P_N$. Every $P_{N}$ has finite rank because the VOA has finite-dimensional graded spaces. For an initial vector in $P_{N}$, evolve the finite carrier with the actual compressed generator

## 5. Complete finite instruments and their loss record

For a finite bounded instrument $K_{y}$ with $\sum K_y^*K_y=I$ and bounded $[L_0,K_y]$, set $A_y=P_NK_yP_N$ on $P_{N}H$. Then $\sum A_y^*A_y\le P_N$. Define the genuine additional Kraus operator

Indeed, move $L_{0}$ across $K_{y}$ and use complete normalization; the commutator remainder is bounded by the displayed sum. Consequently $\ell_N\le(E+C_{\mathrm{inst}})/(N+1)$. Comparing the full Stinespring output with the finite one plus its orthogonal failure label gives squared vector difference exactly $2\ell_N$, hence output trace-norm error at most $2\sqrt{2\ell_N}$. The smooth bounded-instrument class is response-separating. For any finite bounded local Kraus family, use one common nonnegative normalized smooth smearing kernel $f_{\epsilon}$. Its square root has bounded first commutator: the Sylvester equation $\sqrt{D}\,X+X\sqrt{D}=[L_0,D]$ has the norm-convergent solution $\int_0^\infty\exp[-t\sqrt{D}]\,[L_0,D]\,\exp[-t\sqrt{D}]\,dt$, bounded by $\lVert[L_0,D]\rVert/(2\sqrt{\delta})$. This is $X=[L_0,\sqrt{D}]$ on the energy core. The square root supplies the loss Kraus operator. **Branch normalization for the P14 cutoff instrument**

The complete Kraus instrument and its native-drift dilation satisfy the joint flagged-channel estimate. Its conditional outputs are the subnormalized maps in the complete flagged output. Normalization at a selected outcome uses that outcome's probability in the bound below.

Let $\sigma_y=K_y\rho K_y^*$ and $\tau_y=P_N\sigma_y P_N$ for an input $\rho$ supported on $P_{N}$. Write $p_y=\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_y$, $\ell_y=\operatorname{Tr}(Q_N\sigma_y)$, and $q_y=\operatorname{Tr}\tau_y=p_y-\ell_y$. The sum $\ell=\sum_y\ell_y$ is the source's retained-loss probability. On the common enlarged output space the original full instrument has a zero failure branch, and the finite instrument has its actual additional $A_{\mathrm{fail}}$ branch. Their joint trace-norm discrepancy is at most $2\sqrt{2\ell}$, including every label and its subnormalized state. Dephasing or selecting a label is trace-norm contractive, so this is also a valid bound for any selected subnormalized branch. It does not normalize that branch.

If $p_y>\ell_y$, both ordinary branch probabilities are positive and

$$
\lVert \sigma_y/p_y - \tau_y/q_y\rVert_1 \le 2\sqrt{\ell_y/p_y}.
$$

To prove this, purify $\sigma_y/p_y$. Project the source factor onto $P_{N}$ and normalize; the pure-state overlap is $\sqrt{1-\ell_y/p_y}$. The trace-norm distance of the two pure states is $2\sqrt{\ell_y/p_y}$, and partial trace is contractive. For pure $\sigma_{y}$ this bound is exact. If $q_{y}=0$ there is no normalized finite output on that label and no such comparison is defined. The additional finite failure label has no normalized reference counterpart because its reference probability is zero.

More generally, let two positive subnormalized branch outputs $\sigma,\tau$ satisfy $\lVert\sigma-\tau\rVert_1\le\delta$, with $p=\operatorname{Tr}\sigma>0$ and $q=\operatorname{Tr}\tau>0$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
|p - q| &\le \delta, \\
\lVert \sigma/p - \tau/q\rVert_1 &\le 2\delta/p.
\end{aligned}
$$

The latter follows by adding and subtracting $\tau/p$ and using $\operatorname{Tr}\tau=q$. A lower bound $p\ge s>\delta$ ensures $q>0$ and gives $2\delta/s$. Interchanging $\sigma$ and $\tau$ gives the alternative denominator $q$; the stated safe bound suffices. Prior dynamics and coefficient errors may first be added at the complete-channel/subnormalized level and only then propagated with the declared probability floor.

A rare-branch family shows why the denominator is indispensable. On a two-level output with $P=|0\rangle\langle 0|$, let $\sigma_\epsilon=\epsilon|+\rangle\langle +|$. Then $p=\epsilon$, $\ell=\epsilon/2$, $\tau=(\epsilon/2)|0\rangle\langle 0|$. Its subnormalized discrepancy vanishes with $\epsilon$, while its normalized branch discrepancy is exactly $\sqrt{2}$. A complete realization takes a pure input $|0\rangle$ and Kraus $K_1=\sqrt{\epsilon}\,|+\rangle\langle 0|$ and $K_2=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{1-\epsilon},1)$; their effects sum to $I$. The same rare-branch behavior persists as $\epsilon$ tends to zero. No branch-independent normalized error tending to zero follows from a small total loss alone.

### A finite-energy input not already in the cutoff

The displayed dynamical theorem assumes the initial vector lies in $P_{N}$. To use it for a general normalized finite-energy vector $\psi$ with energy $E$, include initial preparation/projection explicitly. $$

$$

Unitary evolution preserves that initial difference. Adding it to the source theorem, with $E_{N}$ as the prepared cutoff input energy, gives a valid convergent sequence. Alternatively retain the initial projection's failure flag as another complete instrument. Its preparation, failure and retries belong in the ledger. ## 1. Complete common-clock character identity

The root-normalized modular identity in P.13.9 and $\eta^{24}=\Delta$ imply exactly

$$
\begin{aligned}
\chi_L(q) &= j(q) + r_L - 720 \\
&= J(q) + r_L + 24, \\
r_L &= \text{number of norm-two lattice vectors}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $\dim(V_L)_0=1$, $\dim(V_L)_1=r_L+24$, and for every $n\ge 2$ the coefficient $\dim(V_L)_n$ is the same Moonshine coefficient. Equality here is the entire convergent function for $0<q<1$, not a finite-order expansion. Candidates with equal $r_{L}$ have equal multiplicity at every eigenvalue of the same physical Hamiltonian; a grading-preserving Hilbert-space unitary intertwines their free Hamiltonians. Consequently every retained record depending only on that spectral measure, including arbitrary temperature derivatives, is identical.

This does not assert that their operator products, local nets, lattice marks or controlled response maps are intertwined by that grading unitary. The strict observable functor constructed above retains those data.

## 2. A concrete exactly degenerate pair

Take the two original Niemeier classes with root systems

$$
\begin{aligned}
R_A &= A_5 + A_5 + A_5 + A_5 + D_4, \\
R_B &= D_4 + D_4 + D_4 + D_4 + D_4 + D_4.
\end{aligned}
$$

Both have rank twenty-four and Coxeter number six. $A_{r}$ has $r(r+1)$ roots; $D_{r}$ has $2r(r-1)$ roots. Hence both root counts are 144 and both weight-one spaces have dimension 168. Their complete characters are $J(q)+168$, at the same normalization and physical clock.

The lattice current source, however, obeys the actual VOA zero-mode brackets. Its Cartan states are $h(-1)1$ and its root states are $e_{\alpha}$ for $\lVert\alpha\rVert^2=2$. The lattice vertex formula and its sign cocycle give

$$
\begin{aligned}
{}[h(0),e_\alpha(0)] &= (h,\alpha)e_\alpha(0), \\
{}[e_\alpha(0),e_\beta(0)] &= \epsilon(\alpha,\beta)e_{\alpha+\beta}(0) \\
&\quad \text{if } (\alpha,\beta)=-1,
\end{aligned}
$$

with the Cartan bracket when $\beta=-\alpha$ and zero when no root sum exists. These are the simply-laced compact-current Lie algebra after the usual Hermitian real-form choice. Orthogonal root components commute. Because the roots span the full rank twenty-four in this pair, there is no residual abelian current factor. Thus the weight-one current algebras are

$$
\begin{aligned}
g_A &= \mathrm{su}(6)^{4} \oplus \mathrm{so}(8), \\
g_B &= \mathrm{so}(8)^{6}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Their complexifications have respectively five and six simple ideals. This invariant is preserved by every VOA isomorphism, since an isomorphism preserves weight one and the product $u_{0}$ v. The two sources are therefore not equivalent under the package-isomorphism category despite their entire identical rotation spectra.

$$

This statement is unchanged by the irrelevant scalar phase of a tomographically reconstructed unitary channel. Therefore a finite process-tomography family at this one registered angle determines the simultaneous commutant dimension; no infinitesimal derivative recovery is needed. ## 4. Populated source matrices and normalization certificate

The two literal triangular arrays below are the primary integer Gram records, at the common root-length-squared-two normalization. Each is exactly even, positive definite and determinant one. The rational LDL enumeration visits respectively 18,011 and 16,233 search nodes and exhausts all nonzero vectors of norm at most two. It finds 144 roots in each source. The graph joining roots with nonzero inner product has components of ranks/root counts (4,24),(5,30),(5,30),(5,30),(5,30) in the first case and six copies of (4,24) in the second. This independently populates the root types and their orthogonal source support. The exact recurrence below generates every finite root coordinate and determines its norm and component rank.

For an explicit source-coordinate current construction, use the weight-one basis $h_i=b_i(-1)1$ for the twenty-four lattice basis vectors and $e_{\alpha}$ for the 144 certified roots. Its positive Gram matrix is $S=\operatorname{diag}(G,I_{144})$. Let

$$
\epsilon(a,b) = (-1)^{\sum_{i>j} a_i b_j G_{ij} + \sum_i a_i b_i G_{ii}/2}.
$$

These are integer lattice coordinates. The exponent is bilinear over the integers, so $\epsilon$ is an associative sign cocycle; its commutator is $(-1)^{a^T G b}$, as required by lattice locality. For a root $\alpha$, $\epsilon(\alpha,-\alpha)=-1$. The source zero-mode matrices are exactly

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_\alpha h_i &= -(G\alpha)_i\, e_\alpha, \\
E_\alpha e_\beta &= \epsilon(\alpha,\beta)\, e_{\alpha+\beta} \quad \text{if } \alpha^{T} G \beta = -1, \\
E_\alpha e_{-\alpha} &= -\sum_i \alpha_i h_i, \\
E_\alpha e_\beta &= 0 \quad \text{otherwise}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Cartan $H_{i}$ acts by $(G\beta)_i$ on $e_{\beta}$ and by zero on all $h_{j}$. The zero-mode source formula gives these entries before any response comparison. Direct substitution in these finite matrices gives the physical adjoint relation $E_\alpha^\dagger=-E_{-\alpha}$ in the $S$ metric, and $[E_\alpha,E_{-\alpha}]=-H_\alpha$. Hence $X_\alpha=E_\alpha-E_{-\alpha}$ and $Y_\alpha=i(E_\alpha+E_{-\alpha})$ are Hermitian. One root from every opposite pair gives 144 such Hermitian controls; with the twenty-four $H_{i}$ they form a complete 168-dimensional real current basis.

Conjugating by the positive square root $S^{1/2}$ places these matrices in an orthonormal physical basis. This is one fixed source coordinate conversion, not a change in the root normalization or the physical clock. The compact $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ generated by each opposite root pair unitarily conjugates $X_{\alpha}$ and $Y_{\alpha}$ to $H_{\alpha}$. The simply-laced root strings give $H_{\alpha}$ spectrum contained in $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$; hence both root controls have norm at most two. Since $G_{ii}$ is two or four and $\beta$ has norm two, integral Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|(G\beta)_i|\le 2$, so the Cartan controls have the same norm bound. Divide every source matrix by the common number three and use the fixed angle $1/4$ as above. The physical source norm is then at most $2/3$. No candidate-specific gain is chosen from a desired comparison result.

The complete source preparation space includes the vacuum and $H_1$, of dimension 169. It embeds in 256 levels, or eight qubits, with explicitly unused levels. A binary pointer gives a 512-dimensional finite dilation; a sequence of tomography settings uses fresh pointers/copies or an owned reset. The non-scalar native Hamiltonian on the vacuum-plus-current space is $\hbar\omega\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,\dots,0)$, together with registered padding and apparatus energies. Preparation/readout use the exact drift-tracked dilation constructed above. Current gates preserve $H_1$ and commute with this native field Hamiltonian. Tables, physical source preparation energy, clock accuracy, field support, all outcomes and discarded/fresh supplies are charged for the actual number of settings and repetitions.

These are global current controls on the owned circle support. They are not claimed to be operations in one small interval algebra. The strict net functor retains the local observable structure, while this finite current protocol uses the separately declared whole-circle support. No unproved instantaneous spatial propagation or fixed local-gate depth is implied.

**Exact root enumeration and component ranks.** Starting from either displayed symmetric matrix $G$, compute its rational unit-lower-triangular factorization by
$$
 d_i=G_{ii}-\sum_{k<i}\ell_{ik}^2d_k,\qquad
 \ell_{ji}=\frac{G_{ji}-\sum_{k<i}\ell_{jk}\ell_{ik}d_k}{d_i},\quad j>i.
$$
Direct substitution reconstructs $G=LDL^{\mathsf T}$, with $d_i>0$ and $\prod_i d_i=1$ in both cases. The integer diagonal entries are even, so the resulting lattice is even, positive and unimodular in the fixed metric.

Enumerate the integer coordinates in reverse order $i=24,\ldots,1$. If $x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{24}$ are fixed and $R_i$ is the remaining squared norm, set
$$
 c_i=\sum_{j>i}\ell_{ji}x_j,\qquad
 q_i=\left\lceil\sqrt{R_i/d_i}\right\rceil,
$$
$$
 \lfloor-c_i\rfloor-q_i\le x_i\le\lceil-c_i\rceil+q_i,
 \qquad R_{i-1}=R_i-d_i(x_i+c_i)^2\ge0.
$$
Start at $R_{24}=2$ and retain all such integer choices in increasing order. At a leaf discard the zero vector. The identity
$$
 x^{\mathsf T}Gx=\sum_{i=1}^{24}d_i(x_i+c_i)^2
$$
shows both soundness and exhaustive coverage. Positivity bounds every interval finitely. Evenness forces each nonzero retained vector to have norm exactly two, so the generated set is precisely the full root set $\mathcal R(G)$. All square-root ceilings are characterized by the integer inequality $(q_i-1)^2<R_i/d_i\le q_i^2$, with $q_i=0$ when $R_i=0$.

Join two distinct generated roots when $\alpha^{\mathsf T}G\beta\ne0$. Taking connected components and ordinary rational row elimination gives the following complete finite calculation:

| Input | Recursion nodes | Roots | Component $(\text{rank},\text{root count})$ | Root-span rank | Weight-one dimension | Current commutant dimension |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|

| $G_B$ | $16{,}233$ | $144$ | six copies of $(4,24)$ | $24$ | $168$ | $6$ |

The recurrence fixes every root coordinate; the displayed matrices fix every input. A nonzero inner product is exactly an edge, so no orthogonal component can be omitted by the traversal.
