## Theorem P.16.3a: General measurable prohibition classification

**Local subparts.** The parenthesized subparts of P.16.3a below supply the measurable-classification clause. Selection and realization are supplied by the subsequent common construction in this insertion.

### C0. Authority, scope, and fixed data

The controlling result is **Theorem P.16.3 (Finite-Kernel Classification of Prohibition Access)**, which establishes the finite access equivalence, finite closed-class criterion, finite K1/K2/K3 exclusions, and compatibility countermodels. The construction here extends it to the measurable setting with the necessary continuum qualifications. The full problem has three parts: selection of a dynamics law fixing the structure on P, continuum classification, and realization of the selected kernel.

This scope respects **Definition P.16.1** (candidate post-update targets), **Definition P.16.3** (a base-relative, certificate-relative cost, when its realizer and reduction premises are supplied), **Theorem P.16.1**, **Proposition P.16.2**, **Remark P.16.2**, **Corollary P.16.1**, and **P.16.9**. A static cost does not specify a transition law. The mathematics below permits any registered measurable cost; identifying it with the certificate-relative cost of Definition P.16.3 requires that definition's independent premises. A kernel on attempted-update requests is not silently a kernel on completed physical self-models.

No environmental support hypothesis is assumed. The distinctions below preserve **Hypothesis 14.5.8**, **Proposition 14.5.8b** (cost preference does not establish support exclusion), **Proposition 14.5.8c** (conditional boundary charging under weak recovery limits), and **Proposition 14.5.8d** (window-local laws need not glue).

#### Registered mathematical domain

Let $(\Theta,B)$ be a standard Borel space, let $U:\Theta\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable, and put

\[
P=\{U=\infty\},\qquad A=\{U<\infty\}.
\]

Both sets are measurable; assume both are nonempty. Let K be a Markov probability kernel on this one fixed state space. Its homogeneous discrete-time chain has law $P_{x}$ from x. A changing base, controller, budget, or environment must already be included in $\Theta$, or a separate lumpability/intertwining proof must justify the reduced K. None is supplied by the symbol U.

For a kernel $L$ and a finite positive measure $\lambda$, write $(\lambda L)(B)=\int L(x,B)\,\lambda(dx)$. The notation $0\ne\lambda<\infty$ means a nonzero finite positive measure. A stationary probability satisfies $\pi K=\pi$. All claims about sample times concern $n=0,1,2,\dots$ under the registered clock; they do not assert exclusion at intervening physical times.

Standard Borelness ensures the usual countable-time path-law construction from the consistent iterated-kernel finite-dimensional laws. The proofs below use only these iterated integrals, countable unions, monotone/dominated convergence, and explicitly stated topological assumptions.

### C1. Exact access and finite invariant-measure classification

#### Theorem P.16.3a(1) (Measurable access and killed invariant mass)

1. The following pointwise statements are equivalent:

\[
\forall x\in A:\quad
\mathbb P_x(\exists n\ge1:X_n\in P)=0,
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.1}
\]

\[
\forall x\in A:\quad K(x,P)=0.
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.2}
\]

2. Assume (P.16.3a.C1.2). Define the Markov restriction R on A and the substochastic restriction Q on P by

\[
R(x,B)=K(x,B)\quad(x\in A,\ B\subseteq A),
\qquad
Q(x,B)=K(x,B)\quad(x\in P,\ B\subseteq P).
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.3}
\]

Then

\[
\exists\pi\text{ stationary probability for }K\text{ with }\pi(P)>0
\iff
\exists\,0\ne\mu<\infty\text{ on }P:\ \mu Q=\mu.
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.4}
\]

Every finite Q-invariant measure has zero leakage into A:

\[
\int_P K(x,A)\,\mu(dx)=0.
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.5}
\]

Its extension by zero to $\Theta$ is $K$-invariant and, after division by $\mu(P)$, is a stationary probability supported in the measure-theoretic sense on $P$.

3. More exactly, every stationary $\pi$ decomposes as

\[
\pi=\nu+\mu,
\quad \nu=\pi|_A,\quad\mu=\pi|_P,
\quad \nu R=\nu,\quad\mu Q=\mu,
\quad\nu(A)+\mu(P)=1,
\tag{P.16.3a.C1.6}
\]

where either summand may be zero. Conversely, every pair of such finite invariant positive measures with total mass one gives a stationary $\pi$ by extension and addition.

Consequently:

- Every stationary probability vanishes on P exactly when Q has no nonzero finite invariant positive measure.
- At least one stationary probability for K exists exactly when R has a stationary probability or Q has a nonzero finite invariant positive measure.
- If Q has no such measure, the stationary probabilities of K are precisely the zero-extensions of stationary probabilities of R. In particular, uniqueness on the whole space then means existence and uniqueness on A; it is not implied by exclusion alone.

##### Proof

If (P.16.3a.C1.2) holds, $K(x,A)=1$ for every $x\in A$. Induction gives $K^n(x,A)=1$ for every $n\ge 1$: if it holds at $n$, then

\[
K^{n+1}(x,A)=\int_A K(y,A)K^n(x,dy)=1.
\]

Thus each event $\{X_n\in P\}$ has probability zero, and so does their countable union. Conversely, (P.16.3a.C1.1) implies $K(x,P)=P_x(X_1\in P)=0$ for every $x\in A$. This proves item 1.

The restrictions in (P.16.3a.C1.3) are measurable kernels on the trace sigma-algebras. $R(x,A)=1$ and $Q(x,P)\le 1$. If $\pi$ is stationary and $B\subseteq P$ is measurable, then

\[
\pi(B)=\int_\Theta K(x,B)\pi(dx)
       =\int_P Q(x,B)\pi(dx),
\]

because $K(x,B)\le K(x,P)=0$ for $x\in A$. Hence $\mu=\pi|_P$ satisfies $\mu Q=\mu$. If $\pi(P)>0$, this $\mu$ is nonzero and finite.

Conversely, suppose $0\ne\mu<\infty$ and $\mu Q=\mu$. Evaluate this identity on $P$:

\[
\mu(P)=\int_PQ(x,P)\mu(dx)
       =\mu(P)-\int_PK(x,A)\mu(dx).
\]

Finiteness makes the subtraction legitimate. Therefore (P.16.3a.C1.5) holds. Since the integrand is nonnegative, $K(x,A)=0$ for $\mu$-almost every $x\in P$. For any measurable $B\subseteq\Theta$,

\[
\begin{aligned}
(\widetilde\mu K)(B)
 &=\int_PK(x,B\cap P)\mu(dx)
   +\int_PK(x,B\cap A)\mu(dx)\\
 &=\mu(B\cap P)+0
 =\widetilde\mu(B),
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(\widetilde\mu(B)=\mu(B\cap P)\). Normalize by $0<\mu(P)<\infty$. This proves (P.16.3a.C1.4), including the extension direction and its zero-leakage step.

For a stationary $\pi$, its $P$ restriction is $Q$-invariant, so the preceding zero-leakage calculation applies to $\mu=\pi|_P$. For $B\subseteq A$, stationarity now gives

\[
\pi(B)=\int_A R(x,B)\pi(dx)+\int_PK(x,B)\pi(dx)
      =(\nu R)(B).
\]

Thus $\nu R=\nu$. Conversely, extending a finite $R$-invariant $\nu$ by zero is $K$-invariant because $A$ has no outgoing mass to $P$. The same is true for $\mu$ by (P.16.3a.C1.5). Their sum is stationary. Any nonzero finite invariant summand normalizes to a probability, proving all existence and uniqueness assertions. ∎

**Why finiteness matters.** A $\sigma$-finite invariant measure of infinite total mass does not satisfy the cancellation step $\mu(P)-\mu Q(P)$; both quantities may be infinite. Counting measure for bilateral translation on the integers is an invariant infinite measure although there is no invariant probability. Such a measure does not answer the stationary-probability question in (P.16.3a.C1.4).

#### Corollary P.16.3a(2) (Recovery of the accepted finite theorem)

If $\Theta$ is finite, K always has a stationary probability. Without any no-access assumption, every stationary probability vanishes on P exactly when every closed communicating class is contained in A. Under (P.16.3a.C1.2), classes cannot meet both A and P; hence the criterion becomes “there is no closed communicating class contained in P,” exactly as in Theorem P.16.3.

##### Proof

Here are the finite facts, included to expose exactly where finiteness enters rather than importing them into the measurable theorem.

For a finite Markov matrix, form its directed graph with an edge $x\to y$ precisely when $K(x,y)>0$. Its finitely many strongly connected components form a finite acyclic graph. Every vertex has a finite directed path to a sink component; sink components are the closed communicating classes. Let $C$ be their union and $T$ its complement. Choose, for each $x\in T$, one path to $C$. Finiteness permits a common length bound $m$ and a strictly positive lower bound $\varepsilon$ on the products of the finitely many chosen path probabilities. Because $C$ is closed,

\[
\inf_{x\in T}\mathbb P_x(X_m\in C)\ge\varepsilon,
\quad
\sup_{x\in T}\mathbb P_x(X_{jm}\in T)\le(1-\varepsilon)^j.
\]

For stationary $\pi$, $\pi(T)=P_\pi(X_{jm}\in T)\le\pi(T)(1-\varepsilon)^j$, hence $\pi(T)=0$.

On each nonempty closed irreducible finite class $C_{i}$, Cesàro averages of any row law have a convergent subsequence in the finite probability simplex. If $\eta_N=N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\delta_xK^n$, then $\eta_NK-\eta_N=N^{-1}(\delta_xK^N-\delta_x)$, so every subsequential limit is stationary. A stationary law on $C_{i}$ is positive at every state: it is positive somewhere, and stationarity along any positive-probability path transports positivity to every state. It is unique. Indeed, for positive stationary laws $\pi$ and $\rho$, let $c=\min_x\pi(x)/\rho(x)$. Then $\pi-c\rho$ is nonnegative, stationary, and zero at some point. If nonzero, the just-proved positivity would make it positive everywhere, a contradiction. Thus $\pi=c\rho$ and normalization gives $c=1$.

Since all stationary mass lies on the disjoint closed classes, restriction to each class and normalization gives exactly a convex mixture of these class laws. A class law gives positive mass to P precisely if its class meets P. Finally, under (P.16.3a.C1.2), a communicating class meeting both A and P would contain a path from A to P, contradicting C1. Thus each class is wholly on one side. Equivalently, P.16.3a.C1.4 says that a finite invariant measure for Q exists precisely when there is a closed class in P. ∎

### C2. Escape, survival, uniformity, and invariant laws are different properties

#### Theorem P.16.3a(3) (Survival classification and exact uniform criterion)

Assume pointwise no-access (P.16.3a.C1.2), and define

\[
\tau_A=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in A\},\qquad\inf\varnothing=\infty.
\]

For $x\in P$ and $n\ge 0$,

\[
s_n(x):=Q^n\mathbf1(x)
 =\mathbb P_x(\tau_A>n)
 =\mathbb P_x(X_n\in P).
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.1}
\]

In particular,

\[
\forall x\in P:\ \mathbb P_x(\tau_A<\infty)=1
\iff
\forall x\in P:\ s_n(x)\longrightarrow0.
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.2}
\]

Either equivalent condition implies that Q has no nonzero finite invariant positive measure, and therefore every stationary K-law gives P mass zero. The converse is false.

The following uniform statements are equivalent:

\[
\sup_{x\in P}s_n(x)\to0;
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.3}
\]

\[
\exists m\ge1,\ \varepsilon>0:\quad
\inf_{x\in P}\mathbb P_x(\tau_A\le m)\ge\varepsilon;
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.4}
\]

\[
\sup_{x\in P}\mathbb E_x\tau_A<\infty.
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.5}
\]

Under (P.16.3a.C3.4),

\[
s_n(x)\le(1-\varepsilon)^{\lfloor n/m\rfloor},
\qquad
\sup_x\mathbb E_x\tau_A\le m/\varepsilon.
\tag{P.16.3a.C3.6}
\]

The pointwise condition (P.16.3a.C3.2) implies, for every *fixed* initial probability $\lambda$ supported on $P$, that $\int s_n\,d\lambda\to 0$. It does not imply a bound uniform over all initial laws: that bound is exactly (P.16.3a.C3.3), because Dirac initial laws are allowed.

##### Proof

The iterated substochastic kernel integrates exactly the paths whose first $n$ steps remain in $P$. It therefore gives $P_x(\tau_A>n)$, with $Q^0 1=1$. Because $A$ is absorbing as a measurable region, a path that enters $A$ cannot subsequently be in $P$, outside a single countable union of conditional null events. Thus $\{X_n\in P\}$ and $\{\tau_A>n\}$ agree up to null sets. The events $\{\tau_A>n\}$ decrease to $\{\tau_A=\infty\}$; continuity from above proves (P.16.3a.C3.2).

If $\mu Q=\mu$ is finite, then $\mu Q^n=\mu$ and

\[
\mu(P)=\int_Ps_n(x)\mu(dx).
\]

Under pointwise $s_n\to 0$, dominated convergence makes the right side tend to zero, so $\mu=0$.

Put $a_n=\sup_x s_n(x)$. The kernel composition identity and positivity imply $a_{n+k}\le a_na_k$. If $a_n\to 0$, choose $m$ with $a_{m}<1$ and put $\varepsilon=1-a_m$. Conversely, $a_m\le 1-\varepsilon$ gives $a_{jm+r}\le(1-\varepsilon)^j$ for $0\le r<m$, proving (P.16.3a.C3.6). The tail-sum identity for positive integer hitting times gives

\[
\mathbb E_x\tau_A=\sum_{n\ge0}s_n(x)\le m\sum_{j\ge0}(1-\varepsilon)^j=m/\varepsilon.
\]

If $\sup_x\mathbb{E}_x\tau_A=M<\infty$, Markov's inequality gives $\sup_xP_x(\tau_A>n)\le M/n$, proving (P.16.3a.C3.3). Finally, dominated convergence gives the fixed-initial-law statement, and taking $\lambda=\delta_x$ proves the assertion about uniformity over initial laws. ∎

**No absorption, no marginal shortcut.** Even without (P.16.3a.C1.2), $Q^n1$ still equals the probability of avoiding $A$ through time $n$ when starting in $P$. It need not equal $P_x(X_n\in P)$, because a path may leave and return. The two-state deterministic cycle $p\to a\to p$ has $\tau_{A}=1$ from $p$ but visits $P$ at every even time. This is why (P.16.3a.C1.2) is explicit in C3.

**A harmonic survival function is not an invariant measure.** Under no-access, $h(x)=\lim_nQ^n1(x)=P_x(\tau_A=\infty)$ satisfies $Qh=h$ by bounded convergence. It is a right-harmonic function. The invariant-mass criterion instead asks for a finite *left*-invariant measure $\mu Q=\mu$. The examples below show that $h\equiv 1$ can coexist with no such nonzero $\mu$.

#### Exact counterexamples

All the following spaces are standard Borel. Disjoint unions carry their usual disjoint-union Borel structure and topology. Unless otherwise specified, $U=0$ on $A$ and $U=\infty$ on $P$; thus their set meanings are unambiguous abstract mathematical witnesses, not physical realizations of completed prohibited self-models.

1. **No access does not imply escape or invariant exclusion.** Take $A=\{a\}$, $P=\{p\}$, and the identity kernel. $A$ is absorbing, $p$ never escapes, and $\delta_{p}$ is stationary. This is the countermodel of Theorem P.16.3.

2. **Pointwise escape need not be uniform.** Let $A=\{a\}$, $P=\{1,2,\dots\}$, and use deterministic countdown: $1\to a$, $k\to k-1$ for $k\ge 2$, $a\to a$. Then $\tau_A=k$ from $k$ and $s_n(k)=1_{k>n}$. Every point escapes in finite time, but $\sup_ks_n(k)=1$ at every $n$. The only stationary probability is $\delta_{a}$, and every fixed initial probability converges to it in total variation, with no uniform rate over starting points. This also proves that pointwise escape does not imply a uniform mean-hitting-time bound.

3. **Closed noncompact P, no finite invariant measure, and no escape.** Let $\Theta=\{a\}\sqcup[0,\infty)$, $A=\{a\}$, $P=[0,\infty)$, with $a$ absorbing and $T(x)=x+1$ on $P$. $P$ is closed and noncompact. If $\mu Q=\mu$ is finite, then $B_0=[0,1)$ has no predecessor in $P$, so $\mu(B_0)=0$. For $B_j=[j,j+1)$, $j\ge 1$, invariance gives $\mu(B_j)=\mu(B_{j-1})=0$. These disjoint $B_{j}$ cover $P$; hence $\mu(P)=0$. Nevertheless $s_n(x)=1$ for every $x\in P$ and every $n$. By C1, $\delta_{a}$ is the unique stationary probability for $K$, so invariant exclusion is nonvacuous, but no point of $P$ escapes or converges weakly to $\delta_{a}$. The bounded continuous indicator of the clopen component $P$ has expectation one along every such trajectory and zero under $\delta_{a}$. The kernel is Feller. It is also K1/K2-compatible; with reference measure $\delta_{a}$ plus Lebesgue measure and this $U$, its Gibbs law is $\delta_{a}$ and it is Gibbs-reversible. Thus these compatibilities do not repair the failed escape implication.

4. **A positive-probability route to A from every point is insufficient in a continuum.** Use the same space with

\[
K(x,\{a\})=\epsilon(x)=2^{-(x+2)},\qquad
K(x,\{x+1\})=1-\epsilon(x)\quad(x\in P).
\]

Every x has a direct positive chance of escape. But

\[
\mathbb P_x(\tau_A=\infty)
=\prod_{j\ge0}\bigl(1-2^{-(x+j+2)}\bigr)>0.
\]

Indeed every factor has $t=2^{-(x+j+2)}\le 1/4$, and $\log(1-t)\ge -2t$ there, while $\sum_jt<\infty$. The partial products decrease to a limit bounded below by $\exp(-2\sum_jt)>0$. The same strip argument as in example 3 gives $\mu Q=\mu\Rightarrow\mu=0$: $B_0$ has no predecessor, and each later strip receives mass only from the preceding zero-mass strip. Thus all stationary laws are safe even though escape fails with positive probability. In the finite theorem, finitely many positive paths produce a common $m$ and a positive minimum $\varepsilon$; it is exactly that finite reduction which fails here.

5. **Invariant exclusion can be vacuous.** Let $A$ and $P$ be two disjoint copies of $[0,\infty)$. Move $x\to x+1$ on $A$ and send each $P$ point in one step to coordinate $0$ in $A$. Every $P$ point escapes in one step. The strip proof shows $R$ has no invariant probability, and $Q=0$ has no nonzero invariant measure. Hence $K$ has no stationary probability at all. “Every stationary probability gives $P$ zero mass” is true but asserts no existing law.

6. **Uniform escape does not give uniqueness on A.** Let $A=\{a,b\}$, $P=\{p\}$; $a$ and $b$ are absorbing and $p\to a$. $P$ escapes in one step, but every mixture $t\delta_a+(1-t)\delta_b$ is stationary. There is no common attracting invariant law for all starting points.

7. **Uniqueness does not give attraction.** Let $A=\{a,b\}$, $P=\{p\}$, with $a\to b$, $b\to a$, and $p\to a$. $P$ escapes in one step, and $(\delta_a+\delta_b)/2$ is the unique invariant probability. From $a$, laws alternate between $\delta_{a}$ and $\delta_{b}$, so neither weak nor total-variation convergence occurs in the discrete topology. Cesàro averages do converge, which is a different assertion.

8. **Weak attraction is weaker than total-variation attraction.** Let $A=[0,1]$, append an isolated point $P=\{p\}$, and set $T(x)=x/2$ on $A$, $T(p)=0$. The unique stationary probability is $\delta_{0}$. To verify uniqueness on $A$, invariance gives $\int x\,d\pi=(1/2)\int x\,d\pi$ and hence $\int x\,d\pi=0$, forcing $\pi=\delta_0$. For every $x\in A$, $T^n(x)\to 0$, so $\delta_{T^n(x)}\Rightarrow\delta_0$; the same holds for any initial law by bounded convergence. For $x>0$, however, the total-variation distance $\sup_B|\delta_{x/2^n}(B)-\delta_0(B)|$ is one at every finite $n$.

9. **Even uniform Wasserstein attraction to A need not mean hitting A.** On $\Theta=[0,1]$, put $A=\{0\}$, $P=(0,1]$, and $T(x)=x/2$. The same expectation proof gives the unique invariant law $\delta_{0}$ and $W_1(\delta_xK^n,\delta_0)\le 2^{-n}$ uniformly in $x$. Nevertheless $s_n(x)=1$ for every $x\in P$: $A$ is never reached at finite time. The forbidden indicator is discontinuous at $0$. Here $P$ is not closed, so weak convergence does not control its mass. This witness is separate from example 3, which deliberately makes $P$ closed and noncompact.

10. **Sampling is not continuous-time avoidance.** On the circle, let A be the point of phase 0, P its complement, and let a deterministic continuous-time motion make one full rotation per unit time. At integer times the sampled kernel is the identity and has no access from A. At every noninteger time before the first revolution the path lies in P. A theorem about K at the registered sample times supplies no claim about this intervening motion.

#### Logical summary

Under pointwise absorption of A:

\[
\text{uniform escape}\Rightarrow
\text{pointwise a.s. finite hitting}
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{pointwise decay of }\mathbb P_x(X_n\in P)
\Rightarrow
\text{every invariant law has zero }P\text{ mass}.
\]

Every displayed reverse implication that is not stated as an equivalence fails in the numbered examples. One-step no-access and zero ever-access from A are equivalent by C1 and are the premise for this chain of implications. They do not themselves imply any later property. Existence, uniqueness, weak attraction, total-variation attraction, and Cesàro attraction are separate questions about R and, for attraction from P, about entrance into A. A nonzero finite Q-invariant measure detects stationary occupation of P, not all kinds of persistent motion within P.

### C3. Additional sufficient conditions for existence and attraction

#### Proposition P.16.3a(4) (Explicit optional existence/mixing premises)

The following are sufficient premises, not consequences of $U=\infty$ on $P$ and not universal necessities.

**(a) Compact Feller existence.** If A is a compact metric space in its own declared topology and R maps continuous functions to continuous functions, R has a stationary probability. The assertion needs compactness of A itself (or another tightness argument); compactness of a larger $\Theta$ does not make a nonclosed A compact.

*Proof.* Fix $a\in A$ and take the Cesàro laws $\eta_N=N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_aR^j$. Probability measures on compact metric $A$ have a weakly convergent subsequence; let its limit be $\pi$. For continuous $f$,

\[
\left|\eta_NRf-\eta_Nf\right|
=\frac{|R^Nf(a)-f(a)|}{N}\le\frac{2\|f\|_\infty}{N}.
\]

Both $f$ and $Rf$ are continuous, so passage to the weak limit gives $\pi Rf=\pi f$. Bounded continuous functions determine Borel probabilities on a metric space, hence $\pi R=\pi$. The only compactness fact used here is sequential weak compactness of probabilities on compact metric spaces. ∎

**(b) Uniform minorization on A.** Suppose there are a probability $\nu$ on $A$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ such that $R(a,B)\ge\varepsilon\nu(B)$ for every $a\in A$ and $B\subseteq A$. Then $R$ has a unique invariant probability $\pi_{A}$ and

\[
\sup_{a\in A}\|R^n(a,\cdot)-\pi_A\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le(1-\varepsilon)^n,
\quad
\|\rho-\sigma\|_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_B|\rho(B)-\sigma(B)|.
\tag{P.16.3a.C4.1}
\]

*Proof.* For $\varepsilon<1$, write $R=\varepsilon\nu+(1-\varepsilon)L$ with $L$ a Markov kernel. For probability laws $\rho,\sigma$, the common $\nu$ term cancels and the Markov contraction inequality gives

\[
\|\rho R-\sigma R\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le(1-\varepsilon)\|\rho-\sigma\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.
\]

The space of probabilities is complete in total variation. For completeness of the application, iterates satisfy

\[
\|\rho R^{n+1}-\rho R^n\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le(1-\varepsilon)^n,
\]

so the telescoping geometric series makes them Cauchy; their limit $\pi_{A}$ is a probability, and contraction makes $\pi_AR=\pi_A$. Applying contraction to two invariant probabilities proves uniqueness. Applying it to $\delta_{a}$ and $\pi_{A}$ proves (P.16.3a.C4.1). When $\varepsilon=1$ all rows equal $\nu$ and the result is immediate. ∎

**(c) Adding entrance from P.** If pointwise no-access holds, every $x\in P$ hits $A$ almost surely, and $R^n(a,\cdot)\to\pi_A$ in total variation for every $a\in A$, then $K^n(x,\cdot)\to\pi_A$ in total variation for every $x\in\Theta$. In particular, $\pi_{A}$ is the unique stationary probability of $K$.

*Proof.* Let $H_{x}$ be the probability law of the finite entrance pair $(\tau_A,X_{\tau_A})$ for a start $x\in P$. The Markov property at the finite stopping time, obtained by partitioning over $\{\tau_A=t\}$, yields the bound

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|K^n(x,\cdot)-\pi_A\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le &\ \mathbb P_x(\tau_A>n)\\
 &+\sum_{t=1}^{n}\int_A
 \|R^{n-t}(a,\cdot)-\pi_A\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\,
 H_x(\{t\},da).
\end{aligned}
\]

For each fixed (t,a), the integrand tends to zero, is at most one, and $H_{x}$ has total mass one. Dominated convergence and the survival limit prove the result. Total variation distances between these kernels are measurable on standard Borel spaces: they can be computed as suprema over a fixed countable generating algebra. Convergence from any fixed initial distribution follows by another dominated-convergence integral. An invariant starting distribution must therefore equal $\pi_{A}$. ∎

If, more strongly, the block escape premise P.16.3a.C3.4 holds with $(m,\eta)$ and the $A$-minorization premise holds with $\varepsilon$, then for any $0\le k\le n$,

\[
\sup_{x\in\Theta}\|K^n(x,\cdot)-\pi_A\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
\le (1-\eta)^{\lfloor k/m\rfloor}+(1-\varepsilon)^{n-k}.
\tag{P.16.3a.C4.2}
\]

To prove it, split the time-$k$ law into its mass in $A$ and $P$. The $P$ mass is bounded by the first term; any $A$ conditional law is within the second term after $n-k$ further steps. Taking $k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ gives a uniform geometric bound. No Harris-recurrence or drift theorem is needed for this explicit sufficient branch. More general recurrence, drift, or tightness assumptions can replace these premises only after their own hypotheses are checked.

Conversely, total-variation attraction to an $A$-supported invariant law implies $s_n(x)\to 0$ because the test set $P$ is permitted in total variation. Weak attraction implies the same if $P$ is closed (by the closed-set inequality), or more generally if $P$ is a continuity set of the limiting law. Without such a condition, example C2.9 disproves the implication.

### C4. Measurable cost compatibility and the null-point issue

#### Theorem P.16.3a(5) (K1/K2 pointwise; K3 generally only almost everywhere)

**K1.** Suppose that for every $x\in A$,

\[
K\bigl(x,\{y:U(y)\le U(x)\}\bigr)=1.
\tag{P.16.3a.C5.1}
\]

One may impose the same condition on P, but there it is vacuous because every extended nonnegative value is at most ∞. This is the measurable, almost-sure-row version of cost-nonincreasing support.

**K2.** Suppose that for every $x\in A$,

\[
\int_\Theta U(y)K(x,dy)\le U(x)<\infty,
\tag{P.16.3a.C5.2}
\]

using the nonnegative extended Lebesgue integral. An infinite value on a zero-measure set contributes zero; positive mass on such a set makes the integral infinite.

K1 implies K2, and either premise implies the pointwise no-access condition P.16.3a.C1.2. If the premises are given only almost everywhere in $x$, this argument gives only the corresponding almost-everywhere conclusion; “for every $x\in A$” is material.

**K3.** Let m be a sigma-finite Borel reference measure, $\beta>0$, and

\[
0<Z_\beta=\int_\Theta e^{-\beta U}\,dm<\infty,
\qquad
\pi_\beta(dx)=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta U(x)}m(dx),
\quad e^{-\beta\infty}=0.
\]

Suppose reversibility means equality of measures on $\Theta\times\Theta$,

\[
\pi_\beta(dx)K(x,dy)=\pi_\beta(dy)K(y,dx).
\tag{P.16.3a.C5.3}
\]

Then $\pi_\beta$ is stationary, $\pi_\beta(P)=0$, and

\[
K(x,P)=0\quad\text{for }\pi_\beta\text{-almost every }x\in A.
\tag{P.16.3a.C5.4}
\]

For every initial probability $\lambda\ll\pi_\beta$,

\[
\mathbb P_\lambda(\exists n\ge0:X_n\in P)=0.
\tag{P.16.3a.C5.5}
\]

In general one cannot replace “$\lambda\ll\pi_\beta$” by “$\lambda(A)=1$,” nor replace (P.16.3a.C5.4) by a statement about every $x\in A$.

##### Proof

Under K1 and $x\in A$, $U(y)\le U(x)<\infty$ almost surely, so integration proves K2. Under K2, for any integer $M\ge 1$,

\[
\int U(y)K(x,dy)\ge M K(x,P).
\]

If $K(x,P)>0$ the supremum over $M$ is infinite, contradicting (P.16.3a.C5.2). Thus either condition gives pointwise no-access.

For K3, integrate the symmetric measure over $\Theta\times B$. Its first description gives $(\pi_\beta K)(B)$; its transposed description gives $\pi_\beta(B)$, since every $K$ row has total mass one. Thus $\pi_\beta$ is stationary. Its density is zero on $P$, so $\pi_\beta(P)=0$ and

\[
0=(\pi_\beta K)(P)=\int K(x,P)\pi_\beta(dx).
\]

Nonnegativity proves (P.16.3a.C5.4). For any $B$ with $\pi_\beta(B)=0$, the same stationarity identity gives $K(x,B)=0$ for $\pi_\beta$-almost every $x$. Therefore $\lambda\ll\pi_\beta$ implies $\lambda K\ll\pi_\beta$. Induction shows $\lambda K^n\ll\pi_\beta$ at every $n$, so every registered-time $P$ event has probability zero. Taking their countable union proves (P.16.3a.C5.5). ∎

#### Two null-starting-point counterexamples

**Counterexample C5.N1 (changing one invisible row).** Take $\Theta=[0,1]\sqcup\{p\}$, $A=[0,1]$, $P=\{p\}$, $m=$ Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$ plus $\delta_p$, $U=0$ on $A$ and $\infty$ at $p$, $\beta>0$. Then $\pi_\beta$ is uniform on $[0,1]$. Fix $x_{0}=1/2$ and define

\[
K(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\delta_p,&x=x_0\text{ or }x=p,\\
\delta_x,&x\in A\setminus\{x_0\}.
\end{cases}
\]

The kernel is measurable. The measure $\pi_\beta(dx)K(x,dy)$ is exactly uniform measure on the diagonal $\{(x,x):x\in[0,1]\}$, because the altered row $x_{0}$ has $\pi_\beta$-mass zero. That measure is symmetric, so $K$ is reversible. Yet $K(x_0,P)=1$. Also $\delta_{p}$ is a stationary law in addition to the Gibbs law. Null rows can matter for actually admitted point initializations even though they do not change detailed balance.

**Counterexample C5.N2 (Feller plus full support still need not suffice).** Take $\Theta=[0,1]$, $P=\{0\}$, $A=(0,1]$, $m=$ Lebesgue measure, $U(0)=\infty$ and $U=0$ otherwise, and $K(x,\cdot)=\delta_{1-x}$. The Gibbs law is uniform on $[0,1]$. Reflection preserves that law and is an involution; for Borel sets $B,C$,

\[
\int_B\mathbf1_C(1-x)\,dx
=\int_C\mathbf1_B(1-y)\,dy,
\]

so reversibility holds. The kernel is Feller because $f\mapsto f(1-x)$ preserves continuity. The Gibbs law has full topological support on $\Theta$ and, in particular, relative full support on $A$. Nevertheless $K(1,P)=1$. Here $x\mapsto K(x,P)=1_{\{1\}}$ is upper semicontinuous, not lower semicontinuous. Feller continuity alone controls integrals of continuous functions, not this closed-set indicator.

#### Correct pointwise upgrades

Suppose $\pi_\beta$ has full support relative to $A$ and the function $f(x)=K(x,P)$ is lower semicontinuous on $A$. If $f(x_0)>0$, lower semicontinuity gives a relatively open neighborhood $V$ of $x_{0}$ on which $f>f(x_0)/2$. Full support gives $\pi_\beta(V)>0$, contradicting $\int_Af\,d\pi_\beta=0$. Thus $f$ vanishes at every $x\in A$.

Sufficient conditions for this premise include:

- Strong Feller regularity on $A$, meaning $K$ sends every bounded measurable test function to a continuous function on $A$, applied to $1_P$.
- Weak Feller regularity on a metric $\Theta$, explicitly meaning that $K$ maps $C_b(\Theta)$ into $C_b(\Theta)$, together with $P$ open and full support relative to $A$: this makes $x\mapsto K(x,\cdot)$ weakly continuous, and the open-set inequality gives lower semicontinuity of $K(\cdot,P)$. No unqualified $C_0$-Feller convention on an arbitrary noncompact space is used for this upgrade.
- A direct protocol proof of $K(x,P)=0$ for every admitted $x$, which requires neither Gibbs reversibility nor topological upgrades.

No claim is made that a convenient modification of null rows is physically implemented. The physical kernel's actual exceptional rows must satisfy the asserted condition. On the accepted finite branch with counting reference measure, every $a\in A$ has $\pi_\beta(\{a\})>0$, so the almost-everywhere statement is pointwise and reproduces Theorem P.16.3. An arbitrary finite reference measure with zero-weight $A$ points would require the same null-point qualification.

#### Compatibility does not fix stationary P mass

For any Gibbs probability $\pi_\beta$ above, the identity kernel is reversible and has $\delta_{p}$ stationary for each $p\in P$. The independent-refresh kernel $K(x,\cdot)=\pi_\beta$ for every $x$, including $P$, is also reversible because $\pi_\beta\otimes\pi_\beta$ is symmetric; after one step every initial law is $\pi_\beta$, its unique stationary probability, and $P$ is escaped in one step. Thus K3 does not select the $P$ rows or invariant-mass behavior.

For K1/K2 the same nonentailment already follows from the accepted finite witnesses. It also has an uncountable witness on $\Theta=[0,1]\sqcup\{p\}$ with $U=0$ on $[0,1]$ and $\infty$ at $p$: both identity and independent uniform refresh satisfy K1/K2, with respectively a stationary $\delta_{p}$ or unique stationary uniform $A$ law. For a general continuum $U$ an $A$ minimum need not be attained, so the finite “reset to a minimizer” proof must not be repeated without an attainment premise. None is needed for these explicit witnesses.

### C5. Zero mass, topological support, and weak limits

#### Proposition P.16.3a(6) (Support and approximation caveats with sufficient controls)

Assume a Polish topology only in this section and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures.

**(a) Zero mass does not exclude topological support.** On $\Theta=[0,1]$, uniform $\mu$ has $\mu(\{0\})=0$ but $0\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$. Every relatively open neighborhood of $0$ has positive length. Thus $\mu(P)=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq A$ are distinct statements. In a second-countable space, $\operatorname{supp}\mu$ is the complement of the union of all open $\mu$-null sets and has full $\mu$-mass: the union can be reduced to a countable union using a countable base. Consequently $\operatorname{supp}\mu\cap P=\emptyset$ is equivalent to the existence of an open $\mu$-null set containing $P$, a stronger condition than $\mu(P)=0$. If $P$ itself is open, $\mu(P)=0$ does give support exclusion. A closed null boundary generally does not.

**(b) Weak limits can charge a forbidden boundary.** On $[0,1]$, take $P=\{0\}$, $A=(0,1]$, and $\mu_n=\delta_{1/n}$. Then $\mu_n(P)=0$ for every $n$, but $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_0$ and $\delta_0(P)=1$, since $f(1/n)\to f(0)$ for every continuous $f$. Even stationary laws can behave this way: let $K_n(x,\cdot)=\delta_{1/n}$ for every $x$, so $\mu_{n}$ is its unique invariant law and each $K_{n}$ has no access from $A$; the weak row limit $K_\infty(x,\cdot)=\delta_0$ violates that no-access condition. Thus invariant-law convergence and pointwise weak kernel convergence alone do not preserve the discontinuous $A/P$ predicate.

There is also a single-kernel version. On $[0,1]$, use $T(x)=x/2$ with $P=\{0\}$, $A=(0,1]$. Every finite-time trajectory from $A$ stays in $A$, but its laws converge weakly to the forbidden invariant law $\delta_{0}$. Pointwise no-access is not exclusion of asymptotic boundary accumulation.

These are purely mathematical witnesses. They do not supply the source-specific interpolation-realization certificate assumed in Proposition 14.5.8c, and they do not weaken that proposition's stated qualification.

**(c) Finite Gibbs densities also can concentrate at a null boundary.** On $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue reference measure and $\beta=1$, take the everywhere-finite potential $V_n(x)=nx$ and normalized density

\[
\rho_n(x)=\frac{n e^{-nx}}{1-e^{-n}}.
\]

Each $\mu_n(dx)=\rho_n(x)\,dx$ gives $P=\{0\}$ mass zero. For every $\delta>0$,

\[
\mu_n([\delta,1])
=\frac{e^{-n\delta}-e^{-n}}{1-e^{-n}}\longrightarrow0,
\]

so uniform continuity of any continuous $f$ gives $\int f\,d\mu_n\to f(0)$: $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_0$. If a growing finite penalty specifically at the forbidden point is desired, replace $V_n(0)$ by $n$; a change on this reference-null point leaves every $\mu_{n}$ unchanged. A sequence of finite penalties therefore provides no general boundary-exclusion limit theorem. A *fixed* potential with controlled truncations has a stronger result, stated in (h) below; it must not be confused with an arbitrary changing Gibbs family.

**(d) Total variation controls mass.** If $\lVert\mu_n-\mu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}\to 0$ and $\mu_n(P)\to 0$, then

\[
\mu(P)\le\mu_n(P)+\|\mu_n-\mu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0.
\]

This proves zero P mass, not necessarily support exclusion. Total variation is generally unavailable for an atomic finite grid approximating a non-atomic law: if $G_{n}$ is the finite grid support, an atomic grid law gives it mass one and a non-atomic $\mu$ gives it mass zero, so their total-variation distance is one.

**(e) Uniform boundary-neighborhood control prevents weak boundary charging.** Let $P$ be closed and $N_\delta(P)=\{x:d(x,P)<\delta\}$. Suppose $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ and there is $\omega(\delta)\to 0$ as $\delta\downarrow 0$ such that

\[
\sup_n\mu_n(N_\delta(P))\le\omega(\delta).
\tag{P.16.3a.C6.1}
\]

The open-set inequality for weak convergence gives

\[
\mu(P)\le\mu(N_\delta(P))
\le\liminf_n\mu_n(N_\delta(P))\le\omega(\delta).
\]

Letting $\delta\downarrow 0$ gives $\mu(P)=0$. For a nonclosed $P$, the same condition using distance to $P$ actually controls its closure. It is stronger than separate assertions $\mu_n(P)=0$.

**(f) A fixed closed safe carrier gives support exclusion.** If there is a closed $F\subseteq A$ with $\mu_n(F)=1$ for all $n$ and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, the closed-set inequality gives $1=\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$, so $\mu(F)=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq F\subseteq A$. For example, a common positive-distance guard $d(x,P)\ge\delta_0>0$ yields such a closed safe carrier. Merely saying each $\mu_{n}$ has some safe carrier $F_{n}$ is insufficient, as $F_n=\{1/n\}$ shows.

**(g) A lower-semicontinuous barrier with uniformly bounded mean cost gives zero boundary mass.** Let $V:\Theta\to[0,\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous, $V=\infty$ on $P$, and $\sup_n\int V\,d\mu_n\le C<\infty$. If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$, then

\[
\int V\,d\mu\le\liminf_n\int V\,d\mu_n\le C,
\tag{P.16.3a.C6.2}
\]

so $\mu(P)=0$. To prove (P.16.3a.C6.2), write $\int V\,d\mu=\int_0^\infty\mu(\{V>t\})\,dt$. Every $\{V>t\}$ is open. Apply the open-set inequality pointwise in $t$ and then Fatou's lemma. Since $V\ge M1_P$ for every $M$, finiteness of the limit integral forces $\mu(P)=0$. If moreover $b(\delta)=\inf_{N_\delta(P)}V\to\infty$, Markov's inequality gives the explicit bound (P.16.3a.C6.1) with $\omega(\delta)=C/b(\delta)$. This extra uniform barrier geometry need not hold merely because $V$ is infinite pointwise on a noncompact $P$. Uniformly bounded cost expectations are substantive new data; the divergent values $\int V\,d\delta_{1/n}$ for a boundary-diverging $V$ explain why the boundary witness can evade this sufficient theorem.

**(h) Controlled Gibbs truncations converge in total variation.** Let $m$ be a fixed finite reference measure, $V_{n}\ge 0$ measurable, $V_n\to U$ in $[0,\infty]$ $m$-almost everywhere, $\beta>0$ fixed, and $0<Z=\int e^{-\beta U}\,dm<\infty$. Put $w_n=e^{-\beta V_n}$, $w=e^{-\beta U}$, $Z_n=\int w_n\,dm$. Dominated convergence gives $\lVert w_n-w\rVert_{L^1(m)}\to 0$ and $Z_n\to Z>0$. For sufficiently large $n$,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\int\left|\frac{w_n}{Z_n}-\frac wZ\right|dm
&\le \frac{\|w_n-w\|_1}{Z_n}
       +\frac{|Z-Z_n|}{Z_n}
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence the normalized Gibbs laws converge in total variation to $Z^{-1}w\,m$, which gives $\{U=\infty\}$ mass zero. This includes $V_n=\min(U,n)$. For an infinite reference measure, an integrable dominating envelope for all $w_{n}$ gives the same proof. Alternatively, uniform integrability on finite-measure sets together with a uniform integrable-mass tail bound outside an exhausting family of those sets suffices: first make the tail contribution small, then apply the finite-measure Vitali argument inside. Uniform integrability on bounded regions alone does not prevent probability escaping to infinity.

The concentrating densities in (c) fail the positive limiting-normalizer premise for the unnormalized $w_n=e^{-nx}$: $w_n\to 0$ Lebesgue-almost everywhere and $Z_n\to 0$. Thus (c) and (h) do not conflict.

**(i) Tightness is separate from no-access.** Laws $\delta_{n}$ on a closed unbounded safe sector $A=[0,\infty)$ all have zero mass on an isolated forbidden $P=\{p\}$, but have no weakly convergent subsequence as probabilities on $\Theta=A\sqcup\{p\}$. For any compact set $C$, all sufficiently large $n$ lie outside $C$, so the family is not tight. Equivalently, if a weak probability limit existed, continuous compactly supported tests on $A$ would all have zero integral under it, while the continuous component indicator $1_A$ would have integral one, an impossibility. Tightness or compactness is needed to extract a probability limit; after a limit exists, the boundary controls above are still separate obligations.

##### Finite-horizon predicate control under an approximate coupling

A useful protocol-level sufficient estimate does not rely on weak convergence. Suppose exact states $X_{j}$ and implemented/decoded states $Y_{j}$ share a metric space and are coupled, with

\[
\mathbb P(d(X_j,Y_j)>\delta_j)\le e_j,
\qquad
\mathbb P(X_j\in P)=0,
\]

for each $0\le j\le H$. On $\{Y_j\in P,\ d(X_j,Y_j)\le\delta_j\}$, necessarily $X_j\in A$ and $d(X_j,P)\le\delta_j$. Therefore

\[
\mathbb P(\exists j\le H:Y_j\in P)
\le\sum_{j=0}^{H}\left[e_j+
\mathbb P\bigl(X_j\in A,\ d(X_j,P)\le\delta_j\bigr)\right].
\tag{P.16.3a.C6.3}
\]

This union-bound proof gives the required separate roles of response error and near-boundary mass. An exact retained A/P tag with a verified tag-preserving transition can instead give zero predicate error directly, even when other coordinates are quantized. Neither a fixed-H estimate nor weak response convergence by itself supplies uniform-in-time exclusion, convergence of invariant laws, or a completed-state realization.

### C6. Resolution metadata for the classification component

- **Exact domain:** Every homogeneous discrete-time Markov probability kernel $K$ on a standard Borel candidate/request configuration space $\Theta$ with measurable nonempty partition $A=\{U<\infty\}$, $P=\{U=\infty\}$. Topological claims use the separately stated Polish/compact/Feller or continuity assumptions only where invoked.
- **Premises:** Pointwise no-access $K(x,P)=0$ for all $x\in A$ for the killed-measure and escape classification; finite positive measures for the invariant-mass equivalence; explicit every-row quantifiers for K1/K2; the specified $m$, $\beta$, finite positive normalizer, and symmetric product measure for K3. No implicit physical realization or environmental support premise.
- **Equivalence:** Ever-access exclusion from every $A$ point iff one-step no-access; under that premise, existence of a stationary law with positive $P$ mass iff existence of a nonzero finite $Q$-invariant measure; pointwise almost-sure finite escape iff pointwise killed-survival decay; uniform decay iff a uniform positive finite-block escape probability, equivalently a uniform finite mean hitting time.
- **Budgets and quantifiers:** Every admitted point initial condition and every integer sample time; all stationary probabilities, with their existence separately classified; all fixed initial probability laws for the stated dominated-convergence extensions. No intervening-time, finite-hardware, or all-resolution physical claim is implicit.
- **Verifier:** The proofs of C1–C6, including restriction/extension, finite-mass cancellation, finite graph specialization, tail probabilities, submultiplicativity, the null-row reversibility witnesses, translation strip argument, and explicit boundary-convergence calculations.
- **Falsifier:** A stationary law with positive $P$ mass but no nonzero finite $Q$-invariant measure under pointwise no-access; an asserted pointwise Gibbs exclusion contradicted by C5.N1 or C5.N2; an escape implication contradicted by translation; or any claimed weak-limit predicate preservation lacking hypotheses and contradicted by $\delta_{1/n}\Rightarrow\delta_0$.
- **Basis:** Mathematical extension with self-contained proofs and explicit counterexamples. No physical experiment or external validation is asserted.
- **Baseline and scope:** Theorem P.16.3 supplies the finite baseline. The module respects the scope gates of Definition P.16.3, Remark P.16.2, Section P.16.9, Hypothesis 14.5.8, and Propositions 14.5.8b–d.
- **Nonvacuity:** Uncountable translation, refresh, reflection, contraction, and Gibbs-density examples; the translation witness has an existing unique safe invariant law, so its invariant-exclusion conclusion is not vacuous.
- **Completed component:** Measurable/continuum access, invariant-mass, cost-compatibility, escape, and approximation-boundary classification, including the finite specialization.
- **Precise residual:** This classification module alone does not supply the selected controller or the physical realization. The common typed implemented branch in Sections B, H, D and T supplies those components.

## <a id="theorem-p163b-operational-prohibition-boundary"></a>Theorem P.16.3b: Operational prohibition boundary

This section supplies the genuine boundary used by the selected request dynamics. It does not supply or claim the Definition-P.16.3 reduction certificate. Its extended cost is an independently registered hard constraint. Its underlying host is the concrete ideal finite MPU host of Section H: H.3 proves strict program-length admission, H.4 implements the gates and instruments, H.5–H.6 supply bounded simulation and the finite diagonal wrapper, and H.7–H.8 give the self-model and complete resource/clock types. Everything specific to the live diagonal, its geometry, its prediction family and its candidate semantics is supplied here.

### B.1. Registration, before target classification

Fix the manuscript's positive performance threshold \(\alpha=\alpha_{\mathrm{SPAP}}>0\). Fix the following dimensionless accuracy contract, independently of any candidate membership calculation:

\[
g(\delta)=\delta/\alpha,\qquad 0\leq\delta\leq\alpha.
\]

Thus the allowed Fisher tangent error is one unit at zero performance and decreases linearly to zero. No rescaling is performed after classifying candidates. Use the ordinary probability coordinates of three separately addressed binary receiver probes. Their full identifiable chart is

\[
\Omega=(0,1)^3,\quad
p_\theta(y_1,y_2,y_3)=\prod_{j=1}^3\theta_j^{y_j}(1-\theta_j)^{1-y_j},\quad y\in\{0,1\}^3.
\]

The probability coordinates, ordering of the registers, computational bases and independent-source convention are fixed. The Fisher tensor is

\[
G(\theta)=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac1{\theta_1(1-\theta_1)},
\frac1{\theta_2(1-\theta_2)},\frac1{\theta_3(1-\theta_3)}\right).
\tag{P.16.3b.B1}
\]

Indeed the score of coordinate \(j\) is \((Y_j-\theta_j)/[\theta_j(1-\theta_j)]\). Its squared expectation is \(1/[\theta_j(1-\theta_j)]\); independent coordinates have zero cross-score expectations. Hence the stratum is identifiable, positive definite and Fisher orthogonal. All three factors concern the receiver's own prepared/read-out registers and belong to the self tangent space. If external model coordinates are also retained, append an independent factor and use the corresponding block-orthogonal self/external splitting; no external factor is needed for this witness.

For (M.18), evaluate the tangent norm of the ordinary chart difference at the candidate target:

\[
\|v\|_{\mathcal F,\theta}^2=v^TG(\theta)v.
\tag{P.16.3b.B2}
\]

A stronger uniform estimate below also covers every alternative evaluation point in \(\Omega\). We make no claim that ordinary coordinate differences are invariant under arbitrary nonlinear reparameterization. The result is for this registered chart. Simultaneously permuting identically calibrated registers leaves all norms and tests unchanged. Changes of global phase in a circuit do not change the classical model or its probabilities.

Let

\[
a=\frac14,\quad b=\frac34,\quad q(z)=\frac7{16}+\frac z8,
\qquad z\in[0,1].
\]

The continuum request-configuration space is the compact standard Borel space

\[
\Theta=\{\mathsf s,\mathsf p\}\times[0,1]
\]

with the discrete topology on its first factor. Its injective candidate-target map into the full self-model chart is

\[
j(\mathsf s,z)=(a,a,q(z)),\qquad
j(\mathsf p,z)=(b,b,q(z)).
\tag{P.16.3b.B3}
\]

The full Fisher chart is \(\Omega\), not a rank-deficient claim that the two one-dimensional sheets themselves have three-dimensional tangent spaces. Displacements in (P.16.3b.B2) are ambient chart tangent vectors. The kernel is deliberately registered only on the candidate subclass \(j(\Theta)\).

Fix the base/default \(\theta_0=(a,a,1/2)=j(\mathsf s,1/2)\). At every performance \(PP\in[0,\alpha]\), put \(r=PP/\alpha\) and register the predictor

\[
\Pi^{(PP)}(\theta_1,\theta_2,q)
=\left(a,a,\frac12+r(q-\frac12)\right).
\tag{P.16.3b.B4}
\]

This is a smooth map \([0,\alpha]\times\Omega\longrightarrow\Omega\), and \(\Pi^{(0)}\equiv\theta_0\) is a common default, independent of the target. Thus the zero-performance discrepancy is exactly the full displacement from this fixed default, as M.10.3 requires.

The corresponding nested attainable prediction classes are explicitly restricted classes for this nominated receiver and its fixed binary forecasting program:

\[
\mathscr H_r=\left\{h_t:\ 0\leq t\leq r\right\},\quad
h_t(\theta_1,\theta_2,q)=\left(a,a,\frac12+t(q-\frac12)\right).
\tag{P.16.3b.B5}
\]

Here the two binary forecasts are produced by the fixed program `RETURN 0`. Its two forecast output ports are immutable task-local ports: initialization writes zero, the controller permits only reads and copying until the commit completes, and neither the performance input nor the separate general-purpose interpreter is wired to write those ports. The allowed performance resource controls only the registered mixing gain in the actuator-distribution forecast. Increasing performance permits all earlier gains. The third reported distribution can be generated by mixing a default fair-bit model with the known actuator model with mixing probability \(t\). It need not be sampled in order to store its probability description. For dyadic inputs and gains the description and, if wanted, its sampler have exact finite Boolean implementations.

For a fixed target, every first/second component error is constant over \(\mathscr H_r\), and the third absolute error is \((1-t)|q-1/2|\). Hence the best attainable discrepancy in every component, and its total Fisher norm evaluated at that fixed target, is attained by \(t=r\) and is nonincreasing in \(r\). Formula (P.16.3b.B4) is this optimizer. This proves the calibrated ordering for each fixed target rather than assuming it or arguing from a changed diagonal outcome. The physical output-port restriction makes every permitted same-task forecast belong to the declared class; the host's ability to compute a different bit elsewhere does not enlarge that task's authorized port operations. These are not classes of every possible program that the host could run. Replacing the nominated forecasting algorithm is outside this declared task class. The diagonal wrapper below nevertheless defeats either bit returned by any such replacement if the replacement is tested live; the specific two sheets fix the canonical zero-forecast transcript. There is no universal prohibition-membership algorithm or universal optimal-predictor claim.

The continuum performance coordinate is the M.10.3 calibration of this registered gain budget. It is not asserted to equal a separately measured Brier score or any other empirical accuracy score. The global value of \(\alpha\) is retained from the manuscript, not rederived here. An arbitrary real gain is a mathematical parameter; a finite device represents only finite gains. For midpoint-grid \(z=(k+1/2)/2^n\) and gain \(t=h/2^\ell\), the reported probability \(1/2+t(q(z)-1/2)\) is dyadic and has an exact finite integer description and comparator sampler. Nested dyadic gain classes populate (P.16.3b.B5) at every fixed resolution. For arbitrary \(t\), the approximation \(t_\ell=2^{-\ell}\lfloor2^\ell t\rfloor\) satisfies

\[
|q_t-q_{t_\ell}|\leq 2^{-\ell}/16,
\qquad
\|\Pi_t(\theta)-\Pi_{t_\ell}(\theta)\|_{\mathcal F,\theta}
\leq2^{-\ell}/\sqrt{63}
\tag{P.16.3b.B5a}
