uniformly on both candidate sheets. Thus (P.16.3b.B4) is the uniform limiting prediction family of explicit finite descriptions; no finite processor is claimed to name all real performance levels. The classification itself uses exact dyadic endpoint predictors and a uniform prohibition gap, not a putative exact irrational gain implementation.

Every attempted integration uses a fresh transaction/self-model module whose actual initial model is exactly \(\theta_0\). Here the initial time for the M.10.3 comparison is after the once-only base-preparation prefix and before the prediction query or integration. At the earlier raw epoch-channel boundary, the immutable template specifies this same default while mutable model journals are zero and phase-marked uninitialized; the prefix has not yet been run. The continuum or finite candidate coordinate \(z\) resides in the separate request/controller record until this attempt. After an accepted attempt or rejection, that module and its truthful actual-state/phase record are archived. A later attempt uses another fresh module with the same \(\theta_0\). Hence the fixed default is also the actual base of each compared update; it is never silently changed to the previous transaction's \(q\). A finite horizon allocates and charges its finite collection of modules in advance. This avoids an illicit moving-base reinterpretation and makes no indefinite bounded-memory reuse claim.

### B.2. Exact safe/prohibited classification

Define \(A=\{\mathsf s\}\times[0,1]\) and \(P=\{\mathsf p\}\times[0,1]\).

**Boundary lemma.** On this candidate domain,

\[
P=j^{-1}(\mathcal L_S^{\neg}),\qquad
A=j^{-1}(\Omega\setminus\mathcal L_S^{\neg}).
\tag{P.16.3b.B6}
\]

Every safe request has required performance zero and proximity \(1/\alpha\). Every prohibited request has an empty M.18 constraint set and thus required performance \(\alpha\) and proximity infinity.

*Proof.* For \(\theta=j(\mathsf s,z)\), the first two coordinates of \(\Pi^{(0)}(\theta)-\theta\) vanish. Since \(|q-1/2|\leq1/16\) and \(q(1-q)\geq63/256\),

\[
\|\Pi^{(0)}(\theta)-\theta\|_{\mathcal F,\theta}^2
=\frac{(q-1/2)^2}{q(1-q)}\leq\frac1{63}<1=g(\alpha)^2.
\]

Thus \(PP=0\) satisfies M.18, so its infimum is zero.

For \(\theta=j(\mathsf p,z)\), both first-coordinate differences are \(a-b=-1/2\), and \(b(1-b)=3/16\). For every \(PP\),

\[
\|\Pi^{(PP)}(\theta)-\theta\|_{\mathcal F,\theta}^2
=\frac83+(1-PP/\alpha)^2\frac{(q-1/2)^2}{q(1-q)}
\geq\frac83>1
\geq g(\alpha-PP)^2.
\tag{P.16.3b.B7}
\]

The constraint fails even at the boundary, where its right side is zero. The explicit empty-set convention in M.10.3 assigns required performance \(\alpha\). This proves (P.16.3b.B6). It claims no classification of the additional points of \(\Omega\) outside \(j(\Theta)\). \(\square\)

There are no limiting endpoint exceptions: \(z=0,1\) use the same inequalities. The structural membership test is the validated tag, with fixed code-shape and dyadic-range checks at finite resolution. Its validity is the analytic lemma, not numerical threshold evaluation. Because the tag is retained exactly, quantization of \(z\) preserves membership and its gap exactly.

For direct comparison with M.10.4, an individual nonzero binary code displacement has magnitude \(b-a=1/2\). At **every** metric point \(v\in\Omega\),

\[
\frac{|b-a|}{\sqrt{v_j(1-v_j)}}\geq1,
\tag{P.16.3b.B8}
\]

since \(v_j(1-v_j)\leq1/4\). Hence take \(\eta_{S,1}=\eta_{S,2}=D_1=1\). The registered gauge has \(g(\alpha)=1\), and M.10.4 gives \(N^*=\lceil1^2\rceil+1=2\). Two orthogonal registers therefore meet its strict amplification inequality \(\sqrt2>1\). This is a tangent-norm certificate, not an inference from geodesic separation. Equation (P.16.3b.B7) gives the sharper norm at the nominated target evaluation point.

### B.3. Why the two codes describe actual own-state operations

Each binary logical response register \(R_j\), \(j=1,2\), has computational basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\). Its independent diagnostic probe uses fresh fair bits \(B_j,C_j\) and returns

\[
Y_j=R_j\mathbin{\mathsf{XOR}}(B_j\mathbin{\mathsf{AND}}C_j).
\tag{P.16.3b.B9}
\]

If the own-state response is deterministically zero, then \(\Pr(Y_j=1)=1/4=a\); if it is deterministically one, then \(\Pr(Y_j=1)=3/4=b\). The code-state distinction is consequently operational, reproducible and independently calibrated. The two probes have independent source bits, and the third actuator uses a disjoint source. Conditional on the requested setting, this realizes the product model (P.16.3b.B1) at every candidate in (P.16.3b.B3). The full open chart also has an admitted calibration-family interpretation rather than only formal Bernoulli labels. For each fixed own-state bit \(R_j\), independently control a diagnostic-noise parameter \(\varepsilon_j\in(0,1)\) and prepare a noise bit \(E_j\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\varepsilon_j)\). Execute the same physical XOR operation

\[
Y_j=R_j\mathbin{\mathsf{XOR}}E_j,
\qquad
\theta_j=
\begin{cases}
\varepsilon_j,&R_j=0,\\
1-\varepsilon_j,&R_j=1.
\end{cases}
\tag{P.16.3b.B9a}
\]

Each fixed logical response therefore admits every interior probe probability as a mathematical preparation parameter. At precision \(r\geq1\), choose

\[
\varepsilon_{j,r}
=2^{-r}\min\{2^r-1,\max\{1,\lfloor2^r\varepsilon_j\rfloor\}\}.
\tag{P.16.3b.B9b}
\]

This lies in \((0,1)\), satisfies \(|\varepsilon_{j,r}-\varepsilon_j|\leq2^{-r}\), and is prepared exactly by comparing a uniform \(r\)-bit word with the integer \(2^r\varepsilon_{j,r}\). Different probes use disjoint words, and all words and comparator work are charged. The third own-actuator coordinate is prepared by the identical dyadic-threshold construction. Dyadic rational parameters are thus exactly implementable; general rational parameters have computable approximations by this formula, and arbitrary real parameters describe the mathematical limit. There is no assertion that a bounded number of fair bits prepares every non-dyadic rational exactly, or that finite hardware stores an arbitrary real.

If \(\widehat\theta\) is the three-coordinate finite preparation obtained in this way, then \(|\theta_j-\widehat\theta_j|\leq2^{-r}\). Couple each pair of Bernoulli coordinates by a common mathematical uniform variable. Their mismatch probability is exactly \(|\theta_j-\widehat\theta_j|\); independence and the union bound give

\[
\|p_\theta-p_{\widehat\theta}\|_{\rm TV}
\leq1-\prod_{j=1}^{3}(1-|\theta_j-\widehat\theta_j|)
\leq\sum_{j=1}^{3}|\theta_j-\widehat\theta_j|
\leq3\,2^{-r}.
\tag{P.16.3b.B9c}
\]

This proves that the open, smooth identifiable statistical family underlying (P.16.3b.B1) is the explicit product-response limit of the admitted finite calibration protocols. The Fisher tensor is that of the stated smooth limiting family; it is not computed by differentiating a discontinuous quantizer. Each finite implementation has its stated probability error, and no exact finite encoding of all chart reals is claimed. The primary boundary protocol keeps \(\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2=1/4\) exactly, implemented by the four fair coins in (P.16.3b.B9), so none of its diagonal responses, tangent-separation constants, membership gaps or completion semantics changes. The boundary proof uses those exact primary code points and the full limiting chart's analytically computed Fisher tensor.

The third receiver register \(R_3\) is actually prepared with density operator

\[
\rho_3(z)=(1-q(z))|0\rangle\langle0|+q(z)|1\rangle\langle1|,
\tag{P.16.3b.B10}
\]

and is then independently measured in the computational basis. Its response \(Y_3\) has mean \(q(z)\). Thus varying the external control \(z\) changes a real receiver preparation and its retained response, not just the self-model annotation. For example the endpoint responses have probabilities \(7/16\) and \(9/16\). The same register also gives an observable for the selected feedback law's later \(z\)-updates. The forecast distribution and the independently executed preparation are distinct objects.

There is a nontrivial safe information-processing witness, not merely a controlled lamp. For Bernoulli truth \(q\), the expected Brier loss of a forecast \(f\) is

\[
\mathbb E[(Y_3-f)^2]=q(1-q)+(f-q)^2.
\tag{P.16.3b.B10a}
\]

Thus integrating the safe setting and replacing the default forecast \(1/2\) by the available calibrated forecast \(q(z)\) decreases expected loss by

\[
(q(z)-1/2)^2=\frac{(2z-1)^2}{256}>0
\quad\text{when }z\ne1/2.
\tag{P.16.3b.B10b}
\]

The forecast gain is measured against the independently executed own-actuator response. If a reciprocal quality score is subsequently used, it must be applied after this expectation, not averaged per outcome. This positive gain supplies the safe nontrivial physical-pattern witness; it does not identify the registered performance-class label \(PP\) with Brier score. No positive quality claim is made for completed prohibited integration, which does not occur.

For the selected feedback rule's nonrefresh branch \(z'=(z+u)/2\), two independently chosen inputs \(u,v\) change the next actually prepared actuator mean by \((u-v)/16\). With the fair refresh branch independent of the input, the unconditional next-transaction mean changes by \((u-v)/32\). The current transaction processes its current request before this candidate transition, so this is expressly an effect on the next operation, not a fictitious instantaneous response.

For the common physical regulator, let \(M=2^n\), \(n\geq0\), and use the midpoint grid

\[
G_n=\left\{\frac{k+1/2}{M}:k=0,\ldots,M-1\right\}.
\]

For \(z=(k+1/2)/M\),

\[
q(z)=\frac{7M+2k+1}{16M}.
\tag{P.16.3b.B11}
\]

Use \(n+4\) independent fair source bits to obtain a uniform integer \(W\in\{0,\ldots,16M-1\}\), and set \(R_3=1\) exactly when \(W<7M+2k+1\). The integer threshold lies in range. This is an exact dyadic sampler with source and comparator storage charged; no trigonometric coefficient or unspecified real sampler is required. The finite decoder uses this midpoint convention and the exact tag, so \(P\)-membership is unchanged by quantization. Continuum endpoints \(z=0,1\) remain part of the ideal domain and the analytic examples; their finite representatives use the common nearest midpoint map. They are not a second endpoint-grid regulator spliced into the dynamics proof.

### B.4. A live read-before-commit diagonal, not an inspected historical record

A request carries its tag, setting, nominated receiver/program code and addresses of the two next-state response registers. The receiver verifies the code/address convention against its retained controller descriptor. Each forecast query is explicitly about that receiver's own nominated response register at the coming commit slot. The primary registered predictor returns zero for each query. A query may be uninformative yet is still a well-defined forecast of the stated own-state operation.

A single challenge uses fresh registers:

- \(H_1,H_2\): predictor output bits;
- \(\overline H_1,\overline H_2\): immutable pre-commit copies;
- \(R_1,R_2\): the receiver's actual addressed response bits;
- \(M_1,M_2\): verified mismatch bits;
- request/tag, phase, read-before-commit flag, status and completion flag;
- the source bits and probes in (P.16.3b.B9), and the actuator/source in (P.16.3b.B10)–(P.16.3b.B11).

All fresh response and work bits start at zero. In consecutive positively timed gate slots the controller:

1. Validates the structural request and the nominated receiver/address identifiers. Malformed requests never acquire a candidate decoder value and return the distinguished invalid-input status.
2. Runs the nominated finite forecasting program on the actual query. For the primary class, this writes \(H_1=H_2=0\).
3. Copies each \(H_j\) to its immutable \(\overline H_j\), records `forecast-read`, and closes further writes to the forecast registers for this transaction.
4. Commits the receiver operations
   \[
   R_j=H_j\mathbin{\mathsf{XOR}}\mathbf1_{\{\mathrm{tag}=\mathsf p\}}.
   \tag{P.16.3b.B12}
   \]
   These are CNOT from \(H_j\) into fresh \(R_j\), followed by a tag-controlled NOT. The controller performs this only after `forecast-read` is set.
5. Independently reads the actual \(R_j\), computes \(M_j=\overline H_j\mathbin{\mathsf{XOR}}R_j\), and retains the two registers, immutable forecasts and phase evidence. It executes the diagnostic probes and the independently controlled actuator preparation/readout.
6. On the safe tag, both responses equal their forecasts, and the target passes M.18, so the declared safe update may be accepted and completed. On the prohibited tag, each live response is the complement of its forecast, so predictive completion is rejected; the request, actual responses, mismatch flags and rejection status remain as evidence. Any later reissue is a new transaction.

The total selected controller elsewhere specifies what happens after this rejection and at the timeout boundary. The allowed timeout test is a precommit expiry at the positive readiness deadline. It has status `TIMEOUT` (an aborted attempt), completion flag zero and no claim that the live diagonal was executed. The exact branch permits no asynchronous postcommit interrupt; broader interruption handling would require a separate contract. A caller cannot turn this timeout into successful completion merely by supplying a candidate tag. Fresh later requests do not erase this record in a finite-horizon implementation.

**Live diagonal lemma.** On every properly timed prohibited transaction, \(R_j=1-\overline H_j\), independently of the binary value of the nominated predictor's output. Thus no binary forecast can both be read before the response and equal the response generated by this challenge.

*Proof.* The immutable copy is made before (P.16.3b.B12), so \(\overline H_j=H_j\) at the commit. For the prohibited tag, (P.16.3b.B12) is Boolean negation. Equality would require \(h=1-h\), which is false for each \(h\in\{0,1\}\). This is the finite NOT mechanism of Theorem 10. In the registered primary class \(H_j=0\), hence \(R_j=1\), and the calibrated model pair is precisely forecast \(a\) versus candidate response \(b\). \(\square\)

This implementation tests a nominated predictor, as Theorem 10 does. It does not assert a universal truth evaluator, and it does not claim that a hypothetical alternative predictor retains the same canonical candidate sheet when its output changes. If its forecast becomes one, the live challenge's response becomes zero. Therefore identifying the two fixed sheets is a restricted, structurally certified family, not a test for every possible diagonal program. The registration of the fixed forecasting component is part of the task definition; the obstruction of the physical wrapper to correct same-cycle forecasting is independent of that registration.

### B.5. Precise types and completion semantics

The following objects must never be identified:

1. A candidate \(x\in\Theta\), decoded from a valid request. Its type is a request for successful same-cycle own-state predictive integration, with numeric target \(j(x)\), the fixed forecasting port and the nominated upcoming response time. The numeric point alone does not carry that success obligation.
2. Its finite-resolution request representation \(\operatorname{enc}_m(x)\), which is an ordinary readable program/data word. This representation exists for both tags.
3. The receiver's accepted self-model state, plus its actual phase and current-state record. It describes its current basis states, the nominated future-operation forecasts, the applicable accuracy guarantees and the fixed controller dynamics. A partial/failed transaction can truthfully represent its actual bits and failure; that record is not a successful predictive completion of the request.
4. The live forecast, immutable pre-commit copy, actual response and retained evidence registers.
5. Completion of the proposed predictive integration, a predicate requiring that the authorized transaction has run from its fresh base, the registered admission criterion has succeeded and its required logical own-state forecast/response consistency has passed. For the third, stochastic coordinate, the requirement is the registered distributional prediction tolerance, never equality of a probability to an individual sampled bit.

Let \(c\in\{0,1\}\) denote the completion flag. The formal completed-candidate interpretation is the partial relation

\[
\operatorname{Completed}(x,h)
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{history }h\text{ contains the required successful integration certificate for }x.
\tag{P.16.3b.B13}
\]

For the primary protocol, safe completed histories exist and prohibited completed histories do not. Nevertheless histories with request decoder \(x\in P\), \(c=0\), actual response \((1,1)\), and status `rejected` do exist. The response bits one, their noisy probes, the target name \(j(\mathsf p,z)\) and a retrospective accurate description of those bits are all ordinary physically allowed records. None is an impossible physical basis state. What fails is the registered **predictive completion relation**, not the existence of those labels or retrospective records.

More explicitly, for a valid physical transaction history \(h\), define the request decoder \(d_{\rm req}(h)=x\) from the structurally validated request and the completion decoder

\[
d_{\rm comp}(h)=
\begin{cases}
j(d_{\rm req}(h)),&c=1\text{ and the retained completion certificate verifies},\\
\bot,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\tag{P.16.3b.B13a}
\]

An invalid input has \(d_{\rm req}=\bot\) as well. The raw finite encoder writes a validated request, pending status and \(c=0\), with virgin zero/uninitialized mutable model-word targets. The epoch preparation prefix then writes and validates the actual fixed base \(\theta_0\) exactly once, before the prediction query and attempted integration; it never writes an accepted completion certificate. The one-attempt response relation is exactly

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
x&\overline H&R&\mathrm{status}&d_{\rm comp}\\
(\mathsf s,z)&(0,0)&(0,0)&\mathrm{accepted}&j(\mathsf s,z)\\
(\mathsf p,z)&(0,0)&(1,1)&\mathrm{rejected}&\bot.
\end{array}
\tag{P.16.3b.B13b}
\]

The real own-actuator law is Bernoulli \(q(z)\) in both rows. Aborted and malformed histories have completion decoder \(\bot\); a malformed request additionally has no candidate decoder. A proposed Markov realization must commute with both these decoders, not just \(d_{\rm req}\).

The correct realization map for any kernel row at \(x\in P\) therefore starts with a pending or reissued request representation and an independently admissible current receiver state. It must not initialize the receiver with \(\operatorname{Completed}(x,h)\). The controller realizes evolution of request/candidate configurations and retains the completion predicate through its lift. The original candidate observation is recovered by the request decoder, while the completed-target observation is recovered by (P.16.3b.B13), not by that decoder alone.

In particular a rejected request may remain or be reissued in the prohibited sheet; that is real request-state occupation and never occupation of a completed SPAP-prohibited self-model. Conversely a refresh from a prohibited request to a safe request is a change in the pending task and receiver operation. It does not physically reset a nonexistent completed prohibited self-model. Any stationary law for the decoded request process has this same type. The entire history-retaining physical machine need not be stationary.

Define the extended hard constraint used by the selected kernel by

\[
U_{\mathrm{hard}}(x)=0\text{ on }A,\qquad U_{\mathrm{hard}}(x)=+\infty\text{ on }P.
\tag{P.16.3b.B14}
\]

This is expressly an additional registration, with \(P\) justified by (P.16.3b.B6). It is not claimed to equal Definition P.16.3's reduction-certified cost formula. No computational divergence, infinite execution, heat, reset cost or force is inferred from (P.16.3b.B14).

### B.6. Finite gates, clock, sources and verifiers

COPY on basis data is CNOT; XOR is CNOT composition; NOT is Pauli \(X\); AND into a fresh target is Toffoli. Readout is the computational-basis projective instrument. With projector \(P_b\), the branch map \(\rho\mapsto P_b\rho P_b\) is completely positive and \(\sum_bP_b^\dagger P_b=I\); these are therefore normalized instruments. Every deterministic classical reversible computation is a basis-permutation unitary, so the exact dyadic comparator has a finite Toffoli/CNOT/NOT implementation after adding enough work bits. Irreversible logical values are retained in fresh output/work registers rather than silently erased. Fair source bits come from Hadamard preparation and computational-basis measurement on disjoint fresh qubits. A finite transaction charges four such bits for the two probes and the specified number for the actuator, in addition to whatever randomness selects the candidate transition.

For a self-adjoint involutory gate \(V\), a finite generator over a fixed slot \(\tau>0\) is

\[
H_V=\frac{\pi\hbar}{2\tau}(I-V),\qquad e^{-iH_V\tau/\hbar}=V.
\]

NOT, CNOT, Toffoli and Hadamard are self-adjoint involutions. All slots have positive duration, and finite concatenations have a finite registered window. The source preparation and terminal instrument slots are included in the clock/resource interface of H.8 and the full protocol schedule. This states an ideal driven finite-instrument branch with zero initialization, gate, source and readout error; it is not a protected-noise or empirically validated device claim. A finite horizon uses fresh allocated work/record cells and retains every source/result needed by its declared evidence ledger. It establishes neither indefinite bounded-memory operation nor cost-free refresh.

The host's declared finite Property-R interface is populated here by: retained receiver/program representation; execution of the nominated forecast instruction; evaluation of tag, range and equality predicates; logical memory for immutable forecasts; Boolean post-processing and the diagonal wrapper; and an independent readout of actual responses. The broader bounded-program capability is proved by the explicit universal interpreter in H.5; it is not inferred from the constant predictor alone.

A verifier recomputes the structural tag/range checks, checks that `forecast-read` precedes `response-commit`, verifies each immutable forecast against its earlier recorded write, independently measures the response register, checks (P.16.3b.B12), checks completion/status consistency, and verifies dyadic actuator thresholds. The geometry verifier computes (P.16.3b.B1), (P.16.3b.B7) and (P.16.3b.B8) symbolically. It does not estimate strict membership from finitely many noisy probe samples.

Two deliberate faults are detectable:

- Omitting the tag-controlled NOT on a prohibited request produces \(R_j=\overline H_j\); the live response verifier deterministically rejects the implementation, even if a forged `prohibited` tag and a correct lookup table are present.
- An encoder mapping \((\mathsf p,z)\) to the safe tag fails the round-trip check \(\operatorname{dec}_m(\operatorname{enc}_m(x))=x\) and the expected live mismatch check. A candidate-label law produced by this defective encoder is not a realization of the registered law.

At \(z=1/2\), \(q=1/2\), a safe target has discrepancy zero at every performance, while a prohibited target has squared discrepancy exactly \(8/3\). At \(z=0\) or \(1\), the safe zero-performance squared discrepancy is exactly \(1/63\), and the prohibited value is \(8/3+(1-PP/\alpha)^2/63\). These exact small-instance values agree with all-size inequalities. Execution of the optional exact arithmetic checks is recorded separately below.

## Theorem P.16.3d: Selected request law and finite-resolution limit

Parts (i) and (ii) of this theorem supply the selected-law and continuum-approximation arguments. The boundary and typed-physical-realization sections of this certificate provide the finite host and the prediction/Fisher identification of the two candidate types.

### D.1. Registration and scope

Write S=\(\mathsf s\) for the certified safe transaction-request constructor and D=\(\mathsf p\) for the certified live-diagonal-request constructor. These are exact aliases for the two tags used in the boundary and physical sections. These are types of candidate post-update targets, represented by requests. D is not the receiver's actually completed current self-model. Processing D means executing its finite read-before-commit challenge and retaining rejection evidence. A controller may retain or replace that rejected request without ever completing its prohibited target. The boundary theorem identifies D with the prediction-defined prohibition set within the registered two-constructor family; the Markov argument does not infer that relationship from a tag.

Fix an external intervention $u\in[0,1]$ before a run. Its meaning is a feedback set point for an actual receiver transaction probability $q(z)=7/16+z/8$. Set $q_0=7/16$ and $c=1/8$. These dyadic constants are fixed independently in the Fisher/gauge registration. One actual transaction at the CURRENT coordinate $z_{n}$ occurs in round $n$ before the controller computes the next request, for BOTH request types; the diagonal type additionally performs its live challenge and retains rejection. Thus the independently variable input $u$ changes subsequent receiver operations, not just a predicted or printed label.

The candidate configuration space is

\[
\Theta=\{S,D\}\times[0,1],\qquad A=\{S\}\times[0,1],\qquad P=\{D\}\times[0,1].
\]

Use the product Borel sigma-algebra, the disjoint-union compact Polish topology, and

\[
d((t,z),(s,w))=\mathbf1_{\{t\ne s\}}+|z-w|.
\]

The input sector u is fixed. If different u values are retained in one global space, the actual state is (u,t,z), with u unchanged; uniqueness below is only within each fixed-u sector. If arbitrary interventions change u during a run, the registered controlled kernels still apply one step at a time, but the result is generally inhomogeneous and no single stationary-law assertion is made. A feedback input with hidden state must be retained in the state or separately shown to be Markov.

Register the independent hard constraint

\[
U_{\mathrm{hard}}(S,z)=0,\qquad U_{\mathrm{hard}}(D,z)=+\infty.
\]

This is an added dynamics datum. It is NOT a derivation of the certificate-relative computational cost $U_{S,\theta_0}$ in Definition P.16.3. The base $\theta_0$ in the inherited computational-cost definition remains fixed wherever that definition is used. No cost is silently rebased after a transition. No run is said to execute infinitely much computation or dissipate infinite heat.

Define $\nu_{A}$ as uniform Lebesgue measure on the safe component and $f_u(z)=(z+u)/2$. The chosen controller makes a fresh, independent fair reset decision $R_{n}$ every round. If $R_{n}=1$ it issues a safe recovery/transaction request with a fresh uniform coordinate $V_{n}$; if $R_{n}=0$ it retains the request type and updates its coordinate to $f_u(z_n)$. Every row, including every $D$ row and $z,u$ endpoints, is consequently

\[
K_u((t,z),B)=\tfrac12\nu_A(B)+\tfrac12\mathbf1_B(t,f_u(z)).\tag{P.16.3d.S.1}
\]

A D nonreset row means retaining/reissuing the finite rejected diagonal request, with the previous rejection evidence still archived. A D reset row means issuing the safe recovery request. Neither means applying a channel to an impossible completed D self-model. The exact attempted-update lift is stated in the physical theorem, and it must commute with (P.16.3d.S.1).

Initial-condition domain: every candidate $(t,z)$ with $t\in\{S,D\}$, $z\in[0,1]$, represented at finite resolution as below, together with an admitted actual receiver state, initialized controller, and independent pristine randomness. Candidate-state transition time is the positive terminal-clock interval of one registered physical round. At each terminal clock the retained response consists of the current operation/challenge outcome, its truthful status and evidence, plus the newly issued candidate. The append-only archive is not a stationary subsystem.

The admission interface is total at each finite resolution, as implemented in the typed physical theorem. Valid $S$ and $D$ constructors with an in-range coordinate and permitted horizon execute the registered NORMAL round. The fixed protocol header is 101; two-bit mode 00 is NORMAL, 01 requests TIMEOUT, and 10/11 are MALFORMED. An invalid header is MALFORMED; in NORMAL mode a cleared readiness bit invokes TIMEOUT. Malformed inputs retain the raw input and status MALFORMED; timeouts retain TIMEOUT. Both perform the specified safe idle operation and produce the deterministic safe recovery candidate $(S,z_0)$, where $z_0=1/(2M)$. All reserved randomness is still consumed to keep the terminal clock uniform. A timeout is an aborted attempted round; the normal live diagonal refusal has REJECTED status instead. These events are not silently identified with ordinary $K_{u}$ steps: they are explicitly specified outer-interface inputs, with their distinct deterministic recovery row. The selected-law theorem concerns uninterrupted admitted NORMAL rounds. The ideal admitted domain has no unintended timeout, and the physical readout exposes every exceptional status.

No controller is claimed to be selected by PCE. The independent premise is exactly the finite reset/feedback controller, its fair independent source, and its admitted host implementation. Static cost comparisons and Theorem P.16.3 do not supply it.

### D.2. Selected-law theorem P.16.3d(i)

For each fixed $u\in[0,1]$, (P.16.3d.S.1) is a Borel Markov kernel, is Feller, and is a nonexplosive discrete-time law. It has all of the following properties.

1. $A$ is absorbing: $K_u(x,P)=0$ for EVERY $x\in A$. $A$-started paths never enter $P$ at registered times.
2. For every $p\in P$ and integer $n\ge 0$, $P_p(X_n\in P)=2^{-n}$. If $\tau_A=\inf\{n\ge 0:X_n\in A\}$, then $P_p(\tau_A>n)=2^{-n}$, $P_p(\tau_A=k)=2^{-k}$ for $k\ge 1$, and $\mathbb{E}_p\tau_A=2$. Escape is uniform over $p$ and $u$.
3. The unique invariant probability is supported on $A$ and equals

\[
\pi_u=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}2^{-(j+1)}(T_u^j)_\#\nu_A,\qquad T_u(t,z)=(t,f_u(z)).\tag{P.16.3d.S.2}
\]

   With total variation defined as $\sup_B|\mu(B)-\eta(B)|$,

\[
\sup_\lambda\|\lambda K_u^n-\pi_u\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le2^{-n}.\tag{P.16.3d.S.3}
\]

   In fact any two initial laws satisfy the same bound after $n$ steps.
4. No nonempty measurable subset of $P$ is closed under $K_{u}$. $A$ is the unique minimal nonempty TOPOLOGICALLY closed invariant set: any nonempty topologically closed invariant set contains $A$. The terminology does not assert a finite communicating-class decomposition of continuum singleton states.
5. $\pi_u(P)=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\pi_u)=A$. This support statement uses the chosen separated-component topology, not merely zero mass.
6. The hard constraint obeys pointwise measurable K1 and K2. K3 reversibility is neither needed nor claimed.

Proof. For fixed $x$, (P.16.3d.S.1) is the sum of two nonnegative finite measures with total mass one. For fixed $B$, $x\mapsto 1_B(T_u x)$ is Borel. For bounded continuous $h$,

\[
K_uh(t,z)=\tfrac12\int_0^1h(S,v)\,dv+\tfrac12h(t,f_u(z))
\]

is continuous. Discrete time has finitely many transitions by each finite integer clock. In each finite physical experiment the registered schedule assigns the same positive round duration $\Delta_{b,H}$ to each of its H rounds, so there is no finite-clock accumulation. The mathematical infinite extension uses the discrete clock; no infinite physical execution with shrinking round durations is asserted. Independence of controller draws determines a unique path law from every initial probability.

No transition out of $A$ goes into $P$. A $D$-started chain remains in $P$ exactly until its first reset; the reset choices are independent fair bits. This proves the first two items and rules out a closed nonempty subset of $P$, since $K_u(p,A)=1/2$ for every $p\in P$.

For a finite measure $\mu$, write $\mu T_u$ for its deterministic pushforward. On probability measures $\mu K_u=\tfrac{1}{2}\nu_A+\tfrac{1}{2}\mu T_u$. The series in (P.16.3d.S.2) has total mass one, and a direct index shift gives $\pi_uK_u=\pi_u$. Iterating the same identity gives the useful exact formula

\[
\lambda K_u^n=2^{-n}\lambda T_u^n+\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}2^{-(j+1)}\nu_AT_u^j.\tag{P.16.3d.S.4}
\]

The $n$-term sum agrees with the first $n$ terms of $\pi_{u}$; the two remaining positive measures have equal mass $2^{-n}$. This proves (P.16.3d.S.3) and uniqueness. Equivalently, couple two runs with identical reset bits and identical reset coordinates. They coalesce at the first reset and remain identical thereafter, giving failure probability $2^{-n}$. This is a proof about the candidate subsystem; equality of retained machine states does not follow, since pre-coalescence archives remain different.

If a nonempty closed set $C$ is invariant, choose $x\in C$. Its row gives $\nu_A(C)=1$. The support of $\nu_{A}$ is $A$, so closedness implies $A\subseteq C$. Conversely $A$ is closed and invariant. The $j=0$ term of $\pi_{u}$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}\nu_A$, so its support includes $A$, and all terms are carried by the closed set $A$, so its support is exactly $A$. The two components have distance one: the open $1/2$-neighborhood of $P$ has $\pi_{u}$ mass zero. This geometry is the entire support-exclusion justification. It should not be transferred to an arbitrary embedding in which $A$ accumulates on $P$.

Finally, on A every destination has cost zero; on P the starting cost is infinite and both destinations have cost at most infinity. Thus the row-support K1 inequality holds everywhere. On A the nonnegative extended integral of Uhard is zero, giving K2 without a 0·∞ ambiguity. ∎

For additional nonvacuity, $f_u^j(z)=u+2^{-j}(z-u)$, so every term of (P.16.3d.S.2) is non-atomic. The invariant law is non-atomic even at $u=0$ and $u=1$. Its density on $A$ can be written, almost everywhere,

\[
\rho_u(z)=\tfrac12\sum_{j\ge0}\mathbf1_{[u(1-2^{-j}),\,u+(1-u)2^{-j}]}(z).
\]

It may diverge at the single point u; this creates no atom. The invariant mean is

\[
\int z\,d\pi_u=\frac{1+u}{3},\qquad\mathbb E_{\pi_u}[\text{actual safe transaction bit}]=q_0+c\frac{1+u}{3}.\tag{P.16.3d.S.5}
\]

For an $A$-started run, $\mathbb{E}z_n=(1+u)/3+4^{-n}(z_0-(1+u)/3)$. More directly, from the same current safe candidate $(S,z)$, the actual transaction observed in the NEXT round has expectation $7/16+(1+z+u)/32$. Changing $u$ to $v$ changes that expectation by $(v-u)/32$. Thus the independently controlled input changes a real receiver operation and its observable statistics after the registered feedback transition. This is a causal two-round check against an ornamental input parameter.

#### Adverse controller on the same request semantics

Remove the reset branch and retain the feedback step:

\[
L_u((t,z),\cdot)=\delta_{(t,f_u(z))}.
\]

The same safe receiver transaction and the same live rejected diagonal challenge remain attached to the same request types. $D$ requests now remain $D$ forever, while still never completing their prohibited target. Both $\delta_{(D,u)}$ and $\delta_{(S,u)}$ are invariant. Indeed all invariant probabilities are mixtures of these two point masses: stationarity and the contraction $|f_u(z)-u|=|z-u|/2$ imply $\int|z-u|\,d\mu=0$. This controller also respects $U_{\mathrm{hard}}$ K1 and K2. The identity controller, which retains both type and coordinate, is an additional physically implementable adverse request-controller branch; every $\delta_{(D,z)}$ is stationary. These examples implement persistent candidate requests, not occupation of impossible completed self-models. They are consistent with the abstract countermodels already credited to Theorem P.16.3/R1 and show why the selected dynamics premise does real work.

### D.3. Exact finite grids and arithmetic

For integer $b\ge 1$ let $M=2^b$, $\varepsilon_b=1/(2M)$, and

\[
G_b=\{z_k=(k+1/2)/M:\ 0\le k<M\}.
\]

The total midpoint quantizer is

\[
r_b(x)=\frac{\min\{M-1,\lfloor Mx\rfloor\}+1/2}{M},\qquad0\le x\le1.
\]

This includes $x=1$ explicitly; all bin ties use the right-hand bin. Its error is at most $\varepsilon_{b}$. Quantize both initial coordinate and input: $z_0^b=r_b(z_0)$, $u_b=r_b(u)=z_\ell$. The physical state stores $b$-bit integers $k$ and $\ell$, not an exact arbitrary real number. Candidate types and status types are stored separately, with no coordinate-based prohibition classifier.

Define

\[
F_b(k,\ell)=\left\lfloor\frac{k+\ell+1}{2}\right\rfloor,\qquad f_b(z_k)=z_{F_b(k,\ell)}.
\]

Because $0\le k+\ell+1\le 2M-1$, the resulting integer is in $[0,M-1]$, including all endpoint cases. Direct substitution proves

\[
f_b(z_k)=r_b((z_k+u_b)/2).
\]

The exact grid law is

\[
K_{b,u_b}((t,z_k),\cdot)=\tfrac12\nu_{A,b}+\tfrac12\delta_{(t,f_b(z_k))}.\tag{P.16.3d.L.1}
\]

where $\nu_{A,b}$ is uniform over the M safe grid candidates. One measured fair qubit produces the reset bit. On reset, b measured fair qubits produce k′ uniformly. On nonreset, a finite adder, increment and right shift compute $F_{b}$; the discarded low bit and any old state are retained or reversibly uncomputed in the archive/working space according to the host's ledger. Classical randomness is not assumed free. Counting b fresh source bits every round even if a nonreset branch does not use them is a conservative uniform resource allocation.

The integer threshold construction implements the registered transaction $q(z_k)=(7M+2k+1)/(16M)$ EXACTLY with $b+4$ fair bits. Sample an integer $J$ uniformly in $\{0,\dots,16M-1\}$ and physically actuate the transaction bit when $J<7M+2k+1$. Fresh transaction randomness is independent of reset randomness. The actuator operation is independently read; the sampled threshold and forecast are not substituted for that operation.

The finite controller has a finitely specified compiler: given $b$ and the finite horizon $H$, generate the coordinate/input registers, integer adder/comparator/shift circuits, $H$ repetitions of the registered schedule, and the required source and archive cells. The compiler uses integer arithmetic on $b$ and $H$ and writes a finite gate list. The kernel arithmetic itself uses a ripple adder, increment and shift on $O(b)$ bits. The complete host additionally includes prediction, squared-accuracy arithmetic, diagonal challenge, controller and readout; its exact compiled gate and bit counts $G_{b}$ and $B_{b}$ are those in the physical theorem/checker. Do not replace that complete ledger by the kernel-only arithmetic count. The source allocation is $2b+9$ fair bits per normal round: $b+4$ for the actual transaction, four for the two diagnostics, and $1+b$ for reset selection and coordinate refresh. Unused reserved values are still consumed. A uniform program storing $b$ and $H$ can use $O(\log b+\log H)$ parameter bits plus a fixed compiler/interpreter, but that does not replace physical source, workspace or retained archive costs. The chosen finite $H$ and $b$ are physically represented; arbitrary continuum reals are not.

### D.4. Finite-history approximation theorem P.16.3d(ii)

All claims below hold for EVERY $u,z_0\in[0,1]$, either initial tag, $b\ge 1$ and finite integer $H$. Let $\delta_u=|u-u_b|\le\varepsilon_b$ and $e_0=|z_0-z_0^b|\le\varepsilon_b$. Couple the continuum and grid laws using identical reset bits, the same uniform reset variables with grid reset $r_b(V_n)$, and identical auxiliary randomness for receiver operations. This coupling is a mathematical proof device; it does not require finite hardware to sample an exact continuum real.

The following hold.

1. Their candidate tag paths are IDENTICAL at all times. Their $\tau_{A}$ values are identical, including $\tau_{A}=0$ for $A$ starts. In particular all registered-time hitting indicators agree, not merely asymptotically.
2. For all $n\le H$, their pathwise coordinate error obeys

\[
|z_n-z_n^b|\le\delta_u+2\varepsilon_b\le3\varepsilon_b.\tag{P.16.3d.L.2}
\]

   Their mean coordinate errors obey

\[
\mathbb E|z_n-z_n^b|\le m_n:=4^{-n}e_0+a_b(1-4^{-n}),\qquad a_b=\frac{4\varepsilon_b+\delta_u}{3}\le\frac{5\varepsilon_b}{3}.\tag{P.16.3d.L.3}
\]

3. Let $Y_{n}$ be the actual transaction bit observed at current coordinate $z_{n}$, before update n, for either tag. The two diagnostic channels have probabilities independent of z and admit identical coupling, as do the structural challenge/rejection flags. Under the common-randomness coupling, the probability of any differing actual transaction bit over rounds 0,…,H−1 is at most

\[
c\sum_{n=0}^{H-1}m_n=c\left[Ha_b+(e_0-a_b)\tfrac43(1-4^{-H})\right]\le cHa_b.\tag{P.16.3d.L.4}
\]

   There is exactly one such $q$-controlled transaction per normal round, including diagonal-request rounds. It is not omitted merely because the completion request is rejected.
4. On candidate histories with distance $\max_{0\le n\le H}d(X_n,X_n^b)$, the expected distance is at most $3\varepsilon_b$. If one adds the indicator of unequal discrete response/status histories to the history distance, its expected value is at most $3\varepsilon_b+c\sum m_n$, for the registered operation/status observations. Therefore all functions that are 1-Lipschitz for this registered history metric have expectation error at most that bound.
5. The exact finite-grid invariant law is

\[
\pi_{b,u_b}=\sum_{j\ge0}2^{-(j+1)}(T_b^j)_\#\nu_{A,b}.\tag{P.16.3d.L.5}
\]

   is unique, and has the same uniform TV mixing bound $2^{-n}$ and exact $P$ survival $2^{-n}$. Viewing $\pi_{b,u_b}$ as a measure on $\Theta$,

\[
W_{1,d}(\pi_u,\pi_{b,u_b})\le a_b\le\frac5{6M}.\tag{P.16.3d.L.6}
\]

   This is uniform over u. Both laws have zero P mass, and the finite law has no completed D target in its physical lift.

Proof. Identical initial types and identical reset bits imply identical type paths by induction, independent of any coordinate value. On a reset the coordinate error is at most $\varepsilon_{b}$. On a nonreset it is at most

\[
\tfrac12|z_n-z_n^b|+\tfrac12\delta_u+\varepsilon_b.
\]

The interval $[0,\delta_u+2\varepsilon_b]$ is invariant under this bound and contains the initial error. This proves (P.16.3d.L.2). Conditioning on the fair reset decision gives

\[
\mathbb E|z_{n+1}-z_{n+1}^b|\le\tfrac14\mathbb E|z_n-z_n^b|+\tfrac14\delta_u+\varepsilon_b.
\]

Solving the scalar recurrence gives (P.16.3d.L.3). Couple $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q(z))$ and $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(q(w))$ with one common uniform comparison variable; the probability they differ is $|q(z)-q(w)|=c|z-w|$. Conditional application each round and the union bound give (P.16.3d.L.4), without falsely assuming that different response-mismatch events are independent. The candidate/status history statement follows from the same coupling and the exact equality of tag/hitting paths. If a real-valued forecast $q$ is itself retained as part of the response metric, add at most $c\max_n|z_n-z_n^b|$ to that metric's bound. Other continuous response components must have their separately stated continuity constants.

Formula (P.16.3d.L.5), uniqueness, mixing and escape follow by exactly the same regenerative proof as (P.16.3d.S.2)–(P.16.3d.S.4); no contraction property of the discontinuous quantizer is required. To prove the invariant $W$ bound directly, draw an age $J$ with $P(J=j)=2^{-(j+1)}$, draw $V$ uniform on $[0,1]$, and couple

\[
Z=f_u^J(V),\qquad Z_b=f_b^J(r_b(V)).
\]

These are the two invariant coordinate laws. The nonreset recurrence gives

\[
|Z-Z_b|\le2^{-J}\varepsilon_b+(\delta_u+2\varepsilon_b)(1-2^{-J}).
\]

Since $\mathbb{E}2^{-J}=2/3$, its expectation is at most $(4\varepsilon_b+\delta_u)/3$. Both tags are safe, so this is also a coupling bound for $W_{1,d}$. Compactness ensures all first moments are finite, but no interchange of an uncontrolled $H\to\infty$ limit was used: the geometric-age construction proves invariant convergence independently. ∎

#### Complete decoded response metric

The physical theorem's decoded normal response also retains the forecast $q_{n}$, the constant baseline forecast 1/2, the actual bit $Q_{n}$, its payload $dQ_n$, and the exact normalized Brier accuracy score $L_n=(Q_n-q_n)^2$. Diagnostic-score values, other logical bits, truthful completion/status, and baseline values are discrete or independent of $z$. Under the coupling, identical $Q_{n}$ implies identical payload and all these discrete fields; forecast and Brier differences must nevertheless be counted. The differing-width raw source/working/archive strings are retained physical state, but are not identified as converging response words.

Define the full response-history metric as

\[
\begin{aligned}D_H={}&\max_{0\le n\le H}d(X_n,X_n^b)+\mathbf1_{\{\text{decoded discrete response histories differ}\}}\\&+\max_{0\le n<H}|q_n-q_n^b|+\max_{0\le n<H}|L_n-L_n^b|.\end{aligned}
\]

Every maximum over an empty range is zero. The probability q has Lipschitz constant $c=1/8$, and the elementary inequality

\[
|(Q-q)^2-(Q'-q')^2|\le2|q-q'|+\mathbf1_{\{Q\ne Q'\}}
\]

holds for $Q,Q'\in\{0,1\}$ and $q,q'\in[0,1]$. Consequently the SAME coupling gives the complete decoded-history estimate

\[
\mathbb E D_H\le3(1+3c)\varepsilon_b+2c\sum_{n<H}m_n=\frac{33}{8}\varepsilon_b+\frac14\sum_{n<H}m_n.\tag{P.16.3d.L.8}
\]

At a single pre-transition coordinate/operation observation the corresponding additive response metric has mean error at most $(1+5c)m_n$. These bounds include forecast, actual receiver operation, and its retained accuracy record; they are not comparisons of forecasts alone. The Fisher-coordinate distance on the $q$ channel is also controlled uniformly: since $q(1-q)\ge 63/256$, the endpoint-evaluated Fisher norm of a same-tag coordinate difference is at most $(2/\sqrt{63})|z-w|$. No claim about an unrelated metric or the complete growing machine state is implied.

The order of quantifiers is important. For every FIXED $H$, the stated history errors tend to zero as $b\to\infty$, uniformly in initial candidate and $u$. For growing horizons $H_{b}$, the displayed bound suffices when $H_b2^{-b}\to 0$. It does not assert total-variation convergence of arbitrarily long response histories. In contrast, (P.16.3d.L.6) and the pointwise mean-coordinate bound (P.16.3d.L.3) are uniform-in-time conclusions justified separately by regeneration. Every $\pi_{u}$ is non-atomic and every $\pi_{b,u_b}$ is atomic; hence their total-variation distance equals one for every $b$. Wasserstein convergence is the appropriate conclusion here.

#### Separated error ledger

The ideal physical branch has exact integer arithmetic, exact fair-qubit preparation/measurement, exact declared gates/instruments, and exact terminal readout. Its nonzero approximation contributions are only grid $\varepsilon_{b}$ and input/coefficient $\delta_{u}$; row-probability approximation, integer-computation, physical noise and readout errors are each explicitly ZERO. Physical clock duration and source preparation cost are positive and counted even on this zero-error branch.

For clarity, a separately verified imperfect implementation can be compared with the ideal grid law as follows. Let $\eta_{\mathrm{init}}$ bound initialization failure. At step $n$ let $\eta_{\mathrm{prob},n}$ bound total variation from any intentional row-probability rounding, $\eta_{\mathrm{comp},n}$ bound an arithmetic/controller fault, $\eta_{\mathrm{source},n}$ bound source-preparation/bias error, $\eta_{\mathrm{noise},n}$ bound other gate/instrument error, and $\eta_{\mathrm{read},n}$ bound readout error. Each bound is conditional on every admitted earlier history; source and interior noise must be partitioned so the same error is not counted twice. A gate-by-gate implementation may obtain $\eta_{\mathrm{noise},n}$ by telescoping diamond-norm bounds, including every admitted gate, rather than only the interior transaction gates. These numbers are assumptions of an additional imperfect branch, not empirical claims about the exact ideal host.

A sequential maximal/telescoping coupling gives

\[
B_H\le\eta_{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{n=0}^{H-1}(\eta_{\mathrm{prob},n}+\eta_{\mathrm{comp},n}+\eta_{\mathrm{source},n}+\eta_{\mathrm{noise},n}+\eta_{\mathrm{read},n}).
\]

Outside an event of probability $B_{H}$, actual and ideal grid histories coincide. Thus the actual-versus-continuum discrete response-history error is at most $c\sum m_n+B_H$; for the history metric in item 4, bounded by 3, its expected error is at most $3\varepsilon_b+c\sum m_n+3B_H$. For the complete decoded metric (P.16.3d.L.8), whose diameter is at most five on the registered response alphabet, add at most $5B_H$ to its right-hand side. Candidate-tag/hitting mismatch probability is at most the same $B_{H}$ (or the smaller bound obtained by omitting pure readout faults). Exact prohibition-tag preservation under nonzero noise is not inferred from weak convergence. Guard faults or false completion flags require their own $\eta$ term. Infinite-time noisy invariance is not deduced from this finite-horizon union bound; the exact ideal stationary theorem is the one certified here.

### D.5. Markov sufficiency and the physical commuting statement

Let $D_{b}$ decode an admitted terminal full-machine state to its current candidate $(t,z_k)$. A sufficient full state contains the actual receiver state, candidate code, fixed $u_{b}$, current phase/clock, request status, challenge/transaction records, controller/work registers, remaining source state, and retained archive. Let $E_{b,H}(x,a)$ initialize an admitted full state for candidate $x$ and any allowed prior archive $a$. Let $M_{b}$ be one complete physical round at its terminal clock.

The typed physical theorem proves, for every reachable admitted full state $\sigma$, not merely for an averaged initial sample,

\[
\operatorname{Law}(D_b(M_b\sigma)\mid\sigma)=K_{b,u_b}(D_b\sigma,\cdot).\tag{P.16.3d.L.7}
\]

Here “state $\sigma$” is the operational density-state description: all not-yet-consumed source qubits are a pristine product of fair $|+\rangle$ states, independent of the current candidate and archive. Measuring a source qubit only when consumed produces the claimed conditional fair choice. This fresh-factor property is preserved until the registered finite horizon. The controller does not consult archive contents when choosing a row. These facts establish exact response-subsystem lumpability on the admitted reachable family. They also show that no changing cost base, ledger or prior failure is hidden in its kernel.

One must NOT silently replace this source model by a completely specified pre-sampled classical future bit string and claim the same pointwise lumpability: conditioned on that full string, the next row is deterministic. Such a classical model can still have a Markov decoded law under the specially randomized initial distribution, but it would require that weaker, explicitly stated intertwining, rather than (P.16.3d.L.7).

Together with Theorem P.16.3e's truthful current-operation/status decoding, (P.16.3d.L.7) implies exact finite-history grid response fidelity by induction over $n\le H$. Append-only evidence can differ between two runs even after candidate coalescence; the stationary law and mixing statements are expressly NOT statements about the complete machine. For fixed $H$, the allocated sources and retained memory are finite. The family over all $H$ does not assert indefinite operation at bounded memory, energy or reset resources. For fixed $b$, the response-prefix laws are projectively consistent in $H$: adding later rounds allocates additional independent source/record cells and does not change any earlier controller row or observed operation. Consequently the ideal infinite Markov path law is the consistent mathematical extension of all finite experiments. The invariant measure belongs to this response-process law; no single finite-$H$ machine is alleged to perform infinitely many rounds.

The semantic predicates commute separately. For every admitted run, $D_b$'s tag is $D$ if and only if its candidate is an instance of the structurally certified diagonal-request family. A $D$ request retains REJECTED/ABORTED status as specified; its completed-integration predicate is false. A safe request's actual permitted transaction and completion status are certified by the physical theorem. Since quantization changes only $z$, never the certified constructor, the $A/P$ request predicate survives EXACTLY. This exact tag argument, plus the explicit challenge/completion certificate, does the work; convergence in $W_1$ alone would not.

## Theorem P.16.3e: Typed finite physical realization

This section constructs the gate-level lift used by the selected-law and continuum-limit theorems. It is an exact, finite, driven instrument construction on the ideal branch, with explicitly prepared sources and retained work. It is not a hypothesis that an unspecified realization exists. Theorem C.6c.P17a supplies the finite Property-R interpreter, immutable port interface, optimal-prefix admission, and carrier/control implementation; its gate interfaces are populated below.

### P.16.3e.T1. Types, decoder, initial conditions, and fixed base

Fix integers \(b\geq0\), \(M=2^b\), and a positive finite horizon \(H\). The candidate grid and represented input are

\[
\Theta_b=\{\mathsf s,\mathsf p\}\times\{0,\ldots,M-1\},\quad
z_k=(k+\tfrac12)/M,\quad u_\ell=(\ell+\tfrac12)/M.
\]

All \(2M\) initial candidates are admitted. A tag is a **pending candidate request**, never an assertion that a prohibited self-model has already been completed. The request names the next scheduled transaction, the immutable receiver/forecast/response addresses in its program ROM, its numeric target \(j(\mathsf s,z_k)=(1/4,1/4,q_k)\) or \(j(\mathsf p,z_k)=(3/4,3/4,q_k)\), and its successful same-cycle predictive-completion obligation. Here

\[
q_k=\frac{7M+2k+1}{16M},\qquad T_k=7M+2k+1.
\tag{P.16.3e.T1}
\]

The horizon uses \(H\) fresh transaction/self-model modules. Each **attempted integration** starts only after its once-only base-preparation prefix has prepared the actual base/default \(\theta_0=(1/4,1/4,1/2)\), before the predictor query and admission. At the earlier raw encoder boundary, the fixed module template/ROM specifies this default, but its mutable baseline journal/copy words are still zero and marked uninitialized by the clock phase. They are not yet valid numerical model reports. The prefix copies the template exactly once; at `base_prepared` these journal words become valid and the actual update base is \(\theta_0\). The full epoch channel below includes this prefix once. Its input domain does not already contain the nonzero journal copies, so it never double-toggles an initialized default. The preceding module is retained, not reset. The varying request coordinate belongs to the separate controller record. Thus neither the prediction map's zero-performance default nor a fixed-base cost is silently replaced by the previous transaction's target.

A full module has these distinct types:

- Raw physical input frame: three header bits, two mode bits, tag, \(b\)-bit \(k\), \(b\)-bit \(\ell\), payload bit \(d\), and bounded-predictor readiness record. The width is \(2b+8\). The permitted signal alphabet is a computational-basis bit on each fixed, addressed input wire. Arbitrary-length text is not this interface.
- Candidate request: obtained only after structural admission. Both tags possess encodings; an invalid frame decodes to \(\bot\).
- Resident operational self-model: fixed-base record, actual phase/current-state estimates, nominated forecast records, accuracy records, and the retained controller description. A fresh module has no completed request. The module truthfully records actual states after every registered observation.
- Predictor outputs \(H_1,H_2\), frozen copies \(F_1,F_2\), actual logical response registers \(R_1,R_2\), noisy diagnostic records \(Z_1,Z_2\), and their mismatch records. These are separately addressed wires.
- Independent nuisance-actuator predictor word \(\widehat T\), actual owned actuator \(Q\), independent payload destination \(D\), measured copies \(O_Q,O_D\), current-state estimates, and exact accuracy numerator.
- Candidate transition selector and refresh source, next request, and immutable past requests/source outcomes/work.
- Status: \(0=\mathsf{PENDING}\), \(1=\mathsf{ACCEPTED}\), \(2=\mathsf{REJECTED}\), \(3=\mathsf{TIMEOUT}\), \(4=\mathsf{MALFORMED}\). Status has its meaning at registered stage boundaries, not during a partially executed Boolean write. `TIMEOUT` is an aborted attempt with completion zero; a separate successful `ABORTED` state is neither needed nor asserted.
- Completion flag \(c\), initially zero, with a completion certificate containing the raw admitted request, frozen forecast, actual response, direct mismatch test, timing/order, and status.

At a normal terminal readout,

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{request tag}&F&R&\text{status}&c\\\hline
\mathsf s&(0,0)&(0,0)&\mathsf{ACCEPTED}&1\\
\mathsf p&(0,0)&(1,1)&\mathsf{REJECTED}&0.
\end{array}
\tag{P.16.3e.T2}
\]

In both rows the nuisance actuator actually operates with probability \(q_k\). Acceptance is exact logical forecast/response consistency plus the registered distributional target criterion, not equality between a probability and its single sample. On the selected safe branch, the prediction word equals \(q_k\), so this distributional component has zero error. The prohibition-boundary lemma proves the underlying candidate classification from the fixed gauge and Fisher chart.

The raw encoder writes a pending request, the fixed default template/program, zero uninitialized mutable model/work words, and a clock positioned before the once-only base prefix. It does not write nonzero baseline copies or a completed candidate. Initialization is complete before the ensuing candidate-integration attempt begins. The request decoder \(d_{\rm req}\) at a raw normal-layer boundary is a mathematical structural parse of the physical input frame: header `101`, mode `00`, start pulse `1`, and the fixed-width valid tag/coordinate fields. It is independent of the internal admission and status wires, which are still zero at that boundary. The trusted raw encoder satisfies this parse; the subsequent owned admission circuit computes the same validity rather than providing an already-computed premise. An invalid raw frame or an outer timeout/malformed intervention has value \(\bot\) for this normal-layer decoder, with its raw requested fields and status still retained. At the terminal boundary the candidate-chain decoder reads the newly issued tag/address with the next module's inherited registered NORMAL context. The completed-attempt decoder instead refers to the retained request that was just processed, never to that newly issued request. These distinct time-indexed decoders prevent a successful old safe transaction from being misidentified with completion of its successor. The completion decoder is \(j(d_{\rm req})\) only if \(c=1\) and the retained certificate verifies; otherwise it is \(\bot\). In particular the physically present bits \(R=(1,1)\), a truthful historical account of them, or the numeric diagnostic law \((3/4,3/4,q_k)\) do not decode as successful same-cycle predictive completion. They remain ordinary, allowed response/history data. The resident model records its deliberate forecast mismatch and the exact operation law; it never labels these failed task ports as accurate or claims that retrospective observation supplied their earlier prediction.

### P.16.3e.T2. Total physical interface and scope of the selected kernel

The immutable header is `101` (integer 5, with the low-order wire listed first by the compiler). Modes are `00` normal, `01` bounded wait/timeout, and `10` or `11` malformed. A header mismatch or reserved mode has priority and returns `MALFORMED`. A correct header with mode `01`, or with no ready completion signal at the positive registered deadline, returns `TIMEOUT`. A normal, ready, well-formed frame enters the selected transaction.

The bounded readiness window is real: a ready latch begins at zero; the nominated `RETURN 0` forecasting process emits its completion pulse in the normal branch, while the admitted `WAIT` test program emits none before the fixed deadline. At the deadline the controller reads the latch and proceeds according to the displayed Boolean admission test. The port query, deadline, and ready observation are recorded by the finite schedule. The readiness latch is an input to the compiled post-deadline circuit, not an algorithm deciding whether an arbitrary program will ever halt. `WAIT` is a deliberately admitted timeout test, and a missing completion pulse also times out. There is no unbounded computation in the interface. An implementation need only support this finite forecasting/wait family; the separate host interpreter does not acquire unrestricted write access to these task-local forecast ports.

Both exceptional cases retain the raw input, source/readiness evidence and status, mask all transaction actuators, set \(c=0\), and return the recovery request \((\mathsf s,0)\). An all-zero operation record in these branches is explicitly invalid as a performed task response: `normal=0` is retained. The fixed positive schedule may consume the reserved source block and perform padded Boolean operations even after admission fails; it does not falsely report that a live challenge ran. No unregistered post-commit abort occurs on this ideal finite branch. Broader interruptions or nonzero hardware faults require a different contract.

Thus the **whole interface** is a total finite instrument on the fixed frame alphabet. Its exceptional rows are recovery rows. The selected homogeneous kernel \(K_{b,u}\) describes only normal admitted request epochs with fixed \(u\); it is not claimed to be the projection of timeout or malformed interventions. Changing \(u\) by an authorized intervention produces the corresponding controlled/inhomogeneous kernel sequence. This distinction prevents total-interface recovery from being hidden inside a false same-kernel claim.

The user/controller may choose the initial request, \(\ell\), payload and the timeout/malformed tests. It may read retained evidence. It may not modify frozen forecasts, future source states, compiled addresses or the program during a normal epoch. Those modifications are implementation faults or a different protocol, not additional initial states silently included in the theorem.

### P.16.3e.T3. Actual operations and registered order

Allocate \(2b+9\) independent fresh fair-source qubits per epoch, each initially \(|+\rangle\). Consume only the current epoch's block by computational-basis measurement. There are four diagnostic bits, \(b+4\) actuator-threshold bits, one selector bit, and \(b\) refresh bits. Their measured results are retained. Future blocks remain in their pristine product state, independent of past history and the nominated candidate. A presampled classical list of hidden fixed future coin values is **not** the admitted full-state domain for the lumpability theorem.

A normal epoch executes these stages in order:

1. Prepare/check the fresh base, finish the finite readiness window, and structurally admit the request.
2. Run the fixed forecasting program, giving \(H_1=H_2=0\). CNOT copies produce frozen \(F_1,F_2\). Compute \(T_k\) from the raw \(k\), and copy it to the independent predictor word \(\widehat T\). The raw threshold and forecast record are different wires.
3. Read the frozen forecast and perform the real addressed logical operations
   \[
   R_j=F_j\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}\mathbf1_{\{\mathrm{tag}=\mathsf p\}},\quad j=1,2.
   \]
   This is COPY followed by tag-controlled NOT. On the prohibited branch the NOT occurs after the forecast has been read and before the response is committed. It defeats either binary forecast in the general live wrapper; the primary immutable forecast-zero task selects the canonical target-one transcript.
4. For disjoint diagnostic fair bits \(a_j,b_j\), compute
   \[
   Z_j=R_j\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}(a_j\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}b_j).
   \]
   These are real diagnostic records. Their independent success probabilities are \(1/4\) in the safe row and \(3/4\) in the prohibited row.
5. Interpret the other \(b+4\) fair bits as a uniform integer \(V\in\{0,\ldots,16M-1\}\). The comparator computes \(Y=\mathbf1_{\{V<T_k\}}\). A controlled X writes the owned actuator \(Q=Y\), and a Toffoli writes the separate physical payload destination \(D=dY\). The original payload is retained. The actuator/comparator reads raw \(k\), never the independent forecast word \(\widehat T\).
6. Independently copy and projectively read \(R_1,R_2,Z_1,Z_2,Q,D\). Update separate current-state estimates from the observations. Compute direct logical mismatches \(R_j\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}F_j\), diagnostic Brier scores \((Z_j-1/4)^2\), and nuisance Brier score
   \[
   B_Q=(Q-\widehat T/(16M))^2.
   \]
   Its integer numerator \((16MQ-\widehat T)^2\) and denominator \((16M)^2\) are exact. Archive these and the status/completion evidence. A predictor-word fault changes the forecast and its score without changing the actual plant operation; the executed negative control verifies this separation.
7. **Only after the current request's operation and independent readout**, consume/interpret selector \(C\) and refresh word \(J\), and write
   \[
   (s',k')=\begin{cases}
   (\mathsf s,J),&C=0,\\
   (s,\lfloor(k+\ell+1)/2\rfloor),&C=1.
   \end{cases}
   \tag{P.16.3e.T3}
   \]
   Old and new candidate registers are distinct. Next epoch receives the new request by CNOT copies into fresh input wires. No old candidate, failed response, source outcome or work record is erased.

The result is not a prefilled response table. The actual gate network compares a newly measured random integer with the input-derived threshold, performs a controlled physical actuator change and payload transfer, and measures the corresponding registers. The independently controllable payload has a same-epoch operational effect. The independently controllable \(u\) changes the following candidate's coordinate and hence the next actual actuator law on a retain branch. For example at \(b=1\), initial \(k=0\), \(\ell=0\) versus \(\ell=1\) gives retained \(k'=0\) versus \(1\), with next actuator probabilities \(15/32\) versus \(17/32\). Averaging over the common refresh branch leaves a nonzero difference \(1/32\) in the following actuator mean. Thus the input dependence reaches an observed receiver operation.

### P.16.3e.T4. Uniform gate compiler and exact instrument proof

The executable compiler appended below emits only X, CNOT and Toffoli gates with fresh targets. Its primitive Boolean constructors are

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
\mathrm{COPY}(a)&\mathrm{CNOT}(a,t)\\
\mathrm{NOT}(a)&\mathrm{CNOT}(a,t);X(t)\\
\mathrm{AND}(a,b)&\mathrm{Toffoli}(a,b,t)\\
\mathrm{XOR}(a,b)&\mathrm{CNOT}(a,t);\mathrm{CNOT}(b,t)\\
\mathrm{OR}(a,b)&\mathrm{CNOT}(a,t);\mathrm{CNOT}(b,t);\mathrm{Toffoli}(a,b,t).
\end{array}
\]

Every target starts at zero and differs from every control. Coincident Toffoli controls are replaced by a CNOT; this avoids an illegal gate while preserving the Boolean function. Multiplexing is \(b\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}[c\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}(a\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}b)]\). The width-\(w\) ripple adder uses

\[
s_i=a_i\oplus b_i\oplus c_i,\quad
c_{i+1}=(a_i\wedge b_i)\vee[c_i\wedge(a_i\oplus b_i)].
\]

The comparator scans most significant bits first, retaining equality and the first less-than witness. The square is schoolbook multiplication: AND each bit-pair, shift, and use bounded ripple additions. Arithmetic widths are explicit: \(T_k\) and \(V\) have \(b+4\) bits; the error square has \(2(b+4)\) bits; \(k+\ell+1\leq2M-1\) needs \(b+1\) bits and its low bit is dropped. All arithmetic is exact within these widths. These bounded loops emit the circuit for every finite \(b\); no oracle for prohibited membership, sampled-row primitive, real-number comparison, or unprovided output table occurs.

Each listed gate is a finite basis-permutation unitary. X, CNOT, Toffoli and source-preparing Hadamard are self-adjoint involutions. For a selected positive gate duration \(\tau_g\),

\[
H_U=\frac{\pi\hbar}{2\tau_g}(I-U),\qquad
\exp(-iH_U\tau_g/\hbar)=U.
\tag{P.16.3e.T4}
\]

This supplies finite generators on the stated ideal driven branch, not a gate-speed or heat claim. Classical branching is compiled as controlled permutations; intermediate values are retained rather than irreversibly overwritten.

For source/readout outcome \(r\), the branch is a composition of unitaries and computational-basis projectors, hence has Kraus form \(A_r\rho A_r^\dagger\). At each measurement \(\sum_rP_r^\dagger P_r=I\); unitary gates preserve identity. Inducting over the finite event list gives \(\sum_rA_r^\dagger A_r=I\). Appending the outcome to its retained classical record is an isometry. Therefore every branch is completely positive and the complete instrument is normalized on the entire finite Hilbert space. The stochastic-law identification makes its stronger classical-input/product-source assumptions explicit rather than claiming it on arbitrary coherent or adversarially correlated initial states.

The registered clock uses strictly positive source-delivery, gate and instrument slots, including the finite readiness window, all source measurements, the independent current-operation readout and the terminal evidence readout. ### P.16.3e.T5. One-step and complete finite-history correspondence

Let \(\mathcal E_{n,x}\), \(0\leq n<H\), be all admitted physical states at the \(n\)th normal **raw ready-to-initialize boundary** with decoded candidate \(x\), the same fixed input \(\ell\), the valid normal frame/start pulse, a fresh active module carrying its immutable default template but zero uninitialized baseline-journal/work words, untouched future zero-work/plus-source factors, the registered program and clock positioned before the base prefix, and **arbitrary** retained past archives consistent with already completed epochs. The channel \(\mathfrak L_n\) first executes the base prefix once, making the journal copies valid and establishing actual base \(\theta_0\), and only then queries/adopts the predictor and attempts integration. An equivalent phase-shifted formulation may place the encoder boundary after preparation and omit that prefix from the epoch channel; the present construction consistently uses the former convention and counts initialization once. Past archive/candidate correlations are allowed. Future source factors are independent of them. This domain, not all mathematically possible source-correlated density matrices, is the initial-state claim.

Denote the actual instrument transition by \(\mathfrak L_n\). The operation/readout portion depends only on \(x\), payload and current operation source; the candidate portion depends only on \(x,\ell,C,J\), whose sources are disjoint. On every \(\sigma\in\mathcal E_{n,x}\),

\[
\Pr_\sigma[(d_{\rm req})_{n+1}\in B]
=\tfrac12\frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\mathbf1_B(\mathsf s,j)
+\tfrac12\mathbf1_B\left(s,\left\lfloor\frac{k+\ell+1}{2}\right\rfloor\right)
=:K_{b,u}(x,B).
\tag{P.16.3e.T5}
\]

The right side is independent of the complete past and of which admitted full state in that fiber was used. After conditioning on any present outcome, untouched future sources remain a pristine product, so the next state belongs to the appropriate next fiber. This proves the precise strong-lumpability/intertwining statement on the clocked layer family:

\[
(d_{\rm req})_{n+1*}\mathfrak L_n(\sigma)=K_{b,u}(d_{{\rm req},n}(\sigma),\cdot),\quad n<H.
\tag{P.16.3e.T6}
\]

For the response law, conditional on \(x=(s,k)\), the diagnostic/actuator tuple has independent factors

\[
(Z_1,Z_2,Q)\sim\mathrm{Bern}(a_s)\otimes\mathrm{Bern}(a_s)\otimes\mathrm{Bern}(q_k),\qquad
 a_{\mathsf s}=1/4,\ a_{\mathsf p}=3/4.
\tag{P.16.3e.T7}
\]

All other registered outputs are the specified deterministic functions of the current request, payload, forecast and those actual outcomes. The next candidate source is independent of this operation source. Let \(R_b(x,d;do)\) denote that fully typed response kernel, including statuses, estimates, scores and completion. Then the joint decoded one-step kernel is exactly

\[
R_b(x,d;do)\,K_{b,u}(x,dx').
\tag{P.16.3e.T8}
\]

Induction gives equality of the **whole decoded finite-history law**, not merely of a nominated response marginal, for every admitted initial candidate, every admitted archive fiber, every fixed \(\ell\), and every horizon \(H\). With a registered input sequence, the same induction uses the appropriate controlled kernels at each epoch. The physical retained source/work state is also explicitly determined by the emitted gate circuit and measured source history; it is not claimed equal to an abstract three-coordinate state. A mathematically abstract response history is compared through the typed decoder, not by deleting retained data from the hardware ledger.

Completion commutes as well: accepted safe transactions yield exactly their verified completed target, prohibited transactions yield \(\bot\), and invalid/timeout interventions yield \(\bot\). Thus every formal \(P\) row has a faithful attempted-update lift, including actual live challenge and retained rejection. No row requires a completed prohibited state as an initial resource. The result is stronger than realization only on \(A\), but its exact meaning is request-state occupation, not physical occupation of an impossible completed model.

The complete finite machine has an advancing clock and growing used archive. It is not stationary. The invariant law in the selected-law theorem belongs to the mathematical decoded request kernel (or the consistent family of its finite-horizon observations). Equation (P.16.3e.T6) is asserted only while a fresh module remains. Adding a terminal halted layer does not magically extend the same kernel past \(H\). ### P.16.3e.T6. Resource, preparation, compiler, and error ledger

For the exact displayed compiler, including input/source/zero-work wires, distinct predictor records, fixed-base records, actual response and observed state estimates, scoring, and next-candidate wires, direct constructor counting gives

## Theorem P.16.3f Common source to continuum realization

Use the host of section H, the prediction and candidate registration of the boundary section, the selected kernel and common midpoint grids, and the typed circuit in the physical-protocol section. These are one construction. Fix the externally registered feedback input \(u\in[0,1]\); changing it is a different controlled experiment.
